It’s difficult to recognize burnout in employees if you rely solely on visible behavior. It’s precisely the employee who always delivers, meets deadlines, and never complains who is at the greatest risk. That may sound counterintuitive, but assessment data from HRMForce confirms this picture. In this article, we’ll show you which personality profile is associated with an increased risk of burnout, how to recognize that profile early on, and what you-as an HR professional or manager-can do before an employee actually takes time off.

The Numbers: What Does Assessment Data Show?

Data from HRMForce, based on Big Fifty personality assessments, reveals a striking pattern among employees who take leave due to burnout within twelve months:
  • Stress resilience: −31% compared to colleagues who remain sustainably employable
  • Discipline: +24% compared to that same group
  • Reliability: +27% compared to that same group
This means that employees with the highest risk of burnout are not the ones who drop out, complain, or underperform. Rather, they are the people everyone relies on-disciplined, reliable, and dedicated to their duties. But they have significantly lower resilience when work pressure increases.

Why Traditional Warning Signs Fall Short

Most articles on recognizing burnout focus on behavioral changes: taking more sick days, cynicism, reduced productivity, and irritability. These are valuable signs, but they only appear once the problem is already well advanced. For top performers, there’s an additional complication. They mask their symptoms-not intentionally, but because their behavioral profile is precisely tailored to do so. A high level of discipline ensures that they keep performing, even when they’re running on fumes. A high level of reliability means they don’t readily say no or turn down work. And low stress tolerance means they’re under intense internal pressure, while outwardly they still function normally. By the time the classic warning signs become apparent, it’s often already too late to change course without a prolonged absence from work.

Understanding the Risk Profile Through the Big Five

The Big Five personality traits form the scientific foundation of HRMForce’s Big Fifty assessment. This model describes personality based on five main dimensions: Neuroticism, Extraversion, Openness, Agreeableness, and Conscientiousness. Stress resilience falls within the Neuroticism dimension. A low score means that a person becomes overwhelmed more easily, worries more, and recovers more slowly after periods of intense activity. Discipline and reliability fall under Conscientiousness, the dimension that describes how organized, goal-oriented, and responsible a person is. The combination of high Conscientiousness and low stress resilience is precisely what makes this risk profile so insidious. The drive maintains performance levels, while the lower resilience undermines recovery. It’s as if someone with a smaller gas tank is pressing harder on the accelerator.

What this means for HR and managers

Don’t wait for someone to burn out

The most important lesson from this data: don’t wait until an employee burns out. Behavioral patterns indicating a risk of burnout are visible in personality data months in advance. This calls for a shift from reactive to preventive action. Organizations that want to prevent work-related stress would be wise to look not only at workload and engagement but also at employees’ personality profiles. Not to screen for stress resilience, but to provide targeted support where the risk is highest.

Actively engage with high performers

It’s particularly tempting not to ask further questions of employees who are performing well-after all, they’re delivering results. But the data shows that high performance and high risk can go hand in hand. Schedule regular work experience check-ins with your top performers. Don’t just ask, “How’s work going?” but also: “How do you recover after a busy period?” and “What’s taking the most energy out of you right now?” These kinds of questions break the pattern of just plowing through without reflection.

Discussing stress resilience in talent reviews

Stress resilience belongs in talent reviews. Not as a weakness or a reason to assign someone else to the task, but as a risk factor that deserves attention. It’s similar to how you take injury susceptibility into account with an athlete. A Sustainable Employability Scan can provide an objective starting point here. By periodically assessing the state of employees’ employability, you prevent warning signs from surfacing only after absenteeism has already begun.

From Individual Risk to Organizational Policy

Burnout prevention is not just an individual issue. Data from HRMForce makes it possible to analyze risk profiles at the group level. This provides insights that go beyond the individual conversation. Suppose that within a particular team or department, a strikingly high number of employees exhibit a risk profile characterized by high discipline and low stress resilience. In that case, there is a good chance that the work culture or the distribution of tasks within that team constitutes a risk factor. In that case, adjusting work processes is more effective than providing individual coaching to employees. Organizations that want to retain staff for longer can use this approach to build a structural prevention strategy rather than putting out fires after the fact.

Practical Step-by-Step Plan: Recognizing Burnout with Data

As an HR professional or manager, do you want to start identifying burnout risk early on? Here’s a practical step-by-step plan: Step 1: Assess the personality profile. Use a validated personality assessment, such as the Big Fifty Personality Test, to assess scores for stress resilience, discipline, and reliability. Step 2: Identify the risk profile. Pay particular attention to the combination of high discipline and reliability with low stress resilience. This is the profile that is statistically most strongly associated with burnout-related absenteeism. Step 3: Conduct preventive conversations. Engage in conversations with employees who exhibit the risk profile. Do so not out of alarm, but out of concern. Discuss workload, opportunities for recovery, and boundaries. Step 4: Monitor periodically. Burnout risk is not a fixed factor. It changes with work pressure, personal circumstances, and the extent to which someone recovers. Periodic assessments provide insight into trends and shifts. Step 5: Translate findings into policy. Use the data not only at the individual level but also to evaluate team composition, task distribution, and work culture.

Burnout among top performers is no surprise. It is a pattern.

The employee who takes a leave of absence due to burnout was often already visible in the data for months. High discipline, high reliability, low stress resilience. It is a recognizable profile that recurs in assessment data from thousands of measurements. This also means that organizations are not powerless. With the right measurement tools and a preventive approach, the risk of burnout can be identified early on-not by waiting until someone collapses, but by looking at the patterns that precede it.
This article is based on anonymous, aggregated assessment data from the HRMForce platform. The percentages cited are derived from comparative analyses of employee profiles.

PRESS RELEASE Amsterdam, October 2021, hrmforce, a provider of online psychometric questionnaires and solutions, and Pearson Talentlens, a provider of online tests and assessments, have established an integration. As a result, Pearson’s most relevant assessments are now directly available on the hrmforce platform. Organizations can now send various Pearson tests to their applicants and employees directly from the hrmforce portal. The key benefits include time savings, process optimization, and a better understanding of a candidate’s qualities thanks to the additional features.

Making Better Decisions

The demand for this integration comes from the market, where a number of organizations use both Pearson and hrmforce questionnaires.  “hrmforce has about 40 questionnaires available, but on specific topics, Pearson’s questionnaires can still provide additional information to help make better selection and development decisions,” said Floor Hendriks, Managing Partner at hrmforce. “The process of requesting and returning the results, as well as the administrative processing, takes place entirely within the hrmforce platform. The integration saves time and results in an optimal experience for the candidate.”  

A Complete Offering from a Single Source

Martin Hoogland of Pearson notes: “With their questionnaires, hrmforce also complements our portfolio. When you look at our combined offering now, we can answer virtually any question regarding the selection or development of employees. It’s also very convenient for the client that everything can be managed from a single central location.  

The Power of Collaboration

Hendriks is enthusiastic about the partnership. “Pearson is a solid and professional company, and its questionnaires are based on sound scientific principles. The TD-12 (which assesses the risk of dysfunctional behavior) and the Watson-Glaser (critical thinking) are examples of questionnaires that greatly enhance the hrmforce portfolio. These tools enable organizations to make better-informed selection and development decisions. In addition, it’s a pleasure to work with the Pearson team to develop the most suitable joint solution for an organization.”  

About Pearson TalentLens

set.body:
Recruiting the right staff can make all the difference for an organization. Organizations are also more focused than ever on retaining their top talent. Recruitment is a profession in its own right. We regularly receive questions about the recruitment process. For example: What recruitment methods do you use, and which ones yield the best results? For example, what do you do with a 38-year-old prospective employee who was unemployed for over a year during the economic crisis, comes across as somewhat headstrong, but scored the highest of all applicants on an intelligence test? In this article:
  • The Resume
  • The First Interview
  • Structured interview
  • Predictive validity
 

1. At the Start of the Selection Process-The Resume

[ps2id id='the-resume' target=''/] The curriculum vitae (resume) has traditionally been the first screening tool recruiters use to separate the wheat from the chaff. However, things often go wrong right at the start of the selection process. Recruiters are sometimes more easily swayed by a photo or a candidate’s name than by the relevant information on the resume. A study by CVster shows that attractive applicants are invited for an interview much more often than less attractive ones. By sending out about 300 nearly identical resumes from two fictional (attractive and less attractive) male and female applicants, the study found that 43% of the attractive applicants received a positive response, compared to 15% of the less attractive ones. A similar study was conducted regarding the applicants’ backgrounds. A total of 480 nearly identical cover letters were sent to companies in various industries. Of the four senders, three had names that did not sound Dutch. Email tracking software was used to determine whether the emails were opened and whether they received a response. It turned out that emails from applicants with Dutch-sounding names were opened more often and received positive responses more frequently. While the resume may serve as the applicant’s calling card, whether it is also a reliable tool for selecting new employees is a matter of debate.

2. A cup of coffee? The first interview

[ps2id id='first-interview' target=''/] Would you like a cup of coffee? How many times has that question been asked at the start of a job interview? It’s an ideal icebreaker and is meant to put the candidate at ease. As the inventors of the concept of “gezellig” (coziness), we in the Netherlands generally consider the “gezellig” factor an important part of the hiring process. In many organizations, interviewers therefore see it primarily as their task to put candidates at ease and have a “gezellig” conversation over coffee that focuses on personal questions. The fact that “a cup of coffee, tea, or something else?” is an important topic is also evident from how frequently it appears on websites that offer advice to job seekers. “Say no to coffee” is the first of 10 tips the site Hi-Re gives its readers. The Monsterboard website also addresses the topic of “drinking coffee.” The advice is that water is the safest option. “You can burn your mouth on coffee or tea, and when you’re nervous, there’s a high chance of spilling it.”

Candidate experience

Incidentally, there’s absolutely nothing wrong with creating a friendly atmosphere during a job interview. Whether or not the applicant turns out to be the right candidate, it can’t hurt if they feel positive about the hiring process. Negative experiences among applicants can have unexpected consequences. They tell friends and family, complain about the potential employer on social media, and-more than once-decide to stop purchasing products or services from the company they applied to. This happened to a major organization like Virgin. The negative experiences of job applicants cost the company about 5 million in revenue!

Optimal Job Application Experience

Recruitment management took action and established a “gold standard interview program.” From then on, candidates could count on an optimal job application experience. Among other things, this meant that the interviewer had to approach the applicant in a positive manner. From then on, everyone was also given a constructive explanation of why they were not a good fit for a particular position. In addition, rejected candidates received free advice on how they could improve certain aspects of their application. This transformation in the candidate experience quickly paid off. Not only did it result in significantly more satisfied candidates, but it also led to a reduction in recruitment and selection costs and an increase in the number of clients.

Freestyling During an Unstructured Job Interview

The job interview is undoubtedly one of the most commonly used selection methods when recruiting new staff. During a traditional interview, candidates often “freestyle.” The term “freestyling” comes from hip-hop and refers to the way rappers spontaneously complement (or contradict) each other and come up with lyrics on the spot. In an unstructured interview-as it’s called in professional jargon-the process is actually quite similar. The direction the conversation will take isn’t determined in advance. There’s hardly any structure to speak of. The conversation develops primarily based on the candidate’s answers. The interviewer builds on these responses. If you have five candidates visiting, this often results in five different conversations. How do you determine who the best candidate is based on such interviews? Do you rely purely on intuition, experience, or biases, or do rational considerations and measurable factors also play a role?

Insight into the person

Of course, an interview like this-which takes place in a seemingly informal atmosphere and focuses primarily on personal questions-has its advantages. After all, when you’re hiring a new employee, you want to know what kind of person you’re bringing on board, what motivates them, and whether they’ll be a good fit for the organization. Precisely because of the relaxed atmosphere, there’s a good chance the candidate will reveal more about themselves. You get a better sense of their personality. At least, that’s what you’d expect.

Reliability

“Tell me a little about yourself” is therefore a commonly used opening question. Of course, that question isn’t meant to find out why the candidate loves coffee so much, is an Ajax fan, or spends their free time in nature. Above all, you want to know more about their motivation and why this applicant believes they’re the right person for the open position. Most applicants-provided they’ve prepared well-know that when asked such a question, they should enthusiastically talk about their passions and talents and weave this into their answer in a way that makes it perfectly clear why they’re a great fit for the job. One of the sites mentioned earlier even advises: “Don’t talk about yourself.” With a question like this, you can go in any direction-it offers plenty of opportunities-and you should take advantage of that by using your knowledge and experiences to immediately make it clear why the position is a perfect fit for you. In short, how reliable is the answer? How do you see through the smooth talk?

Assessments: Personality Tests

In addition to the personal interview, a personality test can provide organizations with greater clarity on how the candidate’s personality profile translates into their knowledge, skills, and behavior. In such a test, candidates are presented with a list of about 150 questions. The test bases the candidate’s scores on openness, extraversion, neuroticism, agreeableness, and conscientiousness. Together, these form the five most important personality factors for behavior in work situations. Competencies such as leadership, entrepreneurship, customer-friendliness, or helpfulness can be better assessed using such a personality test.

3. Structured Interview

[ps2id id='interview' target=''/] In a structured job interview, the direction of the interview is determined in advance. The interviewer has carefully considered the criteria against which a candidate will be evaluated. The candidate must fit a predefined job profile. Knowledge, expertise, and professional competence are qualities that can be measured against specific standards. Standards and scores are therefore established for all questions. This prevents misunderstandings about who receives a positive or negative evaluation. All candidates are evaluated based on the same questions, criteria, and standards. This significantly reduces the likelihood of subjective judgments-such as first impressions, the halo effect—where you’re “charmed” by a single positive trait of the candidate-or the opposite, the horn effect—where a single negative trait ruins the potential employee’s chances-will play a decisive role in selecting the right candidate.

Higher predictive value

In other words, the reliability of a structured interview is significantly higher than that of the unstructured version and is a better method for predicting job performance. This is also confirmed by the study “Personnel Selection in the Netherlands,” conducted by the staffing agency Yacht in collaboration with the University of Amsterdam.

Characteristics of a Good Interview

In practice, organizations often underestimate the impact of well-prepared and structured interviews. The “coffee chat” is still a widely used method, even though its results are significantly less effective when it comes to selecting the right person for the right position. Only 25 to 38% of hired employees are still performing successfully and to the employer’s satisfaction after one year. With structured interviews, that figure rises to 50% of new employees. According to the study, interviews are therefore only a useful selection tool when they meet four key criteria.
  • Well-prepared and targeted questions regarding the most important job requirements
  • Specific questions about concrete behavior in the past, present, and future, designed to ensure that a candidate cannot get away with just smooth talk.
  • The same questions for everyone
  • The use of a scoring method
 

The right selection method is important

The study confirms, as we also saw in the Virgin example, that choosing the right selection methods influences the ability to attract quality staff. When applicants are treated unfairly, unpleasantly, or indifferently, it has a negative impact on the pool of new applicants. The study further shows that, in addition to structured interviews-in which the questions are SMART (specific, measurable, acceptable, realistic, and time-bound)—aptitude tests and demonstrable work performance also have a higher predictive value.

Effectiveness of Staff Selection Rarely Measured

Only 20 percent of Dutch organizations measure the effectiveness of their recruitment process, according to the University of Amsterdam (UVA) study. Fifty percent of organizations do provide feedback and ask applicants what they thought of the selection process. However, this feedback can only be partially trusted because it is unclear to what extent applicants are being completely honest. Recruiters often rely on their gut feeling and, in many cases, on unstructured interviews. In doing so, they overlook the added value of a structured selection process in which candidates are compared based on an objective scoring system.

Greater Focus on Mental Capacity and Broader Versatility

One of the recommendations emerging from the study is that recruiters should pay more attention to a candidate’s mental capacity and broader versatility. According to the researchers, too much emphasis is placed on specific knowledge and skills. While this is undoubtedly useful for well-defined roles, it is less effective in a dynamic work environment where knowledge and skills must be continuously developed. The researchers believe that the selection methods used in the United States-which place much greater emphasis on a candidate’s personality and intelligence-should serve as a model.

4. Predictive Validity - Schmidt & Hunter

[ps2id id='validity' target=''/] To predict whether you are hiring the right employee-one who will not only perform satisfactorily but will also still be with your organization a year from now-interviews (whether structured or not) are usually insufficient. There are other selection methods that influence the prediction of employees’ future performance. An economic factor also plays a role in attracting the best employees. For example, in their 1998 study “The Validity and Utility of Selection Methods in Personnel Psychology,” Schmidt & Hunter demonstrated that the level of employee performance can vary quite significantly. For example, an average employee might perform up to 40% worse than a high-performing employee. Carefully selecting potential employees can therefore yield significant economic benefits for a company. Schmidt and Hunter analyzed 85 years of research on selection methods. In their meta-analysis, the concept of predictive validity plays a key role. It describes the extent to which you can predict something. This applies not only to future events (prediction) but also to the present or past.

Combining Testing Methods

Schmidt and Hunter believe that assessments such as intelligence tests-also known as cognitive ability tests—are a reliable means of predicting job performance. It scores 0.51 on a scale from 0 to 1. However, when intelligence testing is combined with a structured interview, the predictive value increases to 0.63. Even unstructured interviews, which score relatively low, benefit from being combined with an intelligence or ability test. The predictive validity increases significantly from 0.38 to 0.55. The predictive validity also increases when combined with a work trial or practical simulation. It is precisely by combining different selection methods that the best results are achieved.

What do we do with that 38-year-old, headstrong candidate?

“What do you do with a 38-year-old potential employee who was unemployed for over a year during the economic crisis, comes across as somewhat headstrong, but scores the highest on an intelligence test out of all the applicants?” we asked ourselves at the beginning of this article. Let’s take a closer look at his hiring process as we wrap up. During the traditional, unstructured interview, this person had to contend with an interviewer who had already raised concerns beforehand about the fact that the candidate had been out of the workforce for over a year. The interviewer was also put off by the candidate’s tone, even though the candidate excelled at giving smart, well-thought-out answers. This is a classic example of the Horn effect.

Added Value of an Intelligence Test

This candidate would have had no chance from the outset if the hiring process had consisted solely of an interview. However, by scoring the highest on the intelligence test, it caught the interviewer’s attention. Various studies show that the reliability and predictive power of intelligence tests are high. The test revealed that this person possesses many cognitive skills, which are very important today and usually provide organizations with economic added value. This person is able to process information quickly and knows how to immediately link it to existing knowledge. The intelligent employee can analyze and solve problems and does not shy away from complexity. This benefits productivity. A complex, dynamic environment where quick adaptation is a requirement calls for an employee with a broad range of cognitive skills. Thanks to the added value of a selection tool such as the intelligence test, this person could be properly assessed and hired as an employee.

Frequently Asked Questions:

  • As an HR manager, how can you strike a balance between structured and unstructured interviews to achieve the best results?
    • Combining both interview methods can be effective by supplementing structured questions with informal conversations, ensuring that both objective criteria and personal insights are taken into account.
  • What specific tools or software can improve the accuracy of the selection process?
    • There are advanced HR software packages available that use AI and data analysis to improve the accuracy and efficiency of the selection process. Examples include applicant tracking systems (ATS) and assessment tools.
  • How can you address potential biases in the selection process, especially when using traditional methods?
    • Implementing training on unbiased hiring, using anonymous resumes, and standardizing interview questions can help minimize bias.

The Facet5 personality questionnaire, based on the proven Five-Factor Model of personality, is a powerful tool for gaining insight into a person’s personality traits and behaviors. In this article, we will explore the applications of Facet5 in the areas of leadership and career development, and how these insights can contribute to improving leaders’ effectiveness and supporting individuals’ career growth.

Leadership Development: Self-Awareness and Emotional Intelligence

To foster effective leadership, it is important to develop self-awareness and emotional intelligence. Facet5 helps leaders gain insight into their own personality traits, such as their levels of conscientiousness, extraversion, agreeableness, openness, and emotional stability. By understanding these aspects of their personality, leaders can leverage their strengths and address potential weaknesses to communicate and collaborate more effectively with their teams. Team Dynamics and Building Complementary Teams. Leaders who are familiar with their team members’ personality traits, as measured by Facet5, can better respond to their team’s needs and strengths. By assembling a diverse team with complementary personalities, leaders can foster a balanced and productive work environment. A competency is something you bring to the table in terms of knowledge, experience, personality, skills, or communication abilities. Being a leader means that someone is capable of leveraging available opportunities to advance the process and is also willing to continue developing themselves. Competencies can also be focused on specific areas. Consider, for example, competencies focused on education or healthcare.

The Three Pillars of Competencies

Competencies consist of a combination of three core components that together determine how effectively someone can perform:
Component Description Example
Knowledge Facts, information, and understanding Knowledge of project management methodologies
Skills Practical application of knowledge Creating schedules and monitoring deadlines
Attitude Attitude and motivation Proactive and results-oriented thinking

Development of competencies

Every person has talents. The key is to recognize, develop, and utilize them. In addition, education helps develop knowledge, and membership in an organization, a group of friends, family, and other activities helps people learn new skills. It quickly becomes apparent whether someone has leadership qualities, what this might entail, and whether that person is capable of putting those qualities to use. The environment often determines whether an innate leadership quality will become a competency. Much depends on the opportunities and support people receive. This is certainly true in the workplace. The key question is always whether talent is recognized and its development encouraged-or not.

The 70-20-10 Rule for Competency Development

Research shows that competency development is most effective when it follows this breakdown:
70% On-the-job learning: Practical experience, challenging assignments, new projects 20% Social learning: Coaching, mentoring, feedback from colleagues 10% Formal learning: Training sessions, courses, certifications
 

Development Cycle

A development cycle that is clear to everyone can support this process. By identifying a new colleague’s capabilities starting with the introductory interview, you can make the most of them. A good competency model helps build on this foundation. This can be achieved through internal training, by offering specialized courses and programs, but also by giving people opportunities to further develop within the workplace. Within a clear HRM cycle, two things are very important: giving and demonstrating trust, and transparent policies. Employees who feel challenged to grow and supported in that process perform better. It really is that simple.

Step-by-Step Plan for Effective Competency Development

Step Action Result
1. Assessment Identify current competencies Competency profile for each employee
2. Gap Analysis Difference between current and desired levels Identifying development needs
3. Development plan Formulate specific actions and goals Personal Development Plan (PDP)
4. Implementation Carry out development activities Developing new competencies
5. Evaluation Measuring progress and making adjustments Continuous improvement
 

Competency model

The question, of course, is which model works best. Before you start implementing all kinds of models, it might be better to identify everything that is still unknown. A first step could be a workshop with employees, during which they are specifically asked for suggestions for improvement. Two things often derail this process: first, the fact that the boss leads the workshop, and second, PowerPoint presentations. The first makes people hesitant. The second means they’re already bored before the actual work begins. There’s another way, and embracing a new competency model can be the key to that change-provided it isn’t simply imposed, but rather approached collaboratively from the moment it’s brought up. Encouraging one another to keep improving.

Different Types of Competency Models

Organizations can choose from different approaches, depending on their objectives:
Model type Focus Suitable for
Function-oriented Specific skills per role Specialized roles
Organization-focused Core values and culture All employees
Leadership-oriented Management Skills Managers
Behavior-Focused Observable behaviors Performance Management

Success Factors for Competency Management

These elements are crucial for an effective competency system:
Management commitment: Visible support and participation from leadership Clear communication: Transparency regarding goals and expectations Practical application: Directly linked to daily work Continuous evaluation: Regular updates and improvements
 

Stay Curious

If you stand still, you’ll miss the train to the future. New developments are coming at a rapid pace. As a manager, it’s important that you remain curious about innovation. Ask questions, seek answers-where possible, together with your employees and the HRM team.
  1. What would you like to change yourself? What does that require?
  2. How can you gather as much useful information as possible from the team?
  3. What role can each employee play in a potential change?
Those who continue to develop themselves and dare to embrace new competencies will gain a firm grasp on these kinds of processes and will benefit greatly from them. It makes the work a lot easier and more enjoyable for both you and your team.

Future-Oriented Skills

The job market is changing rapidly. These skills are becoming increasingly important:

Top 5 future-oriented skills:

1. Digital literacy: Working with new technologies and data 2. Ability to learn: Quickly acquiring new knowledge and skills 3. Emotional intelligence: Understanding your own and others’ emotions 4. Critical thinking: Analyzing information and making informed decisions 5. Flexibility: Adapting to changing circumstances

Frequently Asked Questions About Competencies

How often should a competency profile be updated? Competency profiles should be reviewed annually, with interim updates as needed in response to job changes and new industry developments.
What if an employee shows no interest in competency development? Investigate the cause: lack of time, unclear added value, or the wrong approach. Link development to personal goals and career aspirations.
How do you measure the ROI of competency development? Monitor performance indicators such as productivity, quality, employee satisfaction, and career progression. Compare these metrics before and after development interventions.

Red represents strength, blue represents calm, and yellow represents creativity. The Caluwé test translates this symbolism into a powerful tool that maps out your personality and work style. This test uses six different colors to determine how you think, act, and collaborate within organizations.

Imagine that your colleague always starts new projects full of energy (yellow thinking), while you prefer to work out all the details first before you begin (blue thinking). These differences often cause friction, but the Caluwé Colors Test shows that you complement each other perfectly. By knowing your personality color, you’ll not only understand yourself better but also learn how to collaborate most effectively with others.

What you’ll learn in this article

  • The six colors and what they mean for your personality
  • How the test works and what it measures
  • Practical applications in work and personal life
  • Differences from other personality tests
  • Tips for getting the most out of your color profile
 

What exactly is the Caluwé color model?

Professor Léon de Caluwé developed this test to measure how people think about change and collaboration. The test is based on the belief that every person has one or two dominant “thinking patterns,” which can be translated into colors.

The test doesn’t measure what you can do or what you know. It examines how your brain processes information and makes decisions. For example, do you think logically first (blue), or do you jump right in (red)? This preference determines your color profile.

What makes this method unique is that there are no right or wrong answers. Each color has valuable qualities that organizations and teams need. A successful team combines different colors to effectively address all aspects of a project.

The test was developed based on years of research into change processes in companies. De Caluwé discovered that conflicts often arise because people put on different “lenses” when looking at problems. By making these lenses visible through colors, teams can collaborate more effectively.

Discover our color test

The six colors explained

 

Blue Thinking

People with a blue thinking style value structure and logic. You analyze thoroughly before making decisions. Details are important to you, and you want to understand how systems work.

A blue thinker first examines all available data. You ask critical questions and look for proven methods. In meetings, you’re the one who asks, “Have we researched this?” or “What are the risks?”

This thorough approach has major advantages. Projects you lead usually have a solid foundation. You prevent costly mistakes by thinking things through in advance. Colleagues appreciate your reliability and expertise.

The downside is that you sometimes wait too long to take action. While you’re still researching, the opportunity may have already passed. Other colors can help you act more quickly when the situation calls for it.

Yellow Thinking

Yellow thinking stands for creativity and innovation. You see opportunities everywhere and enjoy coming up with new solutions. Brainstorming energizes you, and you’re willing to take risks to achieve a breakthrough.

As a yellow thinker, you’re often the first to ask, “Why don’t we do it differently?” You dislike routines and are constantly looking for ways to improve. You inspire others with your enthusiasm for new ideas.

This trait makes you valuable in situations that require change. You see opportunities that others miss and aren’t afraid to experiment. Startups and innovation projects desperately need your way of thinking.

The challenge for yellow thinkers is completing projects. You quickly get excited about the next idea before the current one is finished. Collaborating with blue or green thinkers helps you actually carry out your ideas.

Red Thinking

Red stands for action and results. You tackle problems head-on and prefer concrete solutions. Long discussions frustrate you because you want to see progress.

Red thinkers are natural leaders in crisis situations. You make decisions quickly and motivate others to take action. “Let’s just do it” is your motto. This attitude ensures that projects actually get completed.

Your strength lies in turning plans into results. While others are still talking, you’ve already gotten started. This pragmatic approach often yields quick successes.

The risk is that you’ll act too quickly without fully considering all the consequences. Collaborating with blue thinkers helps you avoid overlooking important details. Thorough preparation prevents you from wasting time later on solving avoidable problems.

Green Thinking

Green thinking focuses on people and collaboration. You pay attention to the team’s atmosphere and make sure everyone feels heard. Harmony and consensus are important to you.

As a green thinker, you see the person behind the employee. You understand that good results come only when people feel engaged. In conflicts, you look for solutions that are acceptable to everyone.

This people-oriented approach builds strong teams. Your colleagues feel safe to make mistakes and share ideas. This leads to greater creativity and engagement within the organization.

The downside is that you sometimes compromise too much. Not every situation allows for endless discussions about everyone’s opinion. Learning from “red thinkers” helps you make difficult decisions when necessary.

White Thinking

White thinking stands for neutrality and a broad perspective. You view situations from a bird’s-eye view and help others see different perspectives. Objectivity is your strength.

White thinkers are natural coaches and advisors. You ask the right questions, enabling others to arrive at insights on their own. In complex situations, you help bring structure to the process without taking sides.

This skill makes you valuable in change processes. You can weigh different interests against one another without becoming emotionally involved. Teams rely on your objectivity to make better decisions.

The downside is that you sometimes come across as too distant. People also want to know what your own opinion is. Learning to take a stand at the right moment strengthens your influence.

Pessimistic Thinking

Pessimistic thinking analyzes what could go wrong. You spot risks and problems before others notice them. This critical perspective protects organizations from costly mistakes.

Pessimists ask the tough questions that others prefer to avoid. “What happens if this fails?” or “Have we really thought this through?” Your skepticism leads to better decisions.

This trait is indispensable for important projects. You prevent teams from sailing blindly on a wave of optimism. By identifying problems early on, solutions can be devised before it’s too late.

The challenge is not just to point out problems, but also to contribute to finding solutions. Pure criticism without alternatives demotivates teams. Combine your realism with constructive suggestions.

Discover our color test

How does the color test work?

The test consists of various statements, and you’ll be asked to indicate to what extent you agree with each one. There are no time limits, because the test measures your natural preference, not your speed.

A typical question is: “When solving problems, I start by gathering all available information.” You indicate whether this is completely true, somewhat true, or doesn’t apply to you at all.

The questions are designed to measure your automatic responses. It’s not about what you think is right, but about what you do spontaneously. That’s why honesty is crucial for a reliable result.

After completing the test, you’ll receive a color profile. This shows your primary color (usually 30-40% of your profile) and your secondary colors. Most people have two dominant colors that together define their work style.

Discover our color test

Practical Application

 

Working in a team

Teams work better when they understand their color distribution. A project team consisting solely of yellow thinkers generates many ideas but achieves little. A team consisting solely of blue thinkers analyzes thoroughly but lacks creativity.

The ideal composition combines different colors: yellow for innovation, blue for analysis, red for execution, and green for collaboration. Each team member contributes based on their strengths.

Conflicts often arise from color differences. The yellow thinker wants to experiment, while the blue thinker wants more research. By recognizing this as a color difference rather than a personal conflict, teams can discuss issues more constructively.

Project leaders can assign tasks based on color preferences. Let the blue thinker conduct the risk analysis and the red thinker oversee the schedule. This improves both quality and satisfaction.

Leadership Style

Your color profile determines your natural leadership style. Red leaders make quick decisions and expect immediate results. Green leaders involve everyone in decisions and ensure consensus.

Both styles have their place, depending on the situation. In crisis situations, red leadership works better; during complex changes, green leadership is more effective. By knowing your profile, you can consciously switch between styles.

Also learn from other colors. A natural red leader can learn to put on the green glasses sometimes. Involve your team more in decisions when support is important. This increases your effectiveness as a leader.

Guiding Personal Development

The test reveals where your natural talents lie, but also where you can grow. Perhaps you’re strong in analysis (blue), but you can learn to act more quickly (red).

Development doesn’t mean changing your personality. It’s about expanding your repertoire. Stay true to your strong colors, but also practice other patterns for situations that call for them.

Consciously choose situations that challenge your weaker colors. As a blue thinker, occasionally participate in brainstorming sessions (yellow). As a yellow thinker, push yourself to see plans through to completion (red). This practice will make you more versatile.

Making Career Choices

Different professions suit different color profiles. Financial analysts often have a lot of blue, creative directors a lot of yellow, and project managers a lot of red. But these aren’t hard and fast rules.

Look at the core tasks of a position and compare them to your profile. Does the job require a lot of creativity while you’re primarily analytical? Then the work will be more exhausting than if it matched your profile.

Look for roles that leverage your strong colors but also challenge your weaker ones. This fosters growth without burnout. A job that’s a perfect fit for you can become boring after a while.

Discover our color test

Differences from Other Personality Tests

The Caluwé Colors Test distinguishes itself from tests like the MBTI or DISC through its focus on change and collaboration. While the MBTI measures personality types, the Colors Test examines thought patterns within organizations.

DISC measures behavior in social situations. The color test goes deeper by examining how you process information and make decisions. This makes it more specifically applicable to work-related situations.

Another difference is flexibility. MBTI is based on fixed personality types. The color test recognizes that people can develop different patterns. Your profile can change through training and experience.

The test is also less categorical. Instead of placing you in a single box, you receive percentages for each color. This provides a more nuanced picture of your personality.

Discover our color test

Scientific Basis and Reliability

Professor de Caluwé based his theory on extensive research into change processes in organizations. He analyzed hundreds of cases to identify patterns in how people respond to change.

The test has been validated across various cultures and organizations. Studies show that the results are stable over time, yet sensitive enough to measure development.

Universities use the test in their management programs. Major consulting firms apply it in organizational development. This widespread acceptance demonstrates its scientific rigor.

A word of caution: no personality test can perfectly predict behavior. The color test provides insights, not absolute truths. Use the results as a starting point for development, not as an unchangeable judgment.

Discover our color test

Common Mistakes and Misconceptions

 

“My color determines what I’m capable of”

This is a dangerous misconception. Your color profile reveals your preferences, not your limitations. A blue thinker can learn to be more creative, and a yellow thinker can become more structured.

“I need to improve my weak colors”

Development doesn’t mean eliminating weaknesses. Focus first on further developing your strong colors. These give you the most return and energy.

"All yellow thinkers are the same"

There is enormous variation within each color. Two yellow thinkers can be very different. The test provides general guidelines, not a detailed portrait.

"The test tells me what kind of work I should do"

The test provides guidance, not rules. Successful people in every role have different color profiles. Much depends on how you apply your colors.

Discover our color test

Making the Most of Your Color Profile

Start by accepting your natural profile. Don’t fight your dominant colors-learn to use them consciously. Know when you need analytical blue and when action-oriented red works better.

Develop an awareness of situations that require different colors. An important presentation might call for more red (decisiveness) even if you’re naturally green (consensus-oriented). Practice this flexibility.

Seek out complementary partners. If you’re strong in yellow (creativity), work with people who excel at blue (analysis) or red (execution). This will increase your collective effectiveness.

Use the language of colors to communicate more effectively. Instead of saying, “You’re too slow,” say, “This calls for more red thinking.” This makes feedback less personal and more constructive.

The Caluwé Colors test offers a powerful way to better understand yourself and others. By knowing your profile, you can make more conscious choices in your work and collaborations. The secret lies not in having the “right” colors, but in cleverly combining different thinking patterns.

The benefit of this insight extends beyond just work. In personal relationships, it helps you understand why people react differently. A red person wants to act immediately, while a green person wants to talk first. Both approaches have value.

By appreciating and combining different colors, we create stronger teams and achieve better results. The test shows that diversity in ways of thinking is an asset, not a problem to be solved.

Discover our color test

Frequently Asked Questions

 

Can my color profile change over time?

Yes, your profile can gradually shift through experience and conscious development. Your dominant colors usually remain stable, but the proportions may change. Retaking the test every few years can provide new insights.

Are some colors better than others?

No, every color has unique value. Successful organizations need all colors. It’s not about better or worse, but about the right mindset for the right situation.

How long does the test take?

The average test time is between 15 and 30 minutes. There is no time limit, so take your time to answer honestly. Rushed answers lead to less reliable results.

Can I use the test for recruitment?

Yes, but use it as part of a broader selection process. The test reveals thinking preferences, not competencies or experience. Combine the results with other selection methods to get a complete picture.

Discover your personality now with our personality test and learn how to use your unique thinking patterns to achieve greater success in work and life.

Discover our color test

Competencies in Education

The new competency requirements replace those from 2006. That was the year the Act on Professions in Education (the BIO Act) went into effect. Substantive improvements have been made, making the competency requirements unambiguous, concrete, and more easily assessable. The seven competencies are grouped under the main themes: subject-specific knowledge, subject-specific pedagogy, and general pedagogy. This has made them more recognizable. The competency requirements focus on student learning and the core of the teaching profession. Through their knowledge and skills related to these competencies, teachers demonstrate that they can perform their work as educators-and as members of the professional educational community they form together with their colleagues-in a professionally effective and responsible manner. Competencies and the development of teachers’ competencies are crucial to the quality of education. Developing competencies is only possible if you know where you stand; that is why we have developed a questionnaire that provides insight into this. Read more about the SBL competencies in education in our knowledge center.

Personality Questionnaire

Hrmforce Education has adapted the online personality questionnaire into a specific questionnaire with a report on the following seven educational competencies:
  1. Interpersonal Competence
  2. Pedagogical competence
  3. Subject-matter and pedagogical competence
  4. Organizational Competence
  5. Competent in collaborating with colleagues
  6. Competent in collaborating with the community
  7. Competent in reflection and professional development
After this assessment, you will have a clear picture of both the strengths and areas for development, both individually and within the team. In addition, gaining insight into these competencies contributes to the quality of the school’s education: fewer mismatches between individuals and their roles, greater satisfaction among the teaching staff, and increased motivation for teachers to continue their professional development. Motivated and satisfied teachers have a positive impact on students’ motivation and performance! In addition to the online assessment, we also offer supplementary tools such as in-depth interviews, role-playing exercises, and (nonverbal) assessments. Ask one of our consultants about the options.  

Employee Participation Training

In addition to the personality questionnaire, we have also developed training programs specifically for the education sector. Drawing on our knowledge and experience in the field of employee participation, we create a customized training program for each school or educational institution that effectively contributes to the development of a professional employee participation body within the organization. This equips members with knowledge of all aspects of employee participation and fosters a valuable partner for the competent authority, where support for educational development is central. More information about the Employee Participation Training can be found here.  

Participation Support Service Package

Case Law: Employer Must Reimburse MR Service Package Since the enactment of the Act on Strengthening Administrative Capacity in Education on January 1, 2017, member representatives (MRs) in elementary and secondary education can legally have the costs of a service package reimbursed by the competent authority without the need for a separate facilities agreement. “ School boards must therefore always reimburse the costs of a service subscription. This is according to the ruling of the National Dispute Resolution Committee for Employee Participation on February 25, 2019. The ruling means that MR members who wish to purchase this service do not need to ask their board for permission. Cost Savings Currently, many schools still use service packages individually from different providers. With multiple schools in a foundation, the costs of this are often unnecessarily high. Hrmforce Education is the only provider in the Netherlands to offer this service at the supra-school level.  The benefits then apply to all affiliated schools and school boards. We call this our “Medezeggenkracht Service.” With this, we serve not only the parent-teacher associations at schools but also the school boards, parents, and students by delivering significant cost savings. Effective parent and student participation doesn’t have to be expensive. That way, the money goes where it’s meant to go: the students! Medezeggenkracht Service Package
  • Unlimited (fair use) access to the student participation consultation hours

HRM Solutions

In addition to administering a personality questionnaire, Hrmforce can also support you in the following areas:
  • Competency Development—further developing your teachers’ competencies: by measuring competencies and combining the results with 360-degree feedback, it immediately becomes clear which competencies can be effectively developed and which cannot;

set.title: MBTI in HR. What does it measure-and what doesn't it measure?

set.body:
In the modern workplace, employees continue to learn and develop-both professionally and personally, with a focus on their behavior and competencies. We were already aware of the importance of this, and the COVID-19 crisis has significantly reinforced this understanding. Yet implementation often stalls when it comes to putting these ideas into practice on the job. This is despite the fact that encouraging learning and development-or even behavioral change-among employees is entirely possible. We’ve listed seven closely interrelated success factors.

From Wanting to Actually Doing

Many employers and employees are now aware of the benefits. When employees remain actively engaged in learning and their professional development, it leads to greater job satisfaction, job security, and career opportunities. Numerous studies also show that these employees are more loyal, motivated, and productive. Moreover, it is a key prerequisite for, for example, increasing sustainable employability. Research from Tilburg University also shows that it encourages older employees to continue working longer in a way that is enjoyable for them. Awareness of the benefits and necessity has grown significantly since the COVID-19 crisis, including among employers. Worldwide, a substantial majority of CEOs (70 percent) now recognize the value of lifelong learning. Before the COVID-19 crisis, this figure was alarmingly low (29 percent), as shown by this international study. So the willingness is there, but creating a “learning organization” does not always prove easy in practice. Often, high workloads act as a barrier, preventing employees from “ever getting around to” a learning program, or they are not sufficiently encouraged and supported to continue developing. How can this be achieved? These success factors can provide immediate help.

  1. Enhance and facilitate self-direction

In practice, fostering self-direction among employees has proven to be the crucial factor for companies that have successfully become learning organizations. However, this arises from an interaction between employer and employee. It’s not just a matter of placing responsibility on employees, but also of effectively facilitating them. This often begins with raising awareness, establishing a good cycle of dialogue, and ensuring accessible and appropriate development opportunities. So it takes more than just launching an “Online Academy.” Ensure clear awareness and communication from the employees’ perspective. What’s in it for them? Consider not only their current role but also career advancement opportunities, job satisfaction, or more personal motivations and drivers. This shifts the perception of learning and development from a sense of “having to” to a desire to do so.

  1. Strengthen self-awareness

Employers can effectively facilitate employees’ awareness and self-direction with practical, accessible tools. In addition to providing greater self-awareness of their current situation, online tools can, for example, offer a clearer picture of an employee’s long-term development path-and what’s needed to get there. Most organizations now use online assessments to support the development needs of employees or teams.

  1. Consider 360-Degree Feedback

A concrete example of a powerful tool for increasing self-awareness is leveraging 360-Degree Feedback. After all, good feedback is extremely valuable for greater self-awareness and employee development. It’s not just their own insights that matter, but also those of relevant people in their environment. Think of colleagues, a manager, or, for example, (internal) clients. By drawing more broadly on employees’ professional circles, performance and development opportunities come into focus in a meaningful and accessible way. The “360 degrees” represent the perspectives from which feedback is received regarding, for example, skills, personality, abilities, and motivation. The questionnaires can be tailored to different competency levels and are often used to foster a productive dialogue between employees and managers or to facilitate a modern, customized performance review cycle.

  1. Watch out for fear of failure!

When organizational changes require different learning or development behaviors, it’s important to be aware of a major pitfall. It lies within our brains. At first, changes often immediately encounter resistance in people. This is because, when we experience change, the same parts of our brain are activated as when we think about death. “A change-even a positive one-is primarily viewed by our brains as a loss. That triggers thoughts of mortality, because death is the ultimate loss,” says American researcher Professor James R. Bailey of George Washington University. “When thoughts of death are subconsciously triggered, a whole series of defense mechanisms kicks in to protect our identity, routines, and competencies.” But you can also leverage these principles, for example, by informing and preparing employees in a timely manner. This underscores the importance of good communication-in this case, to allow people to acclimate safely first. Then the brain can adapt flexibly, because, in fact, the brain is constantly changing. The key is to influence this process positively. This can be achieved by connecting changes to employees’ deepest essence and motivations (the “WHY” from Simon Sinek’s Golden Circle model). Beyond WHAT someone does and HOW they do it, what ultimately matters most is WHY someone truly does something. With that awareness, people can consciously work on their development, and their brain structure is positively influenced. HR can facilitate this by seeking methods that help employees and managers consciously reflect on this core question.

  1. Adapt to the Different Types of Conversations

To facilitate effective conversations between employees and managers during times of change or throughout learning and development processes, it’s important to keep the various conversation cycles in mind. After all, in a complete conversation cycle, they engage in different types of conversations (such as Bila+ and development or annual reviews), each at different times and with a different purpose. A (digital) development cycle can facilitate individual or team development. The starting point is usually the job classification system and the job profiles within an organization. The principles of the conversation cycle are built around these. Objectively designed questionnaires can help bring the conversations up to the right level quickly and in a well-founded manner. Read more about the different feedback cycles here.

  1. Provide Appropriate Learning Opportunities

It may sound logical at first, but you must also provide appropriate learning opportunities when learning and development actually need to be facilitated. Across an entire organization, this often involves a diverse range of options, tailored to each target group and to what individual employees want to learn. After all, different people learn in different ways. Not every learning path is suitable for everyone. Therefore, give careful consideration to the learning methods and formats offered. In some cases, an accessible e-learning course may suffice, while in other situations, frontline workers may prefer to learn together in a classroom setting. Discuss this and tailor the learning offerings carefully to the various learning needs. In an online learning environment, assessments can also be offered to increase self-awareness and self-direction. Don’t forget the potential of internal knowledge sharing among colleagues. Don’t underestimate how much knowledge, experience, and expertise exists within your organization. This can be shared through, for example, internal webinars, training sessions, or knowledge-sharing sessions. Or choose a format that addresses frequently asked questions. This can relate to learning and development or simply to the substantive knowledge and experience available internally.

  1. Give employees a meaningful purpose

In a thriving “learning organization,” many of the success factors just mentioned-if done right-are closely intertwined. After all, there can be no self-direction without self-awareness. And there can be no enriching learning journey without appropriate learning opportunities. An important underlying success factor is that employees are given a clear goal to work toward. To achieve this, align the organization’s goal with an employee’s professional-and ideally also personal-goals. Often, the organization’s goal and strategy are clear, but sometimes they need to be better communicated to employees. Employees themselves are often initially a bit unsure about their own goals. To address this, assess the extent to which their talents, motivations, and interests can be aligned with the goals of the organization or their team. Here, too, 360-Degree Feedback can likely be very useful.

In this Friday Q&A Vlog, we received a question about the Ability questionnaires-both the Ability Analysis and the Ability Scan. To what extent do the percentages of correct and incorrect answers reveal anything about a candidate’s results? And what’s the best way to interpret them? We explain it all in the video below. For more videos, check out the hrmforce YouTube channel.

For talent development in education.

Hrmforce Education offers an online tool for structured HR policy. This reduces the risk of a mismatch between employees and their roles and increases job satisfaction-and, consequently, performance. A motivated and satisfied teacher has a positive impact on students’ motivation and performance. Explore the following options: - Choosing a Field of Study - Selection of Teachers and School Leaders - Matching Career Changers - Competency Framework with 360-Degree Feedback - Employee Participation

Choosing a Field of Study

A career choice test is a test used to help students choose their next educational path or career. The test evaluates the student’s interests, skills, and personality and then provides recommendations on which programs are the best fit for them. There are various types of college selection tests available, such as online tests, consultations with a career counselor, and personality tests.

Selection of Teachers and School Leaders

Selecting the right teacher can be very challenging. Sometimes the interview goes very well, but the teacher falls short in practice-or vice versa. By using multiple tools to gather data, the risk of a mismatch is significantly reduced. Using objective tests to measure competencies and matching them to a competency profile you’ve created in advance further minimizes the chance of a mismatch. That’s why hrmforce allows you to use multiple tools (tests, reference checks, structured interview questions) simultaneously without having to engage an assessment firm. This saves a lot of time-and therefore money!

Matching Career Changers

There is a high demand for teachers in primary and secondary education. One way to address this shortage is by recruiting and selecting career changers in education. To assess candidates’ competencies, the qualification requirements have been translated into personality questionnaires. By assessing a candidate’s personality, you gain valuable insight into their strengths and areas for improvement. This allows you to use the questionnaire to select career changers based on their teaching qualities. This reduces mismatches and ensures you select only those with the potential to become effective teachers. It is also possible to use these questionnaires to design a coaching program that helps develop any missing qualities.

Competency-Based Assessment with 360-Degree Feedback

Screening employees means verifying whether a job applicant is trustworthy and suitable for a position. When people hear the word “screening,” they often immediately think of an (online) background check on the person in question. But did you know that other screening methods are much more valuable? With assessments, you can determine not only whether someone is trustworthy, but also whether their talents and personality are a good fit for your organization.

What you’ll learn in this article

  • Why screening is more than just a background check.
  • How assessments work as a screening tool.
  • What other screening methods are available.
  • Practical tips for a smart screening process.

Why screening candidates is becoming increasingly important

The job market is changing. Candidates often present themselves better on paper than in practice. In addition, the risks are increasing: think of confidential data, financial responsibility, or customer contact. A wrong choice costs not only money, but also energy and reputation. Screening helps prevent this by evaluating facts, skills, and behavior.

Screening through assessments

An assessment is a test or questionnaire that objectively measures how someone scores on competencies, personality, and cognitive skills. While a Certificate of Good Conduct (VOG) only indicates whether someone has committed any criminal offenses, an assessment provides insight into future performance and behavioral tendencies.

Examples of assessments

Hrmforce offers various screening modules that you can use during recruitment and selection: → Personality questionnaires : measure behavior, motivations, and work style. These help you determine whether someone is a good fit for your company culture. → Aptitude tests : provide insight into analytical ability, problem-solving skills, and learning ability. → Integrity tests : focus on reliability, sense of ethics, and the risk of inappropriate behavior. → 360-degree feedback : provides a picture of how others perceive someone in practice. By combining these assessments, you gain a comprehensive and objective picture of the candidate, significantly increasing the likelihood of a good match .

Other Forms of Employee Screening

In addition to assessments, there are traditional forms of screening. These remain valuable but have limitations.
  • Reference check: useful for supplementary information, but often subjective.
  • Degree and resume verification: useful for factual verification, but says nothing about behavior.
  • Certificate of Good Conduct (VOG): an official document, but only reflects past behavior, not future risk.
  • Social media check: provides insight into behavior, but carries legal risks.
  • Credit check: relevant for financial positions, but privacy-sensitive.

Legal Rules for Employee Screening

The GDPR (privacy legislation) always applies to screening. This means:
  1. Screening should only be conducted if it is relevant to the position.
  2. Inform the candidate and request consent.
  3. Process results securely and delete them in a timely manner.
Assessments offer an advantage here: they are objective, transparent, and less privacy-sensitive than, for example, a credit check.

Smart Candidate Screening in 2026

A smart approach combines traditional checks with modern assessments. This gives you certainty about both reliability and talent. Tips: → Start with a job profile : determine which competencies and behavioral traits are required. → Choose appropriate assessments : for example, an aptitude test for an analytical role. → Combine checks : A Certificate of Good Conduct (VOG) plus an assessment provides a broader picture than a single method. → Work with a screening partner : such as hrmforce, which offers proven tools and guidance.

Frequently Asked Questions

Are assessments mandatory during screening? No, but they offer objective insights that traditional checks do not provide. How long does an assessment take? From 20 minutes (aptitude test) to several hours for comprehensive personality assessments. Are assessments GDPR-compliant? Yes, provided you process the results securely and use them only for the specific hiring process. What is the average cost of assessments? It depends on the depth: ranging from a few dozen euros per test to packages for complete selection processes.

Conclusion: Screening = Certainty and Looking Ahead

Screening employees in 2026 isn’t just about the past-it’s primarily about future behavior and performance. With assessments, you can identify who truly fits your organization and avoid making the wrong choices.
