A digital performance review cycle is an important tool for facilitating meaningful conversations between employees and managers. For example, it can be used to foster the development of employees and teams through a customized performance review cycle, or to support hybrid work arrangements. But what should you keep in mind when creating a digital performance review cycle? Here are some key considerations.  

Why a digital performance review cycle?

The performance review cycle encompasses all the times a manager talks with employees about their performance and development. Digitizing the performance review cycle using an online platform or tools is valuable for properly documenting these conversations and making them more meaningful. On the one hand, it serves as an easily accessible record of these discussions; on the other, it can function as a clear dashboard for tracking the development of employees and teams. As such, the digital performance review cycle is often used to create a more modern, customized performance review cycle or, for example, to support hybrid work (more flexible work arrangements at home and in the office).  

Workflows for All Components

A modern online tool like hrmforce makes this step forward possible. It functions as a single, comprehensive, and efficient solution for a modern performance review cycle and for facilitating individual and team development within organizations. A key consideration when creating the digital performance review cycle is setting up workflows for the various development cycles that organizations employ. From the daily to-do list (Bila) and a basic development cycle to development and annual reviews, as well as organizing and monitoring the entire annual cycle. That is why all these variations of the performance cycle are represented in hrmforce’s software for the digital performance cycle. They are explained in more detail later in this article.  

A modern performance review cycle is clearly essential

In addition to effectively, centrally, and easily documenting the discussions between employees and their managers, modernizing the content of the performance review cycle is often the reason for choosing a digital performance review cycle. Organizations want dialogue in the workplace to be more flexible, simpler, and more tailored to individual needs. It is also often necessary to modernize the performance review cycle. This is because the traditional approach costs a lot of time and money and often yields little benefit or is even counterproductive, as a seven-year study at VU University Amsterdam revealed as early as 2018. Researcher and HRM lecturer Kilian Wawoe therefore advocates for a more modern approach with a greater focus on development through continuous, motivational coaching. The assessment of these reviews-often referred to as “mandatory” and “judgmental” by employees, managers, and HR professionals-was downright shocking at the time. 90% of HR professionals found the reviews to be of insufficient quality. 95% of managers were dissatisfied with the review cycle, and 66% of employees even reported that such a review cycle caused their performance to decline. The modern performance review cycle was already scoring significantly better back then, and that will certainly be no less true in today’s tighter labor market. Employees appear to want continuous attention to their performance. A continuous dialogue fits this need and results in a massive increase (280%) in employee engagement. Team productivity also appears to rise significantly (26%) with a development-oriented performance cycle, while voluntary turnover and absenteeism due to illness, according to the study, decrease by 41% and 43%, respectively. These are truly remarkable and encouraging figures.  

Ongoing coaching

Another finding highlighted by the researcher is that teams at top-performing organizations all utilize ongoing coaching. Team members receive feedback throughout the year on how they’ve performed and how they can improve. This boosts employee performance and satisfaction while reducing the risk of stress and burnout. “The best teams are never evaluated using a detailed rating scale, but at most with ‘suitable’ and ‘unsuitable.’ Your driver’s license doesn’t indicate how well you drive either: it’s either satisfactory or not. If you then want to become a better driver, you need to be coached based on your driving behavior,” says Wawoe.  

Modern performance review cycle for hybrid work

As mentioned earlier, the rise of hybrid work can also be a reason to implement a digital feedback cycle. After all, as employees and their managers work remotely more often, remote leadership becomes more important. This requires a different approach to feedback and ensures that attention is paid to employee development. Research conducted at Radboud University in 2022 explicitly demonstrated how hybrid work directly influences the performance review cycle. This study also revealed that, in a hybrid work environment, 360-degree feedback is indispensable for gathering relevant information about employees. This is because 360-degree feedback can help employees and managers assess employee performance in a simple and accessible way. In this way, employee performance is assessed not only by a manager but by multiple people with whom an employee interacts. These could include, for example, colleagues, suppliers, or customers. This can be structured differently for each employee or development goal. This way, an individual receives feedback from various perspectives, creating a more complete picture of how they perform, both in the physical workplace and while working remotely. Users of hrmforce can utilize the 360-degree feedback questionnaire. Read this article for practical tips on how to apply this in practice.  

Digital Performance Review Cycle in Practice

The starting point for setting up a digital performance review cycle is usually the job family structure and job profiles within an organization. The principles of the performance review cycle are built around these. Objective questionnaires can help ensure that the reviews are conducted quickly and in a well-founded manner at the appropriate level. An important consideration is effectively facilitating the various types of conversations required. In addition to in-person meetings, this often involves shorter remote digital interactions. A digital performance review cycle can also serve as a solid foundation for the approach, with in-person meetings added as needed. Keep in mind the different conversation cycles that are needed: each takes place at different times and serves a different purpose. Consider, for example, these types of conversations and their characteristics:
  • Bila: The daily to-do list with specific work agreements reached during a bilateral meeting. This can take place between a manager and an employee, but also between colleagues. In addition to general notes, it’s helpful to specify for each agreement who will carry out what and when.
  • Bila+: For the basic development cycle of (often operational) employees. They and their managers want to be able to initiate these discussions themselves to provide input on topics such as: Work, Learning & Development, Health & Fitness, Collaboration & Leadership, and Family & Social Contacts. With this input, a concrete action list can be established. It is also valuable to be able to document the history and progress immediately.
  • Development Meeting: As part of an agile development cycle, it’s helpful if development meetings can be scheduled based on individual needs. For trainees, for example, every two weeks; for a senior employee with extensive experience, perhaps once a year or every six months. Key components of a development review include: Education & Training, Documents, Job Profile (hard & soft skills), 360-degree feedback, and the Development Plan (by competency and result area).
  • Annual Review: For a development cycle in which an annual review is conducted to evaluate performance and establish development agreements. In addition to these components, employee well-being can also be assessed. The performance agreements and competencies can then be assessed separately. Afterward, a single development plan is created. It is beneficial if each annual review can be digitally signed by both the employee and the manager.
  • Annual Cycle: The traditional review cycle consists of a planning, performance, and evaluation meeting. All components from the four cycles just described are included in the Annual Cycle. This can be supplemented with additional open-ended questions for each phase, for both the employee and the manager. In this way, the entire traditional cycle is digitally accommodated. As a result, the Annual Cycle becomes a very comprehensive and complete form of evaluation and development.
Setting up the digital appraisal cycle with one or more of these components requires a robust development platform. Hrmforce supports all of the components mentioned. This provides you with a well-thought-out appraisal cycle as the foundation for truly valuable conversations between managers and employees.

On average, an assessment accounts for 40-60% of an employer’s final hiring decision. This method offers companies an objective way to evaluate candidates on competencies that are difficult to measure during a standard job interview. The importance of assessments is growing as employers become increasingly selective. Wrong assumptions cost companies an average of 15,000 euros per failed hire, because competencies such as leadership and teamwork only become apparent after several months. Assessments help reduce these risks by testing behavior and skills in advance.

Key Factors That Determine the Weight

The weight of an assessment depends on five key factors: the position you’re recruiting for, the methodology you use, the assessors’ experience, the combination with other selection tools, and the organizational culture. Together, these elements determine how much influence the assessment will have on your final decision.

Job level determines the weight

For management positions, assessments carry more weight than for operational roles. A director is selected 70% based on assessment results, because leadership qualities are difficult to assess in a one-hour interview. For commercial roles, this percentage is around 50%, as sales skills can also be tested in a practical setting. Technical positions often assign a lower weight of 30-40% to assessments. Here, programming skills and degrees carry more weight. The complexity of the position therefore plays a direct role in the weight assigned to assessments.

Methodology Influences Reliability

Structured assessments with multiple exercises carry more weight than simple personality tests. An assessment center featuring role-plays, case studies, and presentations is given greater weight because it measures behavior in various situations. Psychometric tests alone are less predictive of job performance. The duration of the assessment also plays a role. A full-day program provides a more reliable picture than a two-hour test. Employers therefore place greater emphasis on comprehensive assessments that truly challenge candidates and put them under pressure.

Proven Benefits of Assessments in Recruitment

Research shows that assessments increase the likelihood of successful hires by 30-40%. This method better predicts job performance than resume screening or unstructured interviews alone. The secret lies in objectively measuring competencies that are crucial to the role.

Objectivity reduces bias

Assessments reduce subjective decisions based on first impressions or biases. An experienced assessor evaluates behavior according to set criteria, ensuring that all candidates have equal opportunities. This benefit is particularly important when dealing with a diverse pool of applicants. Studies show that structured assessments reduce discrimination by 25%. Female candidates receive fairer evaluations than in traditional hiring processes. Candidates with an immigrant background also benefit from this objective approach.

Predicting Job Performance

Assessments predict job performance with 65% accuracy, compared to 30% for unstructured interviews. This predictive value stems from the fact that assessments test competencies directly related to the position. Candidates must solve problems, make decisions, and collaborate under time pressure. The combination of different assessment components further increases reliability. A candidate who performs consistently across all exercises is likely to perform well in the actual role as well.

Different Types of Assessments and Their Weighting

Assessment combinations are given the highest weight because they provide the most realistic picture of candidates. Personality tests are supplementary and never account for more than 30% of the final decision. Cognitive tests carry significant weight for roles that require analytical thinking.

Assessment combinations

Assessment centers combine multiple exercises that simulate real-life situations. This method is given the highest weight because assessors can observe behavior in various contexts. Each exercise focuses on specific skills such as leadership, communication, or problem-solving. The in-depth observation justifies the high weighting in the selection decision.

Cognitive Tests for Analytical Roles

Cognitive tests measure logical thinking, memory, and processing speed. These tests carry significant weight for roles that involve processing complex information. Financial analysts, engineers, and consultants are selected 40-50% based on cognitive test results. The predictive value of cognitive tests is high for intellectual roles. Candidates with higher scores perform better on tasks that require abstract thinking. This direct relationship between test results and job performance explains the significant weighting.

When assessments carry less weight

Assessments carry less weight for specific roles or circumstances. Technical specialists are primarily evaluated based on subject matter expertise and experience. Creative roles require portfolio reviews in addition to assessments. Organizational culture also determines the weight given to assessments.

Technical expertise comes first

For IT positions, engineers, and specialized roles, assessments carry less weight. Technical skills and experience account for 60-70% of suitability. A programmer is evaluated on coding quality, not just on leadership potential. Assessments serve as a supplement but rarely determine the final decision. Certifications and degrees carry more weight here than behavioral competencies. A candidate with proven technical expertise but lower assessment scores may still be selected. The balance shifts toward hard skills over soft skills.

Creative roles: different evaluation methods

Graphic designers, marketers, and writers demonstrate their abilities through portfolios and practical assignments. Assessments have difficulty measuring creativity, so they carry less weight. A creative professional is evaluated based on previous projects and original ideas presented during the interview. The emphasis is on inspiration and craftsmanship rather than standard competencies. While assessments can measure teamwork and communication, they account for no more than 30% of the total weight in creative hiring decisions. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=IG9stionnNI

Practical Tips for Determining Weighting

You determine the appropriate weight for assessments by analyzing the job requirements and clarifying the organizational goals. Start with a thorough job analysis to identify which competencies truly predict success. Then combine different selection methods for the best results.

Job Analysis as a Starting Point

Make a list of critical competencies for the role. A sales manager needs different skills than an HR consultant. Determine which competencies you can assess through interviews and which require an assessment. Complex skills, such as conflict resolution, are given greater weight in the assessment. Talk to current employees and managers about success factors. They know from experience which traits lead to strong performance. This input helps determine the appropriate weighting for different selection components.

Combining Selection Methods

Use assessments as part of a broader selection process. Combine them with structured interviews, reference checks, and practical assignments. This mix provides a more complete picture than any single method alone. The assessment can account for 40-50% of the weighting, but other components remain important. Test your weighting system by tracking results. Did candidates with high assessment scores perform better after being hired? Adjust the weighting based on these experiences. This way, you’ll develop a selection process that works for your organization.

Costs versus Benefits of In-Depth Assessments

Comprehensive assessments cost between 500 and 2,000 euros per candidate, depending on complexity and duration. This investment pays for itself through better hires and lower turnover costs. A bad hire costs an average of 15,000 euros in recruitment, training, and lost productivity. The proven benefit of assessments lies in the increased likelihood of successful hires. Companies that systematically use assessments experience 25% less employee turnover in the first year. This savings more than offsets the additional costs of a comprehensive selection process.

Frequently Asked Questions About Assessment Weighting

Can assessments be discriminatory? Well-designed assessments actually reduce discrimination because they use objective criteria. Be sure to use culturally neutral exercises and trained assessors. How much weight should an assessment carry for entry-level positions? For entry-level positions, assessments carry less weight (30-40%), because potential is more important than experience. Focus on learning ability and motivation. What if a candidate performs poorly on the assessment but excels in interviews? Review the specific competencies that were measured. Low scores on critical skills are a red flag, regardless of interview results. H3: Can assessments predict job performance 100%? No, assessments are tools, not crystal balls. They increase the likelihood of making good choices but do not guarantee future performance. Do you want to optimize the weighting of assessments for your organization? Start with a thorough analysis of job requirements and measure the results of your current selection process. That way, you’ll build a methodology that truly works for your team.

More and more organizations and leaders are embracing the power of connective leadership. Above all, this means working based on trust, mutual connection, and the freedom to experiment. For leaders, this often involves exploring their new role through the lens of “Secure Base” leadership. A personality test (Big50) provides many valuable insights in this regard. The nine characteristics of connective leadership can now also be identified through this test.

What is connective leadership?

It’s hard to ignore. In recent years, we’ve been hearing more and more about connective leadership. And it’s truly more than just a trend. That’s because organizations are changing at a rapid pace. We’ve moved away from hierarchical structures and toward increasingly “agile” ways of working. This places different demands on employees, but certainly on leaders as well. As a result, Secure Base Leadership (SBL) has become one of the most influential leadership approaches today. Managers ensure a good balance between safety and challenges for employees. They inspire them, instill confidence, and challenge people to experiment, develop resilience, and build connections. In the process, mistakes are allowed so that, ultimately, people’s untapped potential can be unlocked. In fact, many earlier insights in the fields of organizational psychology, leadership, developmental psychology, and-for example-change management have been integrated into this newer vision. It is a practical application of existing insights into an effective leadership style for the modern workplace. Agility and resilience are key characteristics of this approach.

Origins and Conditions

The leadership style was introduced in 2012 by Professor George Kohlrieser, Susan Goldsworthy, and co-author Duncan Coombe (in the book *Care to Dare*) because agility and resilience were increasingly recognized as prerequisites for success for organizations and employees. This approach links a growth- and development-oriented mindset among leaders to clear incentives to foster greater boldness. For example, by rewarding team efforts, encouraging team members to ask for help, or supporting people’s courage to keep experimenting-even when initial results may be somewhat disappointing. At its core, attachment plays an important role within this vision, just as secure attachment provides a solid foundation for children. This fundamental principle has been extended to the workplace. At SBL, trust and giving people space are key principles, but that sounds easier than it often is for managers, especially in the early stages. It also requires clear expectations and agreements. And, of course, it requires managers to have the skills to effectively fulfill their new role based on a more “human-centered leadership” approach. This also means letting go of old habits and learning and developing new skills. “Leaders who apply the Secure Base principles provide their employees with a good balance between security and challenge. As a Secure Base Leader, you are a source of inspiration, you challenge others to reach their full potential, and you instill trust,” Kohlrieser writes in his book.

Fully in line with HR Trends 2023

The search for this new role and balance between security and challenge is not just a quest for managers, but for the entire organization. This is also immediately reflected in the HR Trends 2023 report from research firm Gartner. This annual study of HR developments shows that in 2023, HR leaders must primarily take into account: increasing economic pressure, scarce and more expensive talent, global supply constraints, and change and uncertainty. To address these challenges effectively and successfully, five priorities for HR in 2023 have been identified:
  1. Leadership and Managerial Effectiveness Ensure proper guidance for employees through “human-centered leadership.”
  2. Organizational Design and Change Management Change is a constant in the workplace. Teach people how to cope with it and its impact on their work and well-being.
  3. Alternative approaches to employee development : Younger generations view work differently. Support people’s personal development in a flexible manner and work together to create a career path that aligns with their ambitions and the organization’s goals.
  4. Recruitment Remains Important Half of all organizations expect the “war for talent” to continue to intensify. New recruitment strategies therefore remain important.
  5. The Future of Work : Working with external (and hybrid) workforces continues to require adaptability in the way we work and do business.
SBL’s “care and dare” principle is reflected in all these points. Sometimes literally, as with the “human leadership” mentioned in the first point, and sometimes more indirectly-but certainly no less important. After all, this type of leadership also contributes to recruitment, for example. After all, those who embody the principles of connective leadership-which is what employees are looking for today-are more attractive as employers.

Strengthening Through Personality Testing (Big50)

The development of connective leadership in organizations and among managers can be reinforced with the insights provided by the Personality Test (Big50). This is the most widely used (and researched) personality theory, and for most organizations, the Big50 competencies serve as an ideal starting point for taking a more competency-based approach to the development of employees and leaders. These insights are valuable for translating a personality profile into competencies (to be further developed), for example in the area of connective leadership. Nine characteristics are central to this process. For each competency, an indication is provided of the extent to which an individual can develop that competency. This is based on their personality and on the five key personality factors that influence behavior in work situations. To apply this to the field of SBL as well, we at hrmforce have further expanded the personality test to include the leadership report for connective leadership. In this way, the Big50 personality test continues to evolve. For example, a few years ago we also added Teamflow to provide greater insight into team roles within organizations. Nine Characteristics of Connective Leadership In the book *Care to Dare*, Kohlrieser identifies nine competencies of an authentic and successful Secure Base Leader. An SBL…
  • Always remains calm and does not let themselves be driven by primitive emotions. This prevents a sense of insecurity or unpredictability.
  • Accepts the individual. Appreciation and respect for others are the starting point.
  • Always sees the potential in others and focuses on the long-term development of employees.
  • Listens and seeks dialogue by asking open-ended questions.
  • Communicates with powerful messages. This makes communication unambiguous, clear, and direct.
  • Focuses on the positive. Seeks out opportunities and benefits. Risk-taking is encouraged.
  • Offers opportunities to take risks and develop talents.
  • Is more focused on intrinsic motivation than on monetary rewards. Personal growth and development are central.
  • Demonstrates approachability. Even when absent, people can reach out to their manager if necessary.
These nine characteristics demonstrate the emotional commitment of a manager who has employees’ best interests at heart. It is reminiscent of the family members from our childhood who helped us grow and develop-who instilled confidence in us and with whom we shared feelings of care and joy. For there is a strong causal link between the leadership we experienced in childhood and how we later approach life, work, and relationships. As early as 1966, the renowned developmental psychologist William E. Blatz highlighted the importance of a “Secure Base” for young children. This foundation later fosters the healthy development of qualities such as entrepreneurship, creativity, innovation, and resilience. SBL extends this principle to the entire organization.

Measuring corporate culture is an effective way to understand-and, if necessary, change-your company’s corporate culture. Over the past year, HR technology has made this type of cultural analysis easy to implement. In this article, you’ll learn more about culture analysis and the benefits of measuring corporate culture within HR. Finally, we’ll provide a few examples of HR technology that’s popular for analyzing corporate culture.

Greater Focus on Cultural Analysis

The increase in data volumes, the rise of HR technology, and the shift in focus toward employees’ value drivers-linked to the various facets of the company’s vision and business results-have led to an increasing emphasis on cultural analysis. More and more companies are using technology to analyze and change their corporate culture.

What is cultural analysis using HR technology?

Within HR, cultural analysis is primarily used to gain insight into the corporate culture. After all, it is only possible to change the corporate culture once a solid understanding of the current culture has been established. Technology can simplify the process of measuring corporate culture. This is achieved using datasets and smart algorithms. The collected data not only provides insight into the current culture-a so-called baseline measurement-but the analysis also maps out the path toward the ultimate goal.

Difference from Traditional Analyses

New HR technologies offer added value in their analysis compared to traditional analyses. Traditional analyses accurately pinpointed the problem areas. For example, they made it clear exactly why employees were unhappy in their roles. However, a traditional analysis was unable to translate these findings into a solution; it did not provide a step-by-step plan for increasing employee happiness.

Not Just Insights, but Solutions

HR technologies examine all facets of the corporate culture and align them with the company’s objectives. This allows you to define the goal, map out a path to achieve it, and identify how the company will benefit from this change. Modern cultural analyses therefore not only expose the problems but also point the way toward change-change that ensures the corporate culture is aligned with the company’s vision. And both employees and the company benefit from this.

Benefits of Cultural Analysis

Cultural analyses aren’t just useful for improving corporate culture so that it aligns well with the corporate vision; there are additional benefits in the area of HR. For example, cultural analyses make it easier to hire suitable staff, assess the skills of current employees, and implement smarter talent management.

Hiring the Right Employees

Those who understand the ideal corporate culture can use that knowledge to select new employees. By evaluating applicants against the criteria established by the analysis, you can choose new employees who are a good fit for the intended corporate culture. In the long term, this not only leads to a more enthusiastic team and lower turnover but also to better business results. After all, staff who are in the right place and have the right attitude ensure greater efficiency.

Skills can be accurately measured

Unlike traditional analyses, cultural analyses using HR technology also reveal employees’ soft skills. By measuring these skills and assessing them against the organizational culture and corporate vision, any gaps become apparent. These issues can then be addressed in a targeted manner through training or, for example, by increasing employee engagement.

Smarter talent management

A thorough understanding of the corporate culture is essential when recruiting new staff, promoting current employees, or parting ways with former employees. Such decisions are made easier by utilizing cultural analyses. A culture analysis provides insight into an employee’s alignment with the company’s vision and culture.

Examples of HR technology in the field of cultural analysis

HR technology that intelligently performs cultural analysis is still in its infancy. Hrmforce specializes in organizational assessments using data analysis, algorithms, and AI. Using AI, corporate cultures are analyzed and the skills of individual employees are assessed based on specific metrics. This helps address issues within the current organizational culture and challenges in recruiting new staff. The company offers an assessment tool that allows you to quickly and efficiently evaluate your company and workforce. The platform offers various apps and services that, based on data analysis, ensure employees experience greater engagement at work. Strong engagement contributes to greater job satisfaction. And a satisfied employee is able to make a valuable contribution to the organization. In collaboration with data scientists and organizational psychologists, surveys have been developed to provide insight into employees’ values. Through this analysis, all kinds of workplace issues-from low motivation to high absenteeism due to illness-can be identified and resolved.

The Future of Cultural Analysis

It is expected that more and more companies will recognize that a strong corporate culture is a key differentiator for success. The possibilities for cultural analysis will therefore continue to expand in the future and be applied in increasingly sophisticated ways. In the future, it may become necessary to use HR technology to analyze corporate culture if you want your company to continue developing and take your results to the next level.

Culture Analysis Within Your Company

In practice, you’ll find that all change begins with your employees’ behavior. Using HR technology, you can map out your staff’s value drives. This gives you insight into what your employees consider important, the importance they attach to these values, and how they influence others with these ideas. Would you like immediate insight into your employees’ value drives? You can assess them right away using an online assessment. In addition to these tests, our website offers various assessments that allow you to map out different aspects of your company. After all, insight is the first step toward change.

Employers and employees are eager to adopt a more hybrid work model: a more flexible balance between working from home and in the office. A key consideration here is remote management. It’s also important to continue supporting employee development in a hybrid work environment. This requires a flexible, modern feedback cycle between managers and employees. In this context, 360-degree feedback is extremely valuable for employees who are working from home more and more often.

Hybrid work is here to stay

Hybrid work-or working independently of location and time-is becoming increasingly common. It is not new and existed even before the COVID-19 crisis. Due to this crisis, many people have started working more from home, in a home office, or at different times, and many employees and employers have actually found this to be a very positive experience. As a result, hybrid work is definitely here to stay, and many organizations are now structuring their work around this model. Moreover, thanks to digitalization, hybrid work will become possible for an increasing number of employees and employers in the future. Meanwhile, a growing number of studies show that working from home does not come at the expense of productivity (which often actually increases!) and that it has a positive impact on employees’ well-being and their work-life balance. Due to the benefits of the hybrid work model, about 80 percent of employees want a combination of remote and in-office work in the future, according to this Cisco study. Dutch employees, in particular, prefer to work from home one to two days a week. For this international study, 28,000 people from 27 countries were surveyed, including 1,000 from the Netherlands. More than half (52%) of Dutch employees believe that the quality of their work has improved, and 58% say their productivity has increased. According to 70 percent, hybrid work provides a better work-life balance.

Key Considerations

Nevertheless, there is still work to be done to fully capitalize on the opportunities of hybrid work. According to only one in five (19%) of the Dutch respondents in the survey, their employer is “very well prepared” for a future with hybrid work. Globally, that percentage is slightly higher (25%). Maintaining employee engagement is seen as a particularly important challenge. In particular, remote leadership and continuing to support the development of employees and managers are key areas of focus. And this is despite the fact that continuous learning and development are high on the priority list at many organizations. This makes a modern, customized review cycle with a smooth workflow all the more important for dialogue and development discussions between managers and employees. After all, these conversations must be increasingly flexible and tailored to individual needs.

360-Degree Feedback

Giving and receiving feedback also takes on a different form when people work (together) remotely. To organize this effectively, 360-degree feedback is extremely valuable. It can provide employees and managers with valuable feedback and help ensure that employees’ development goals continue to be realized, even when working remotely. It’s an accessible way to assess employee performance. In this process, performance is evaluated not only by the manager but also by multiple people with whom the employee interacts. These can include, for example, colleagues, suppliers, or customers. This way, people receive feedback from different perspectives, creating a more complete picture of their performance. Questionnaires for 360-degree feedback are available online, and users of hrmforce can access the 360-degree feedback questionnaire. Read this article to learn how this works in practice. An online personality test can also be very useful for enhancing hybrid work. One example is the Big Fifty (Big50) personality test, based on the most widely used (and researched) personality theory. After taking an online test that takes about twenty minutes, individuals will know much more about their competencies, and this also provides valuable insight into the opportunities and pitfalls employees may face in a hybrid work model.

The Best of Both Worlds

With the help of online tools, employers and employees can effectively set up the hybrid work environment. Currently, there are many discussions about how to implement this. Working both in the office and at home can each have advantages that can be leveraged in a hybrid model. Many employees are more productive at home; they no longer have to commute and can more easily balance work and personal life. At the same time, being physically present at work on a regular basis also has its advantages. You interact with colleagues more often and more easily, and it’s simpler to come together as a team. A meeting via Teams is, after all, different from being together in person at the office. This creates a clearer distinction between work and home, which can sometimes be beneficial. Employers also see additional benefits. It aligns with a greater focus on attracting talent, saves costs (less office space!), reduces traffic congestion, and supports corporate social responsibility.

Government Policy

Meanwhile, the government is also working on an “Agenda for the Future of Hybrid Work.” This agenda outlines the developments and factors needed to achieve a good hybrid balance. A key building block is the recent SER advisory report on hybrid work in the future, which was prepared at the government’s request. In it, the SER (Social and Economic Council) recommends giving employees sufficient say to take advantage of the opportunities offered by hybrid work. In addition, employers must have sufficient flexibility to tailor hybrid work arrangements to individual needs. This way, everyone can take advantage of the opportunities that hybrid work offers, according to the SER.

Risks and Coordination

In addition to the benefits, hybrid work can also have drawbacks. As the boundaries between work and private life blur, employees run the risk of burnout and health issues. Social cohesion within an organization can also be jeopardized if too many employees work remotely for extended periods. “Managing, consulting, and brainstorming become more complicated. Work is also a social process, and ideas often arise through interaction,” explains Professor of Labor Law Femke Laagland, who is also a government representative on the SER. The SER therefore recommends that employers and employees consult together on the possibilities for remote work, in a way that suits the organization. It is also possible to establish collective agreements: at the sector level, in collective bargaining agreements, or at the company level with the works council or employee representatives. Laagland: “These shouldn’t be detailed agreements, but rather a general framework that managers and teams can use as a starting point. Consider, for example, a guideline specifying a minimum number of days per week that people are in the office. Or a framework outlining factors that are important when assessing whether working from home is feasible. The exact details will then depend on the specific roles within the teams and their work processes.”

Clear Agreements

At the moment, many employers-and employees as well-are still feeling their way when it comes to hybrid work. Helen Pluut, a researcher in Organizational Behavior at Leiden University, has also observed this. She has been conducting research on flexible work and work-life balance for a long time. “Hybrid work has major advantages, but it does need to be managed properly. By implementing clear policies and establishing agreements on the minimum amount of time you must spend in the office, you lay a foundation that can then be adapted flexibly. Do this at the lower levels of the organization, discuss it openly, and address it as a team,” advises Pluut. According to the researcher, a healthy corporate culture also has a major impact on the success of the hybrid work environment. Leadership by example and support from managers are essential in this regard. “If you feel that you can’t advance your career unless you’re constantly available, policy will remain nothing more than words on paper. Managers really play a crucial role here. Their attitude and behavior determine how work is done and to what extent people feel free to work from home occasionally. I would also like to advocate for making work-life balance a standard topic of discussion during performance reviews. Key questions to ask include: Is what you’re doing sustainable? Can you keep this up? Not everything is measurable, but you can make it part of the culture.”

Anyone who has to choose a major at the start of or during their career faces a major challenge. After all, how do you know if a degree program is really the right fit for you? And how do you avoid making the wrong choice? This happens quite often. A good college major assessment test offers a solution and helps you make a better choice that aligns with your personality, intelligence, and motivations.

Why take a college major selection test?

Choosing a degree program is an exciting and important moment. For high school students, this usually happens during or at the end of high school. But even during their careers, people are increasingly choosing to pursue a degree to change direction or to seek further depth and specialization. Many employers facilitate this to encourage employee development or, for example, to enhance long-term employability . A college selection test helps with making a career choice or selecting a specific (advanced) degree program. This is by no means a luxury, as recent research shows that many people would like better guidance in making this decision. As many as 1 in 5 students feel they did not receive sufficient guidance in this regard. As a result, as many as one-quarter have at some point started a program of study without completing it. In practice, career guidance in schools often proves to be too limited. In higher professional education (HBO) and university education, the dropout rate is even higher (50.9 percent!), mainly due to choosing the wrong program. As a result, 31 percent drop out as early as the first year because the program does not meet their expectations, according to the Dutch Education Inspectorate. Students primarily indicate that their course selection could be improved through a college selection test and, for example, assistance from a professional college selection advisor or a conversation with someone who has just graduated.

Different Types of Tests

Anyone who wants to make a well-informed choice of study program that suits their personality, intelligence, and motivations can take a college selection test. These tests come in various forms. The free online tests are rather superficial, so you shouldn’t expect too much from them. If you want to take a well-structured test, you can easily take a good general career choice test for a small fee. At hrmforce, you also have the option to expand this assessment with a deeper focus on your personality, intelligence, and motivation. This can also include online feedback for additional explanation. This can be extremely valuable when making such a choice, especially since it can have a major impact on your life and career. What’s more, what makes hrmforce’s career choice test unique is that it-finally-objectively maps out all Dutch degree programs in this field. Not only are a participant’s interests assessed, but their answers are also compared to a normative group. This provides particularly valuable insights.

Benefits of College Choice Tests

Taking a well-researched college selection test offers several benefits. First and foremost, it helps you make a well-considered career choice or select a degree program or further education. This reduces the likelihood of dropping out or feeling dissatisfied with the choice you’ve made. The test can also help identify programs or careers that someone had not previously considered or was unaware of. Even in cases of doubt or uncertainty, it provides a better understanding of the requirements and potential future career demands. In addition to providing insight into academic programs and careers, a good college selection test also enhances self-awareness-for example, by clarifying one’s own interests, skills, and strengths. This helps in choosing a program of study or even developing a personal career plan. In this way, students are also better prepared for their future careers.

A Challenge for Academic Advisors

In addition to good career choice assessments, there is another important consideration that can help people make better educational choices. Research from Utrecht University and Leiden University shows that academic advisors can also play a greater role in this regard. This is especially true because, contrary to popular belief, a good choice of study program isn’t made in a single moment. It’s a process, but one that often lacks a clear endpoint, according to the researchers. Even after a study choice has been made, it can still change-and this can actually be very helpful. However, there needs to be room for that flexibility, which is often lacking. The researchers therefore recommend that academic advisors continue to guide high school seniors, even after they’ve already chosen a program. They observed that people sometimes become fixated on a degree choice they’ve made for themselves. In doing so, they tend to ignore conflicting information. For example, if it turns out that the “chosen” degree program doesn’t actually align well with an interest that’s important to them. As a result, people sometimes close themselves off from the realization that a different program might be a better fit for them. It also appears that high school students, in particular, sometimes cling to a “choice” because people close to them (such as parents) believe that the earlier choice suits them better. In addition to providing longer-term, process-oriented guidance, the researchers suggest that academic advisors should also be aware that a student may be clinging to a study choice for the wrong reasons-even against their better judgment. Study advisors should therefore continue to reflect, together with prospective students, on a person’s interests and the programs that align with them. It should also be made clearer that it is not “strange” to change one’s choice of study program. By drawing attention to this, there is a growing awareness that changing one’s choice of study program can also lead to a better choice and better outcomes.

Tip: Forget about the “perfect” choice of study program

Finally, here’s a tip for anyone facing this decision themselves. First and foremost, back up your choice of major with reasons. A decision is made based on feelings, reason, and intuition. A good college major selection test can help with this. To also support the rational side of the decision, it helps to substantiate and justify your choice with arguments. These questions can help:
  • How do I know this program is right for me?
  • Why am I choosing this program? Or why am I considering it?
Here’s another important insight to consider. Prepare thoroughly for your college major decision-a college major assessment and a college advisor can be very helpful in this process. But don’t strive for the “perfect” choice either. After all, a program that perfectly matches who you are and what you want probably doesn’t exist. Many degree programs include courses, theory, or projects that aren’t a great fit for you. This doesn’t necessarily mean the program isn’t right for you. So focus on finding a program that’s “good enough” for you, according to a strategy from Studiekeuzemaken.nl. “Because if you strive for perfection, your doubts will never end.”

Almost everyone in the Netherlands is feeling the effects of the labor shortage this summer: fewer trains are running, you have to wait in line for hours at Schiphol Airport, and in restaurants and bars, you have to wait a long time for your drink. In healthcare and education, too, many HR managers are at their wits’ end. How do you find qualified people to keep things running? Assessments help ensure you hire the right candidates. When Ajax won the national championship in May, the celebration didn’t take place at the Museumplein as is traditional. And it wasn’t even because of COVID-19 restrictions or a forecast of bad weather. No-the organizers simply couldn’t find enough security guards to ensure safety at such a large event. More than a month later, Schiphol Airport announced it was canceling flights due to that same staffing shortage. After all, all travelers must go through security screening, but there aren’t enough security personnel to oversee that process. There is also a shortage of staff at baggage handling. What is happening at Schiphol and at Ajax is indicative of the situation throughout the rest of the Netherlands: the labor market is bursting at the seams. “The Netherlands is grinding to a halt,” wrote NRC Handelsblad in June. While a few years ago it was mainly the healthcare, education, and technology sectors that struggled to find enough qualified staff, now there seems to be no sector that isn’t facing a severe labor shortage. “The shortages are affecting the entire labor market.”  

More Job Openings Than Unemployed People

For the first time since the CBS began tracking these figures, there are now more job openings than unemployed people. “An unprecedented turning point,” as de Volkskrant put it. The problem is particularly acute in the public sector. The numbers don’t lie: right now, there is a need for about 11,000 teachers, 50,000 healthcare workers, 1,400 police officers, and thousands of additional security guards. We all feel the consequences every day. There are too few teachers in the classroom, too few nurses and other healthcare staff at the bedside, too few police officers on the streets, and too few conductors and train operators to keep the trains running. Schools are calling on parents with teaching credentials to step in as teachers; otherwise, the children will have to stay home. The NS is forced to adjust its schedule. And anyone who needs medical or psychological help often faces long wait times.  

Job interviews aren’t enough

For HR managers, staff shortages are a problem that keeps them up at night. After all, how do you find the employees you so desperately need in this unprecedentedly tight labor market? If you think back to the last economic crisis, it’s almost impossible to imagine that just eight years ago, it was commonplace to receive dozens, if not hundreds, of responses to a job posting. Now, the opposite is often true: even if there are candidates to choose from, it’s highly doubtful that any of them will meet the job requirements. It takes time, money, and energy to find employees who are a good fit for your organization. It’s a real shame, of course, when it quickly becomes clear that someone isn’t the right fit for what you’re looking for. In the Netherlands, the job interview is still one of the decisive factors in hiring someone. But the problem is: in such an interview, you often don’t get enough information to assess a person’s qualities. “Job interviews are quagmires of misinformation,” wrote De Correspondent in 2019. The platform reports on a Harvard study in which researchers took a close look at job interviews. Their conclusion: such interviews say more about the employer than about the applicant. “In practice, they yield hardly any information. After all, can you really get to know someone in a half-hour conversation? No.”  

Assessments help you get ahead

Scientific studies have shown that structured interviews offer higher predictive value than “regular” job interviews. Such an interview follows a set pattern, with pre-determined questions that you don’t deviate from. Validated selection tools-such as intelligence tests and personality questionnaires-also provide a more reliable picture of a candidate than a typical job interview. It is therefore a good idea not only to conduct job interviews but also to have candidates take assessments. The word “assessment” literally means “evaluation.” It is a psychological evaluation that determines whether a candidate is suitable for a particular job. The content of the evaluation depends on the position. For example, an assessment may consist of a combination of aptitude, personality, and motivation tests. By having candidates take assessments, you increase the likelihood of a good match. You gain an objective picture of the applicant: what competencies, qualities, personality traits, communication styles, and areas for development do they possess? The results help you predict whether someone will thrive in a particular role.  

Scientific Research

A great deal of scientific research is being conducted on assessments. As a result, we’re gaining a better understanding of which types of assessments work best. For example, researchers have discovered that it’s not just personality and cognitive skills that are important predictors of future performance; a person’s motivation and interests also play a role. It’s also important to realize that “higher” scores on an assessment aren’t always better. What matters most is that a person’s strengths and weaknesses are in balance, and that you, as an HR professional, carefully evaluate the fit between the person and the requirements of a specific role.  

Better Job Interviews

If you conduct an assessment before a job interview, you can use the results to help structure the interview more effectively. The initial meeting with a candidate also becomes more relevant, as you can ask follow-up questions about the points that emerged from the tests. In addition, an assessment report helps prevent many discussions among members of the hiring committee. It can be extremely frustrating when one member of the committee isn’t convinced by a candidate, while the rest are convinced of his or her abilities. An assessment provides factual information, which makes the decision-making process run more smoothly.

The Big Five Personality Model: What Is It and How Can You Use It?

Personality models are increasingly being used in the human resources industry. By administering a personality test to a candidate or employee, you gain a clear picture of his or her personality. You can use this insight to determine whether a candidate is a good fit for your company, which role this candidate is best suited for, and to assess whether an existing employee is in the right position within the organization. There are various personality models that you, as a human resources manager, can utilize. One of the best-known and most popular models is the Big Five personality model. You can read more about this model on this page.

Why the Big Five Model Is the Gold Standard

The Big Five personality model distinguishes itself from other models through its scientific foundation. Decades of research have shown that these five dimensions are universal and transcend cultural boundaries. This makes the model reliable for organizations that operate globally.
Advantages of the Big Five Practical value
Scientifically validated Reliable predictions about job performance
Culturally neutral Applicable to international teams
Dimensional (no types) Nuanced picture without stereotyping
Stable over time Long-term planning possible

The Big Five Personality Model: A Brief Introduction

The Big Five personality model is a model based on five personality traits. The model is used in psychological research, as well as in recruitment and selection, analyzing and resolving workplace conflicts, and coaching. It is also a valuable tool for human resources managers. An important characteristic of the Big Five personality model is that the scores on the five personality traits follow a normal distribution. People who take this test are not pigeonholed. For example, they can be somewhat introverted and at the same time somewhat extroverted. This makes the Big Five personality test very reliable and therefore useful.

How does the Big Five personality model work?

As mentioned earlier, there are five personality traits according to the Big Five model. These traits are briefly described below.

The five dimensions in detail

Dimension High-score characteristics Characteristics of a low score Ideal roles
Extraversion Social, energetic, assertive, optimistic Calm, reserved, independent Sales, management, PR
Agreeableness Cooperative, trusting, empathetic Competitive, skeptical, direct Teamwork, healthcare, HR
Diligence Organized, reliable, disciplined Flexible, spontaneous, creative Administration, project management
Emotional stability Calm, confident, able to handle stress Emotional, concerned, sensitive Leadership roles, crisis management
Openness Creative, curious, intellectual Practical, traditional, conventional R&D, design, consulting
Extraversion Extraversion refers to the extent to which a person does or does not need social interaction. Extraverted individuals are sociable, active, and talkative. Introverted people prefer to work alone in a quiet environment. Agreeableness Agreeableness is also referred to as friendliness in the Big Five personality test. This is the extent to which a person is accommodating, tolerant, and helpful. A less agreeable person is often more competitive and sometimes less cooperative. Conscientiousness Conscientiousness refers to the extent to which a person works in an organized and goal-oriented manner. Emotional Stability Emotional stability refers to the extent to which a person is or is not emotionally stable. If someone is not emotionally stable, that person is neurotic. Openness Openness generally refers to the extent to which a person is willing and able to speak openly, but in the Big Five personality test, this concept means something else. In this case, openness refers to the extent to which a person is open to new experiences and/or new ideas. People who score high in this category are often somewhat more flexible than those who score lower.

How Scores Are Interpreted

The Big Five model uses percentile scores that indicate how someone scores relative to the general population:
Score interpretation:
Very high (90-100%): Extreme in this trait; strong behavior in this direction High (70-89%): Clearly present, but not extreme Average (30-69%): Balance between both extremes Low (10-29%): Limited presence Very low (0-9%): Barely present, behavior in the opposite direction

A Personality Test Without Categories

As mentioned earlier, the Big Five personality test doesn’t pigeonhole people. For example, you might be a little extroverted, a little conscientious, and a little open to new experiences and ideas. After taking the test, you’ll see exactly what your scores are for each personality trait. If your score is very high or very low, you fall into one of the extremes for that trait. In this case, for example, you’re not particularly extroverted at all. If your score is average, then you’re a little extroverted, but not very much. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=lc7vN_e36Yc

Practical Applications by HR Process

The Big Five model can be used in various HR processes. Each application requires a specific approach:
HR process Relevant dimensions Specific applications
Recruitment & Selection All five dimensions Job fit, cultural fit, team composition
Career Development Openness, Diligence Learning preferences, career paths
Team building Extraversion, Agreeableness Role Distribution, Communication Styles
Leadership Development Extraversion, Emotional Stability Leadership Style, Stress Management
Conflict Mediation Agreeableness, Emotional Stability Communication Approach, Sources of Tension

Using the Big Five Personality Model: Tips

Would you like to use the Big Five personality test in your organization? If so, we’d be happy to offer a few tips on how to use this test effectively when screening candidates and assessing your staff, particularly job applicants. Tip 1: Give your interviewee time to take the test It’s a shame if the Big Five personality test is rushed through, simply because the test is less reliable in that case. Be sure to tell your interviewee not to spend too long thinking about the questions and answers in the test. Thinking too much actually reduces the likelihood of reliable answers. Tip 2: Choose a reliable test . There are many companies that offer the Big Five personality test. Not all of them provide a reliable test. By choosing a reliable and validated test from a reputable provider, you can be sure that you’ll be able to conduct a thorough assessment. This is important because only a thorough assessment provides a clear picture of a person’s personality. Tip 3: Discuss the test Did you have an existing employee within the organization administer a test to a candidate for an open position? If so, don’t forget to discuss the test. The raw test results are interesting, but someone’s comments on these results are even more so. For example, ask whether he or she agrees with the results, or whether he or she recognizes themselves in the results. Also, ask follow-up questions: Why is your conversation partner actually like this? What does he or she think about this? Is this a good or bad thing? By asking questions about the results of the Big Five personality test, you’ll gain an even clearer picture of your conversation partner’s character. This makes the personality model even more valuable in your work as a human resources manager.

Additional Implementation Tips

Tip 4: Combine with other information
Never use the Big Five as the sole selection criterion. Combine the results with competency-based interviews, references, and work experience to get a complete picture.
Tip 5: Train your HR team
Make sure HR staff know how to interpret and discuss test results. Misinterpretation can lead to discrimination and poor decisions.
Tip 6: Respect privacy and transparency
Be transparent about the purpose of the test and how the results will be used. Respect the right to privacy and store results securely.

Avoiding Common Mistakes

These mistakes are common when using the Big Five model:
Common mistake Why It’s Problematic Better approach
Viewing scores as absolute truth Leaves no room for growth or change Using scores as an indication
Considering only extreme scores important Average scores also contain valuable information View all scores in context
Overemphasizing a single dimension Simplifying complex personality Taking a holistic view of all dimensions
Not discussing the results Missed opportunity for deeper insight Always conduct feedback and reflection sessions

Sample profiles for various roles

These profiles provide an indication of which scores are often associated with success in specific roles:
Role Extraversion Agreeableness Conscientiousness Emotional Stability Openness
Sales Manager High Average High High Average
Bookkeeper Low Average Very high High Low
Creative Director High Average Average High Very High
HR Business Partner High High High High High
Software Developer Average Average High High High
Note: These profiles are indicative. Successful professionals may excel in various areas. Use these as a guideline, not as strict criteria.

Scientific Background and Validity

The Big Five model is based on decades of research and has proven to be the most robust personality model:
Validity Aspect Big Five score Meaning
Test-retest reliability 0.80-0.90 Very stable results over time
Predictive validity for job performance 0.20-0.40 Significant prediction of success
Cross-cultural validity 95%+ of cultures Universally applicable model
Genetic basis 40-60% hereditary Stable biological basis

ROI of Big Five implementation

Organizations that effectively implement the Big Five model see measurable results:
Measured benefits:
25% reduction in employee turnover with better job-person fit 15% improvement in team effectiveness through deliberate team composition 30% higher employee satisfaction with appropriate roles 20% faster onboarding through targeted development plans

Checklist for Big Five implementation

For organizations looking to get started with the Big Five model:
Pre-implementation checklist:
☐ Define clear objectives for its use ☐ Choose a validated, reliable test provider ☐ Train the HR team in interpretation and interview techniques ☐ Develop privacy and data protection protocols ☐ Determine which roles/processes are suitable for assessment ☐ Create a communication plan for employees ☐ Establish evaluation criteria for implementation success

Conclusion

The Big Five personality model offers organizations a scientifically grounded method for assessing personality. Through the five dimensions-Extraversion, Agreeableness, Conscientiousness, Emotional Stability, and Openness-HR professionals can make better decisions regarding recruitment, development, and team composition. The model stands out for its reliability, cultural neutrality, and practical applicability. Unlike typologies, the Big Five does not pigeonhole people but provides a nuanced picture that leaves room for growth and development.

Key points to remember:

Scientific basis: The Big Five is the most well-validated personality model available Practical value: Direct applications in all HR processes No labeling: Dimensional approach respects individuality Culturally neutral: Applicable in diverse organizations worldwide ROI-driven: Measurable improvements in team effectiveness and employee satisfaction

Description

The Organizational Culture Scan helps you determine your optimal culture, aligned with your organization’s strategy. The scan identifies gaps between the actual and optimal cultures, including detailed information about the cause(s) of these gaps. It also highlights valuable additional information-strengths vs. weaknesses, common characteristics, early warning signs, and other notable findings. It provides input for change.

set.title: 4 Reasons Why Healthcare Workers Are Less Satisfied with Their Jobs-and What You Can Do About It
set.body:
To keep your employees productive and healthy, job satisfaction is essential. In the healthcare sector, job satisfaction is increasingly under pressure. That’s why every last Tuesday in January has been designated “Job Satisfaction Day in Healthcare” to raise awareness of this issue. What factors influence job satisfaction among healthcare professionals? And what can you, as an HR manager, do to ensure that your team continues to enjoy their work? About 1.5 million Dutch people work in healthcare. And that group is likely to grow even larger in the coming years: due to an aging population and new treatment options, the number of patients is increasing. If the healthcare sector continues to grow at its current pace, as many as 1 in 4 Dutch workers will be employed in this sector by 2040. That is, if those healthcare workers are even available. While there is a desperate need for staff in doctors’ offices and at patients’ bedsides, more and more people are leaving the field, according to figures from Statistics Netherlands. In December, the NOS reported that healthcare and social services institutions had as many as 67,000 open positions, more than 16,000 more than a year earlier. The number of job openings is now even twice as high as it was in 2018. This is not only because people in their sixties are retiring. In fact, many newly graduated healthcare workers are changing jobs within just two years. For them, a lack of job satisfaction is a major reason for leaving. Job satisfaction is therefore essential for retaining healthcare staff. By focusing on this, we can prevent even more people from leaving the sector. As an employer or HR manager, how do you promote job satisfaction? There’s no one-size-fits-all solution , emphasizes FWG, organizer of the “Day of Job Satisfaction in Healthcare.” But there are certainly a number of factors that contribute to job satisfaction. In this article, we’ll share four reasons why healthcare workers experience less job satisfaction-and we’ll explain what you can do to keep your staff engaged and happy at work.  

Reason 1: High Workload

High work pressure in the healthcare sector is perhaps the most important reason for the lack of job satisfaction. As many as three-quarters of nurses suffer physically or mentally from excessive work pressure. A survey by the IZZ Foundation shows that 1 in 5 healthcare workers is physically exhausted, and 1 in 6 is emotionally exhausted. Because daily tasks pile up, healthcare professionals have less time and rest to provide quality care. They feel like they’re constantly playing catch-up and unable to help patients the way they need to be helped. Yet for many healthcare workers, “helping people” is precisely what motivated them to choose this profession in the first place.   Here’s what you can do Job satisfaction arises when people get as much energy out of their work as they put into it. So, it’s about helping employees find a balance between their “energy boosters” and “energy drainers.” High work pressure is an energy drainer-but if it’s offset by a great team and interesting work, people are more likely to continue enjoying their jobs. Ask managers to work with their teams to identify each person’s energy drainers and energy boosters. You may not be able to completely eliminate work pressure, but it’s often possible to redistribute tasks so that each colleague does the work that requires the least energy from them.  

Reason 2: Lack of a good relationship with managers and coworkers

Great coworkers are worth their weight in gold! Especially when the workload is high, a pleasant conversation over lunch or a joke at the coffee machine can make a world of difference. In a survey by the temp agency Accountemps, as many as 37% of Dutch people cited “nice coworkers” as the deciding factor for a pleasant work environment. Conversely, it’s disastrous when coworkers can’t stand each other or even work against one another. And when a manager fails to recognize and appreciate his team’s efforts, job satisfaction within that team quickly plummets to zero. Here’s what you can do : Invest in your people. That means: organize team outings and peer-review sessions, send a bouquet of flowers to sick colleagues, show your appreciation when people work overtime, and make sure managers regularly check in to see how everyone is doing. Here are some more tips on how to show your staff you appreciate them. Also, take a critical look at whether there’s a “culture of complaining” in your workplace. Complaining can sometimes feel good, but in the long run, it drains employees’ energy. If you notice that your employees are complaining a lot among themselves, bring this up during a team meeting. And agree together on how you can handle this differently in the future.  

Reason 3: Lack of autonomy

Working autonomously is a key factor in job satisfaction. A study of nurses and caregivers in home health care found that employees who can work independently and are given room for their own initiative are more enthusiastic about their work. They’re also less likely to consider leaving the healthcare sector. People want to have a say in how they provide care and how care is organized. Here’s what you can do : The key words here are: trust and letting go. Your employees will only dare to take the lead if you make them feel that they have the freedom to do so. To start, talk to your employees and ask them if they currently feel they have enough autonomy. If not, what do they think is the reason? Clearly agree on the results you expect from them, but give your staff the freedom to decide for themselves how they’ll achieve those results. Don’t constantly look over their shoulders; leave the responsibility with them. Note: don’t just throw them in at the deep end, either. Let them know you’re available in the background to support them.  

Reason 4: Limited opportunities for personal development

Job satisfaction comes under pressure when someone has little room to develop. This is evident from research by PGGM&CO. Young healthcare workers, in particular, expect their employer to offer opportunities for further growth. In this situation, be careful that people don’t become “quiet quitters”: they’ll then only do the bare minimum. Here’s what you can do : Foster a learning organization culture. In a learning organization, learning, development, and innovation are encouraged. Reflection and evaluation are part of daily work; employees regularly take courses, and managers set a good example by discussing problems without judgment and providing constructive feedback. Employees in such an organization are open to new insights and willing to learn from mistakes. Do you want to become a learning organization? In this article, we share 7 success factors for fostering learning and development. Want to get started right away? Explore the option of a development assessment. Through such an assessment, you and your employee can identify his or her talents and potential, and determine which role best suits that person.   Want to learn more about assessments? Then get in touch! At Lamark, you can have digital assessments administered at locations throughout the Netherlands. We welcome your employees warmly and give them personal attention, so they feel completely at ease. Check the Lamark or hrmforce website for the options.
