It is a key predictor of success. And the great thing is that EQ can be developed. That’s why measuring it is valuable not only when recruiting candidates but also when further developing existing employees and teams. These days, it’s easy to measure using an EQ questionnaire.

What exactly is emotional intelligence?

Emotional intelligence (EQ) is the ability to perceive, interpret, and manage your own emotions and those of others. Key skills associated with this include, for example: self-awareness, self-regulation, motivation, empathy, and social skills. In the past, IQ (intelligence quotient) was still primarily considered the most important predictor of a person’s chances of success. At that time, this innate factor was still viewed as a “static given.” We now know that there are multiple forms of intelligence and that EQ, in particular, is the strongest predictor of performance. These insights are actually still relatively new. In 1983, the American psychologist Howard Gardner was the first to propose the idea of multiple intelligences. Since then, we have been discussing different forms or “domains” of intelligence. Consider, for example, social or spatial intelligence. This means that people can be successful in different ways. The term EQ came to the attention of the general public in 1995 through Daniel Goleman’s groundbreaking work *Emotional Intelligence (Why It Can Matter More Than IQ)*. Since then, the importance of EQ has been widely recognized, especially in the workplace.  

The Rapid Rise of EQ

Most employers and employees now view emotional intelligence as an indispensable skill, according to recent research by Capgemini. To be precise, 74 percent of employers and 58 percent of non-managers consider it an indispensable skill. The consulting firm advises employers to build an emotionally intelligent workforce. “This benefits both organizations and employees. To foster an emotionally intelligent workforce, employers must adapt existing training programs and make them accessible to everyone, adjust hiring processes, and apply an EQ lens when promoting and rewarding talent,” according to Capgemini. Furthermore, attention to EQ is expected to increase sixfold over the next five years. This is also closely linked to digital transformation, as EQ in particular is difficult to replace with automation or artificial intelligence (AI).

What are the benefits of a higher EQ?

Key benefits of a higher EQ include improved collaboration among employees and greater job satisfaction. It fosters greater self-awareness and better self-regulation (the ability to control and redirect disruptive impulses and emotions). This is valuable, for example, when facing changes in the work environment. Other benefits include higher employee motivation and greater empathy in the workplace (understanding others and taking their feelings into account). Meanwhile, better social skills can help build connections with others to guide them in a certain direction. This is valuable, among other things, for (personal) leadership and team building.

How can you measure EQ?

Due to the growing understanding of the importance of EQ, organizations are increasingly seeking to measure it among job applicants or for development purposes among existing employees, managers, or executive teams. This can be done relatively easily with an EQ questionnaire, possibly in conjunction with other tests or assessments that provide further insight into a person’s personality, motivations, or cognitive abilities. Based on current scientific insights, hrmforce has conducted its own research into personal characteristics that are strongly related to emotional intelligence. This has led to the development of our own assessment, which takes about ten minutes to complete. The Emotional Intelligence report then provides immediate insight with an overall score (from 0 to 100 percent) and, even more interestingly, scores on various subscales (on a scale of 1 to 10). These include, for example, scores in the areas of: emotion perception, emotion management, emotion regulation, self-motivation, social awareness, optimism, and self-confidence. These concepts are also explained in the report. The purpose of the report is to provide insight into the current situation in order to stimulate personal growth. After all, all these elements can be developed and changed. The results are valuable within the overall competency overview and important for the development of various competencies. More about hrmforce’s EQ Questionnaire is covered in a recent vlog on this topic.

Applying Insights in Practice

There are various reasons to administer the EQ questionnaire to current employees or job applicants. In addition to predicting success, it offers valuable insights for further developing key skills in individual employees. But it can also be useful for team development, which is becoming increasingly important. Or, conversely, when recruiting lateral hires from other professions. In the latter case, a quick assessment of competencies (Competency Check) is desired, but above all, an understanding of the person and their motivation. For this purpose, hrmforce also offers the Motivation Test and the Personality Test (Big50), among other tools. Finally, short tests such as the EQ questionnaire serve as a valuable starting point for dialogue between employees and managers and for improving “the good conversation” between them. This can make the constructive conversation even better—for example, as part of a modern feedback cycle that includes more frequent brief check-ins as part of the ongoing dialogue between employees and managers.

EQ in 2025: Even More Relevant in an Increasingly Digital World

By 2025, emotional intelligence will have become one of the most sought-after competencies in the job market. As (AI) systems take over more and more routine and analytical tasks, employees with high EQ will distinguish themselves through their interpersonal skills.

More organizations are now investing in EQ development programs. The latest EQ assessments not only measure self-reports but also analyze voice patterns, facial expressions, and heart rate during interactions.

In the hybrid work environment of 2025, digital empathy and online emotional leadership have become critical skills. Leaders who can pick up on emotional cues-even through digital channels-demonstrably create more engaged and productive teams.

True employee development touches on the core of what drives them as individuals and how they grow. When you see an employee thrive in a new role, or when someone suddenly realizes where their talents lie-those are the moments that make this work worthwhile. Ideally, you create these moments systematically rather than waiting for them to happen by chance.

Why Traditional Approaches Fail

The problem with many development programs is that they’re based on a one-size-fits-all principle. You send everyone to the same leadership training, organize standard team-building activities, and expect this to lead to growth. The reality is more complex. Take Sarah, for example, a finance manager who, according to her manager, “needs to communicate better.” Three communication training sessions later, little had changed. It wasn’t until it became clear that Sarah’s natural work style is more analytical and she needs different communication approaches that progress was made. She received coaching on how to translate numbers into stories for non-finance colleagues-something that was much better suited to her personality. This illustrates why we use assessment tools like the Big Fifty personality test. This tool measures fifty personality traits that influence work behavior. Instead of guessing what someone needs, you get concrete data on how someone functions.

The Psychology Behind Motivation

This is where it gets interesting for us as HR professionals. Employee development only works if it aligns with intrinsic motivation. The Motivator Test reveals which factors truly energize people. Take Michael, a sales manager whose numbers were lagging. His manager thought he needed to be driven more by financial incentives. However, the Motivation Test showed that Michael is primarily motivated by helping customers and making a social impact. We shifted his focus to consultative selling and customer success stories. His performance improved significantly because his work suddenly took on meaning. These insights are worth their weight in gold because they explain why certain people thrive in certain roles and others do not. It’s not about ability, but about the match between what drives a person and what the job requires.

Cognitive Abilities as a Foundation

Personality and motivation are important, but cognitive abilities form the technical foundation for development. The Ability Scan measures various forms of intelligence relevant to job performance. This goes far beyond IQ. We look at verbal reasoning, numerical skills, spatial reasoning, working memory, and processing speed. These different types of intelligence determine how people process information and solve problems. A concrete example: Lisa applied for a data analyst position. Her resume was impressive, but during the Ability Scan, it became clear that numerical processing was not her strongest point. However, she scored excellently on verbal reasoning and pattern recognition. We advised her to pursue a role in business intelligence where she would interpret data and translate it into strategic recommendations-a role much better suited to her cognitive profile.

Getting the Full Picture

The power lies in the combination of these different assessment tools. Personality tells you how someone works, motivation explains why they do it, and cognitive abilities reveal what they’re capable of. Together, these dimensions provide a complete picture of a person’s potential. For example: someone with high openness to experience (personality), driven by autonomy and creativity (motivation), and strong in divergent thinking (cognitive) is a natural candidate for innovation roles. This seems logical, but how often do you see people in roles where this match is missing?
Development Phase What Happens Your role as an HR professional Practical tools
Orientation The employee explores what’s possible and what they want Facilitating self-awareness through questions and assessments Assessment tools, career conversations, 360-degree feedback
Objective Formulating concrete, achievable goals together Set challenging yet realistic goals and ensure commitment SMART methodology, development plans, success metrics
Implementation Real development takes place Coaching, removing obstacles, monitoring motivation Training, mentoring, stretch assignments
Evaluation Reflecting on what has been learned and what comes next Celebrating progress, setting new goals Progress meetings, peer feedback, self-reflection

Why the elite sports approach works

Elite athletes have something most organizations lack: a systematic approach to talent development. They measure performance continuously, provide immediate feedback, and tailor training based on results. No athlete waits a year for feedback on their performance. You can apply this principle directly to employee development. Instead of annual reviews, implement weekly check-ins. Instead of standardized training, create personalized learning paths. Instead of general feedback, provide specific, actionable tips.

The Art of Giving Feedback

This is where many managers fall short. They give feedback that’s too general (“you need to communicate better”) or too critical (“you did a poor job presenting that”). Good feedback is specific, behavior-based, and linked to impact. For example: “In yesterday’s meeting, I noticed that you were interrupted three times by colleagues. This happened mainly when you were giving longer technical explanations. For next time: break down complex points into shorter chunks and check in with people along the way to see if they’re following you. This will help you maintain their attention and prevent interruptions.” This type of feedback works because it links concrete behavioral observations to practical tips. The recipient knows exactly what they can do differently. It’s best to use a structured feedback cycle.

The Importance of Context in Employee Development

Employee development doesn’t happen in a vacuum. Organizational culture, the immediate supervisor, the team, and even the physical work environment all influence how people grow. In an organization where mistakes are punished, people will take fewer risks and therefore learn less. In a culture that encourages experimentation, natural learning takes place. As an HR professional, you share responsibility for creating the right conditions.

Psychological Safety as a Foundation

Google’s Project Aristotle demonstrated that psychological safety is the most important predictor of team performance. Teams where people feel safe to ask questions, admit mistakes, and share new ideas perform better. This is crucial for employee development. People learn by experimenting, making mistakes, and learning from them. Without psychological safety, this process is blocked. In practical terms, this means you need to train managers to create safe learning environments. They must learn how to respond to mistakes (as learning opportunities rather than failures), how to model vulnerability, and how to encourage diverse perspectives.

Micro-learning and the Forgotten Power of Repetition

The human brain forgets 75% of new information within 24 hours if it isn’t repeated. This explains why many training programs have little lasting impact. People attend a two-day workshop, get excited, and then fall back into old patterns. Micro-learning solves this by breaking information down into small, repeatable chunks. Instead of a single large training session on giving feedback, people receive a short weekly tip on a specific aspect. This is repeated and applied, helping the information stick. A real-world example: we implemented a micro-learning program for new managers. Every Monday, they received a five-minute video on a specific leadership aspect; on Tuesday, a reflection question; on Wednesday, a short assignment; and on Friday, a reminder to apply what they’d learned. After six months, assessments showed significantly better leadership skills compared to the control group that underwent traditional training.

The 70-20-10 Rule in Practice

The Center for Creative Leadership found that people learn 70% from challenging experiences, 20% from others (mentoring, coaching), and only 10% from formal training. This ratio challenges us as HR professionals to think differently about development. 70% means that real development happens through stretch assignments, new projects, and challenging situations. Your role is to create these learning opportunities. For example: an introverted employee who wants to develop presentation skills can start by presenting to a small, trusted team, then to the entire department, and eventually to external clients. 20% is about learning from others. You can facilitate this through mentoring programs, peer learning circles, or job shadowing. A finance professional who wants to develop strategic thinking can spend a few days shadowing strategic projects to see how senior consultants think and work.

Data-Driven Development Without Forgetting the Human Element

Analytics can enrich employee development, but only if you interpret the data correctly. It’s not about collecting as many metrics as possible, but about finding patterns that provide real insights. For example: you notice that employees on Team A are growing significantly more than those on Team B, despite similar starting points. By digging deeper, you discover that Team A’s manager holds short weekly one-on-one meetings, while Team B has longer monthly meetings. You can use this insight to advise other teams.

Predictive Models for Talent Development

Machine learning can detect patterns that are invisible to humans. What combination of assessment scores, job experiences, and training programs predicts successful career transitions? These insights help you provide targeted advice. But be careful not to reduce people to data points. An algorithm may predict that someone is suited for a leadership role, but it says nothing about their intrinsic motivation to take that step. Human interpretation remains crucial.

What does the future hold?

Employee development is evolving toward even more personalized, flexible approaches. AI will be able to generate individual learning paths that adapt in real time to progress and preferences. Virtual reality makes complex scenarios accessible for safe experimentation. At the same time, we’re seeing a trend back toward more human contact. Paradoxically, more technology creates a need for more authentic, personal contact between people. Automating administrative HR tasks gives us more room for coaching and mentoring.

The Hybrid Future of Learning

The combination of digital and in-person learning offers new possibilities. People can learn theory online and apply it offline, with AI assistants providing real-time coaching. But the human connection-the conversation after a difficult experience, the mentor who challenges you, the colleague who supports you-remains irreplaceable.

Practical Implementation Steps

After ten years of experimenting with different approaches, there are a few principles that consistently work for implementing better employee development. Start small and scale up. Choose an enthusiastic team or department for a pilot. Measure baseline performance and satisfaction. Implement one or two new elements (such as weekly check-ins or assessment-based development plans). Measure again after three months and document what works.

The Critical Role of Managers

Your programs are only as good as the managers who carry them out. Invest heavily in training managers in coaching skills, giving feedback, and conducting development discussions. A well-trained manager can make a mediocre program succeed; a poorly trained manager can cause even the best program to fail. Provide managers with tools and templates, but above all, train them in the underlying principles. They need to understand why certain approaches work so they can adapt when the situation calls for it.

The Long-Term Impact

Organizations that consistently invest in employee development see results that go beyond improved performance. They build an employer brand that attracts top talent. Their people stay longer, grow faster, and take more initiative. But the greatest gain lies in cultural transformation. When development becomes the norm, a learning organization emerges that adapts more quickly to change. In a world that’s changing at an ever-faster pace, this adaptability may well be your most important competitive advantage. It requires patience and perseverance. Cultural change doesn’t happen in six months. But the organizations that embark on this journey create workplaces where people can truly thrive. And that, ultimately, is what it’s all about.

A resume shows what someone has done. An interview shows how someone comes across. But behavior in real-world situations is often harder to interpret. That’s exactly where a DISC assessment can add value-not as a replacement for the interview or the substance of someone’s experience, but as an additional layer that helps provide a more focused discussion of behavior, communication, and team fit.

In short

  • DISC helps make behavioral preferences a topic of discussion during the recruitment process.
  • Never use DISC as the sole selection criterion.
  • Its greatest value lies in better interview questions, a more focused team analysis, and more informed placement.
  • A DISC assessment works best in combination with a resume, cover letter, references, and a structured interview.
  • For teams, DISC can also help identify differences in style, pace, and communication earlier on.
Check out the DISC test from hrmforce

Why recruitment and selection often require more than just a resume and an interview

In many hiring processes, the focus is still primarily on work experience, education, and whether there’s a good rapport during the interview. That makes sense. You want to know if someone understands the job and comes across as likable. At the same time, there’s a risk involved. A candidate may be strong in terms of content but still struggle in practice with pace, collaboration, feedback, or change. Conversely, someone with a less-than-perfect resume might actually be a great fit for the role and the team. Recruitment and selection, therefore, aren’t just about knowledge and experience. It’s also about behavioral preferences. How does someone make decisions? How does someone communicate under pressure? How does someone handle structure, autonomy, or resistance? These kinds of questions are often asked only later in the process, even though they can provide a lot of clarity early on. A DISC assessment can help with this-not by labeling a candidate, but by providing a framework for understanding behavior. This often leads to more insightful conversations and helps prevent you from judging someone based solely on gut feelings.

Important: DISC is not a tool for determining whether someone is a good person or not. It is a resource for discussing behavioral styles. So always use it as a supplement to a careful selection process.

What exactly does DISC measure in recruitment?

DISC examines behavioral preferences. It therefore does not provide a complete picture of a person’s intelligence, professional expertise, motivation, or moral compass. What it does, however, is reveal how a person tends to react when interacting with others and in work situations. In practice, DISC is usually explained using four behavioral colors:

Red

Direct, results-oriented, quick to make decisions, enjoys pace and influence.

Yellow

Enthusiastic, sociable, persuasive, focused on connection and energy.

Green

Calm, caring, loyal, focused on harmony, support, and stability.

Blue

Analytical, meticulous, structured, detail-oriented, logical, and precise.

Need more explanation? Check here for more details on the DISC colors In recruitment, this is valuable because roles often require more than just task execution. An account manager can benefit greatly from persuasiveness and initiative. A financial specialist, on the other hand, often needs to work meticulously, in a structured manner, and with careful thought. A manager, in turn, faces different behavioral challenges than someone in a supportive team role. Still, it’s too simplistic to say that one color always fits one role. A sales role doesn’t automatically require a lot of red and yellow. A controller doesn’t necessarily have to be predominantly blue. Context, team dynamics, and corporate culture always play a role. DISC therefore primarily helps you look more closely and ask more targeted questions. Read also: Which DISC colors go well together?

Where DISC Really Adds Value in the Selection Process

The biggest mistake organizations make is viewing DISC as a quick filter. That does the tool a disservice. Its true power lies precisely in the deeper insights that emerge afterward. Below, you’ll see where DISC often yields the most value in practice.

1. Better interview questions

For example, a candidate with a strong red profile can make decisions quickly and likes to take on responsibility. That sounds appealing, but it also raises questions. How does this person handle dissent? Do they really listen? What happens when processes slow down? By using DISC in advance, you can ask much more targeted questions about specific behaviors. With a candidate who has a pronounced green profile, you can discuss entirely different topics. How does this person handle change? How easily does this person speak up during a conflict? How does this person react when a work environment demands a fast pace and high pressure? This helps you avoid generic interviews where everyone gives socially acceptable answers.

2. Better understanding of team fit

A candidate may look strong on paper but still be a poor fit for an existing team. Not because the person is flawed, but because behavioral styles can clash or, conversely, complement each other. Does a team already have a lot of fast-paced, outspoken people? Then someone who brings calm and is a good listener can actually add a lot. Does a team tend to work slowly and cautiously? Then more decisiveness or initiative may be needed. DISC makes this discussion more concrete. You’re not just looking for “chemistry,” but for what the team truly needs right now.

3. Fewer assumptions during the assessment

Recruiters and managers are quick to draw conclusions based on first impressions. Someone who speaks fluently and comes across as confident is quickly labeled as “strong.” Someone who speaks more calmly or takes longer to think is sometimes unfairly seen as less sharp or less ambitious. DISC helps you look beyond style alone. After all, a quiet candidate can be very decisive. An energetic candidate may struggle with details. An analytical candidate can communicate effectively, but does so in a different way than someone with a high “Yellow” score.

4. Better onboarding after hiring

DISC doesn’t stop at the signature. It’s especially valuable after the hire. You can better guide a new employee if you already know how they communicate, learn, respond to feedback, and prefer to collaborate. This directly links recruitment to onboarding and team development.

How to use DISC responsibly in recruitment and selection

DISC works best as part of a broader process-not as a strict screening tool, but as a conversation starter and reflection tool. This approach often works best in practice:
Step What to Do Why it works
1. Job Analysis Determine which behavioral factors are truly important for the role. You avoid automatically relying on stereotypical profiles.
2. Administer the DISC assessment Have candidates complete the assessment at a logical point in the process. You’ll gain additional insight before delving deeper.
3. Discuss the report Use the results to evaluate behavior using real-world examples. Check here to learn how to read a DISC report. You’ll gain more context than just a profile on paper.
4. Consider the team context Don’t just compare the candidate to the role, but also to the team. Focus on how they complement the team and collaborate, not just on individual style.
5. Make a decision based on the big picture Take the resume, interview, references, and assessment into account together. This makes the process more thorough and more human.

Which DISC profiles are a good fit for which roles?

This is a question that often comes up. However, some nuance is needed here. DISC doesn’t provide a perfect match for every job title. You can, however, consider the behavioral challenges that frequently arise for each role.

Sales and commercial roles

In commercial roles, you often see a need for initiative, persuasiveness, energy, and resilience. Candidates with more red and yellow traits can easily relate to these qualities. But that doesn’t mean a more analytical or calm profile can’t be a strong salesperson. In more complex sales situations, it’s precisely attention to detail, active listening, and in-depth subject matter knowledge that can be decisive.

HR and customer-focused roles

Roles in which empathy, active listening, and relationship management are important often align with profiles that show more green. At the same time, excessive conflict avoidance can also be counterproductive in situations where you need to provide clarity or have difficult conversations. Here, too, DISC helps us look beyond just a likable demeanor.

Analytical and process-oriented roles

In roles where accuracy, structure, and risk awareness are key, you often find that blue behavior is valuable. Think of finance, quality assurance, data, administration, or compliance. But even there, going too far can cause friction. Too much focus on detail can slow down decision-making or hinder flexibility.

Leadership roles

Leadership often requires switching between styles: providing direction, engaging people, listening, making decisions, and staying calm under pressure. A leader, therefore, does not need to have just one distinct “color.” It is precisely the discussion about style, blind spots, and context that becomes valuable here.

What DISC Excels At

  • Making behavior a topic of discussion
  • Generating better interview questions
  • Highlighting team dynamics
  • Strengthening onboarding
  • Providing a clearer framework for collaboration

What to Watch Out For

  • Reducing candidates to a single color
  • Using DISC as a screening tool
  • Drawing stereotypical conclusions too quickly
  • Forgetting the role and team context
  • Underestimating professional suitability

Common mistakes with DISC in recruitment

Confusing DISC with potential or talent

A DISC profile provides insight into behavioral preferences, not necessarily into performance or potential. Someone with a high blue score isn’t necessarily smarter or more meticulous in every situation. Someone with a high red score isn’t automatically a strong leader. Talent arises from a mix of behavior, experience, motivation, skills, and context.

Assigning an “ideal” color to a role too quickly

As soon as organizations say that a role “really needs a red profile,” things get dangerous. Then you start looking for confirmation instead of focusing on the person in front of you. A better question is: What behaviors does this role require in this context, within this team, under this manager?

Not conducting a follow-up discussion

An assessment without a discussion often loses half its value. The report only becomes truly useful when you ask the candidate for examples. Does this sound familiar? When do you see this happen? When don’t you? What does that require of your work environment?

Using DISC only in borderline cases

Otherwise, it quickly feels like an extra hurdle for candidates. It’s precisely when you use DISC in a consistent, clear way within a process that it becomes fairer and more consistent.

Practical Interview Questions Based on DISC

Do you want to effectively incorporate an assessment into the interview? Behavioral questions are key. Not theoretical, but concrete.

Questions about pace and decision-making

  • Can you describe a situation where you had to make a quick decision with limited information?
  • How do you deal with coworkers who take much longer to weigh their options than you do?
  • When do you consciously hold yourself back?

Questions about collaboration and communication

  • What do you need to work well with others?
  • How do you react when someone strongly criticizes your approach?
  • With what type of coworker do you naturally work well, and with what type do you have more difficulty?

Questions about structure and accuracy

  • When do you feel satisfied that something is truly finished?
  • How do you handle unclear instructions or a cluttered work environment?
  • In what situations do you find that your attention to detail helps, and when does it actually slow you down?

Questions about change and pressure

  • How do you react when priorities suddenly shift?
  • What do you do when the atmosphere in a team becomes tense?
  • What causes you stress in your role?

Using DISC for teams rather than just filling individual job openings

A job opening is often more than just an empty seat. It’s also a role within an existing system. That’s why it’s wise to use DISC not only to assess candidates but also to evaluate the team. What’s the team’s current dynamic? Where are the commonalities? Where are people getting stuck? Is there too little momentum, too little structure, too little coordination, or, conversely, too little pushback? When you have that clarity upfront, recruitment becomes less reactive. You’re not just hiring someone who can handle the tasks, but also someone who can make the team stronger.

Do you want to use DISC for candidates or teams?

The DISC test from hrmforce provides a practical starting point for discussing behavior, communication, and collaboration in much more concrete terms. It’s useful for selection, development, and team analysis.

More about the DISC test

When DISC Is Less Appropriate

DISC isn’t the first tool you should reach for every issue. If you want to measure very specific cognitive abilities, you’ll need a different type of assessment. If you want to assess subject matter knowledge, a case study, a trial assignment, or a content-focused interview works better. If you have concerns primarily about integrity or motivation, that calls for yet another approach. DISC is therefore particularly effective when you want to gain insight into behavior, communication, and collaboration. That’s where its value lies. As soon as you expect it to tell you everything about a candidate, you’re placing too much pressure on the tool.

Conclusion

DISC can add significant value to recruitment and selection, provided you use it correctly. Not as a quick judgment. Not as a label. Not as a screening tool to reject candidates. Rather, as a tool to make behavior more concrete, conduct more targeted interviews, and take a more conscious approach to team fit and onboarding. That’s precisely where the value lies for HR, recruiters, and managers. It gives you a better way to articulate what you often already sensed but couldn’t quite put into words. And that often leads to better conversations, more informed decisions, and stronger hires. Do you want to use DISC in recruitment or team development? The workload in elementary and secondary education is high. Teachers in the Netherlands work longer hours than their colleagues in other European countries and are more often faced with large classes of 30 or more students. To express their dissatisfaction, teachers have already taken to the streets and closed their classrooms. Elementary and secondary school teachers constantly face a dilemma. Given the high pressure, it would be wise to take things a little easier. However, who ends up bearing the brunt of this? The students in the classroom. As a teacher, you want to avoid that at all costs. It would go directly against professional ethics. That’s why you make do with what you have and try to make the best of it.  

The government comes to the aid of education

The government is aware that elementary and secondary education are under pressure. The education sector has the highest percentage—22.1%—of people experiencing burnout symptoms. It has therefore been decided to allocate additional funds that can be used to reduce the workload. A school with about 225 students can count on approximately €49,000 in additional funding for the 2019-2020 school year. This money can be used, among other things, to hire additional educational support staff and to invest in IT or digital learning materials. Schools can spend the money as they see fit. This gives them the opportunity to address their own specific challenges. More money for education is great and desperately needed, but will that solve the problems? What can teachers themselves do to carry out their teaching duties with less stress and more energy?  

Tips for reducing your workload:

 
  • Time management: You experience an overwhelming workload when you lack an overview. Time management can help with this. Create a solid weekly schedule, a daily to-do list, and use the time you have effectively. When you’re in control, it leads to much less stress.
  • Priorities: A teacher’s most important task is to educate students. That’s where the priority lies. Your peak focus should therefore be in the classroom. All other matters take a back seat. Meetings, for example, are necessary and useful, but make them efficient. Set a time limit for meetings. You can cover just as many topics in half an hour as you would if you set aside three times as much time.
  • Teamwork: Although teachers usually stand in front of the class alone, you can support one another as colleagues and work together as a team. Work together to solve the problems you encounter. Offer each other advice. As a team, you can also have a greater influence on the school plan. That way, during the school year, you’ll do things that you personally find important-not just because they’ve been mandated by school administration.
  • Self-awareness: What causes you stress? When do you need help from a colleague or supervisor? What inspires you, and what motivates you? What are your competencies, and which ones do you use most in practice? Understanding these issues gives you more control over your own work situation and has a positive impact on stress levels.

Diversity, equity, and inclusion are becoming increasingly important in the modern workplace. Organizations are increasingly focusing on these areas. This offers significant benefits, such as greater innovation, better decision-making, and increased appeal to both employees and customers. You can gain more insight into and better manage diversity issues with hrmforce’s online (DE&I) questionnaire. We use it internally ourselves to conduct assessments. We shared it with two of our female programmers.

The Importance of Diversity and Equality Within Organizations

Diversity and inclusion foster an organizational culture in which all employees feel respected and valued. Regardless of differences such as gender, ethnicity, age, sexual orientation, or, for example, a physical disability. These differences are often the first to come to mind, but it can also involve other differences such as neurodiversity or competencies. Equality means that everyone is given equal opportunities, regardless of these differences. Those who treat differences as equal-or even leverage them-can reap significant benefits from doing so, in addition to making a principled choice. This not only prevents (unconscious) discrimination, for example, in hiring or promotions. A diverse and inclusive work environment also leads to higher employee engagement, greater creativity, and ultimately better business results.

Research on the Benefits

In recent years, extensive research has been conducted on the organizational benefits, yielding striking results. A 2018 McKinsey study shows that companies with greater gender diversity are 15 percent more likely to achieve better financial performance. Companies with ethnic diversity perform as much as 35 percent better. According to the study, this is because diversity at the decision-making level leads to higher-performing teams. An analysis by Harvard Business Review also shows that diversity in teams leads to improved performance-primarily through better problem-solving and strategic thinking. The greater appeal of diverse and inclusive organizations is especially true for younger generations. People from Generation Z (born since the 1990s), in particular, want to be heard and consider it especially important that organizations consciously address diversity and inclusion, as this international study shows.

Online DE&I Questionnaire

To gain a better understanding of diversity, equity, and inclusion within an organization, it is important to be able to measure various related topics. hrmforce’s unique DE&I Questionnaire collects data on how employees experience diversity and inclusion. An organization can use the complete questionnaire or integrate specific questions into existing surveys or, for example, periodic assessments. With these insights, you can take targeted actions within an organization or team to further improve diversity and inclusion. The name of the DE&I Questionnaire, by the way, refers to the English terms Diversity, Equality, and Inclusion . Employees who complete the questionnaire indicate the extent to which they agree with a statement. In addition to direct questions about corporate culture, the questions also cover subtopics such as the organization’s demographic composition, transparency and fairness, recruitment and selection processes, promotion opportunities, pay equity, development opportunities, leadership engagement, and, for example, how the organization handles any incidents or complaints. A connection is also made to employee satisfaction and, for example, the organization’s image. A few open-ended questions can provide particularly valuable input for organizational policy. For example: What additional steps or policy measures would you recommend to create a more inclusive environment for all employees?

What do we measure ourselves?

We also use the DE&I questionnaire in our own organization. One of our findings is that this helps strengthen a culture of openness and respect, in which every employee can be themselves. It also fosters greater engagement because the commitment to equal treatment is valued. And that, in turn, leads to higher employee satisfaction. To put this to the test, we presented a few statements to two of our female programmers. Tilani (Senior Tech Lead) and Uthpala (Senior Software Engineer) have been working for hrmforce as part of our team in beautiful Sri Lanka for 11 and 2.5 years, respectively. How do they experience our work environment?
  1. The diversity of our workforce enhances our work environment.
Both recognize this. Tilani: “If you have the talent, you get the opportunity-regardless of, for example, your gender or other differences. The talents that everyone brings together strengthen our work environment, as many studies have shown. Eleven years ago, I was the first female employee hired onto our team. From there, I was able to advance to Senior Tech Lead. Over the years, I’ve worked closely with people of various nationalities, religions, and ethnic backgrounds. Everyone is treated equally here. We also celebrate holidays from various religions within our organization: Christian holidays like Christmas, but also, for example, the Buddhist Wesak Festival.” Uthpala has experienced this firsthand: “Equal treatment of women and men isn’t common in Sri Lanka, but it is in the IT sector. When I was hired here, there were six other candidates, all men. But we were given the same opportunity, and they chose me based on my talent and work experience.”
  1. Our work environment supports the unique needs of every employee.
“Thankfully, because different people have different needs,” says Tilani. Uthpala: “If I were to have a problem with my leg and couldn’t climb stairs, I’m sure a suitable solution would be found. Then I could work from home temporarily, or if it took longer, accommodations would be made at the workplace. For example, a pregnant woman can also work from home more often if she needs to.”
  1. Our organization is recognized externally for its commitment to DEI.
“I think so,” says Uthpala. Tilani: “Although it’s hard to gauge how the outside world perceives it. You’d have to measure that separately. It’s harder for us in Sri Lanka to assess how it’s viewed in the Netherlands. In any case, the geographical distance isn’t a problem for us. We also feel just as involved. We work closely with our colleagues in the Netherlands and know each other well. We have several online meetings a week and sometimes meet in person as well. That geographical difference doesn’t make any difference either.”

What trends and developments can we expect in the field of HRM in 2026? And how can all of hrmforce’s specialized questionnaires and development tools help organizations with this? We asked Floor Hendriks (managing partner) to share his outlook for the future. With a special focus on, among other things: the consequences of the tight labor market, measuring job satisfaction, and new needs arising from hybrid work. As is tradition, the turn of the year is the perfect time to look back and look ahead. Before we look at the trends and new tools for 2026, let’s first take a brief look back at the past year. At hrmforce, a lot has happened again to help clients work even better, smarter, and more efficiently in the field of HRM.

What stands out most to you from 2026?

“First and foremost, we launched a great many new features for our questionnaires, reports, and HR tools. Every two weeks, we released an update featuring an average of ten new features-ranging from small improvements to major ones, such as the launch of new questionnaires like the one for Diversity & Inclusion. All told, that adds up to about 250 new features. We’re quite proud that we were able to deliver this for our clients once again. This includes new color-coded reports for our questionnaires, specialized leadership reports, new components for the development cycle, and a valuable feature that translates IQ test results into targeted actions. In addition, the design of our portal has been updated and improved. I’m also pleased with that.”

Have many preparations already been made for 2026?

“Definitely. First and foremost, on the technical side. That might sound less exciting, but it’s very important. We’ve been preparing our new server and security environment, which will go live on January 1. With the increasing use of our tools, this is crucial for improving performance. Users will notice this because they’ll be able to work faster with our tools. In addition, we’re ensuring that all data remains secure.”

What are the key HR trends for 2026?

“Recruitment and selection remain a major challenge due to the tight labor market. As a result, workplace happiness and employee retention are becoming even more important issues. To address this, employers will increasingly conduct small-scale surveys to regularly gauge employee sentiment. This allows them to anticipate issues in a timely manner and make adjustments where necessary. In 2026, we also took additional steps to monitor job satisfaction, so that employers can take targeted, data-driven actions in this area. To address various challenges holistically, the (API) integration capabilities of different systems are becoming even more important. We have further developed this capability so that users can continue to work with our specialized questionnaires on their own central platform. The substantive quality and validity of the results remain our key value proposition for clients. Furthermore, hybrid work remains a key theme. Organizations have been practicing this for some time now but continue to evolve in this area. Key areas of focus include remote leadership and continuing to support employee development within the hybrid work environment.”

What do you expect from AI tools for HR in 2026?

“That’s obviously a trend no one can ignore, but you have to use it as a tool and based on your specific needs. We’ve already taken steps in this direction and will certainly continue to do so. For example, for analyzing test results and translating them into recommendations. An ‘AI coach’—with a chat function-will help employees, managers, and HR professionals translate the results into actions tailored to individual employees and teams. That Q&A and recommendation feature is what makes it valuable. For example, if an employee wants to start working on competency development after taking a test, it can be very helpful if they can immediately see which training videos, courses, or modules are recommended for their development plan. Of course, when it comes to data analysis and AI, we take great care to ensure the data privacy that is so important in this context.”

How do you help organizations now that more and more data is available?

“That’s a key focus area, because data only becomes valuable when you use it purposefully to advance your organization’s mission. This means we’re increasingly tailoring measurement results and reports to users’ roles and objectives. For example, we’re introducing updated dashboards for the organizational level, managers, and individual employees. This way, everyone can see the most relevant results at a glance, but in addition to that basic overview, we’ll also be offering expert reports for further analysis. This allows an HR professional, for example, to prepare for an interview based on test results. Or a manager can discover which questions to ask during conversations with employees. For example, if someone scores low on agreeableness and high on directness in a personality assessment, this could cause tension in the workplace. A relevant question might then be how that person handles resistance within the team. Or how the employee convinces others when presenting their ideas.”

So you’ll continue to actively develop all the questionnaires, reports, and tools in 2026?

“Absolutely. People sometimes ask why we do so much. But we’ll definitely keep doing it because we want to and because we find it so important. You can always get more out of the quality of questionnaires and reports to achieve the best measurement results and predictions. In that area, we absolutely cannot and will not stand still. We’re starting the new year full of new energy.”

set.title: The option to set up two-factor authentication-Week 22
set.body: A frequently asked question we receive from IT departments concerns the option for two-factor authentication. The answer is simple: Yes, two-factor authentication is available in hrmforce, and there are two ways to set it up. The first option is to enable the setting specifically for administrator roles. This includes roles such as manager, test manager, and superuser-those who have broad access to the system and manage it on a broader level. In addition, there is a second option: enabling two-factor authentication for all roles within the portal. This means that not only administrators, but also candidates, job applicants, and employees can take advantage of this extra layer of security. DISC shows how people communicate, make decisions, and collaborate. But DISC’s greatest strength doesn’t lie in any one person-it emerges when different DISC colors complement each other.  In this article, you’ll discover which DISC colors work well together, where tension arises, and how to make the most of those differences. Want to brush up on what the DISC colors mean first? Then check out this article:

Similar DISC Colors: Easy Collaboration with Clear Pitfalls

When your behavior resembles that of your collaboration partner, pitfalls can arise.

Red and Red

Two Red styles work quickly and purposefully. They value clarity, pace, and direct communication. In time-sensitive situations, this is a powerful combination. The pitfall: a power struggle. Both want to lead, which can lead to conflicts. There may also be insufficient attention to consensus and details.

Yellow and yellow

Yellow and yellow bring energy, creativity, and optimism. Together, they generate countless ideas and create a lively atmosphere within a team. The pitfall: lack of follow-through. New ideas keep pouring in while ongoing projects are left unfinished.

Green and green

Two green styles form a harmonious and secure partnership. They listen, support one another, and show loyalty. The pitfall: conflicts are avoided. Decisions take a long time, and change moves slowly.

Blue and Blue

Blue and blue deliver quality, structure, and careful analysis. Mistakes are rarely made. The pitfall: “analysis paralysis.” Decisions can be delayed too long due to a drive for perfection.

Strong DISC Combinations: Different Styles That Complement Each Other

In a good team, people with different personality types complement each other.

Red and Green

Red brings direction and pace, while green ensures support and attention to people. This makes the combination very strong for change initiatives. The tension: Red wants to move faster than green is comfortable with, while green wants more coordination than red has patience for. Balance is achieved through mutual understanding.

Red and Blue

Red makes decisions; blue monitors quality and risks. Together, they ensure results that are both swift and well-thought-out. The tension: Blue sometimes finds Red too impulsive; Red finds Blue too slow.

Yellow and Blue

Yellow brings ideas and inspiration; blue makes plans concrete and achievable. This combination is perfect for concept development and innovation. The tension: Yellow feels held back by critical questions; blue gets frustrated by a constant stream of new ideas.

Yellow and Green

Yellow provides energy and momentum, while green fosters calm and collaboration. Teams feel both heard and inspired. The tension: Yellow sometimes moves too fast, while green often finds change too abrupt.

Red and Yellow

This combination excels in communication, sales, and entrepreneurship. Red provides direction; yellow brings influence and enthusiasm. The tension: both sometimes lack structure and attention to detail.

Green and Blue

Green focuses on people, blue on processes. Together, they create a reliable, stable way of working with clear agreements. The tension: blue can sometimes sound too critical, green too cautious.

DISC opposites: where friction arises

Red versus green

Red is direct and task-oriented; green is indirect and people-oriented. Without insight, they can irritate each other, but with understanding, they complement each other perfectly. Red helps make decisions; green ensures others follow through.

Yellow versus blue

Yellow thinks out loud, connects people, and improvises. Blue analyzes, plans, and monitors. Without insight, they clash quickly, but together they deliver creative and realistic solutions.

Which DISC colors best suit certain goals?

Note: The information below is a guideline and does not always apply.

For innovation and new ideas

Yellow for creativity, blue for feasibility, green for buy-in.

For rapid change

Red for direction, blue for quality, green for communication.

For stability and customer focus

Green for collaboration, blue for structure.

For complex projects

Blue for analysis and planning, red for decision-making, green for team cohesion.

How do you get the most out of DISC color differences?

1. Map out team members’ DISC profiles When people understand each other’s styles, mutual respect and better communication develop. 2. Use DISC as a language, not a label Don’t say: “You’re too critical.” Say: “You’re showing a lot of blue right now-can you explain the risks?” 3. Assign roles based on strengths Red for deadlines, yellow for communication, green for support, blue for planning. 4. Consciously balance teams Teams with only red and yellow lack structure. Teams with only green and blue lack momentum. 5. View tension as a useful signal Where there’s friction, there’s often exactly the quality you yourself lack. Differences aren’t a problem-they’re an opportunity. Find out here how to read a DISC report .

Finally: Which DISC colors work best together?

There is no such thing as a perfect combination of DISC colors. It’s not about “right” or “wrong,” but about balance. Similar colors create comfort but are one-sided. Different colors create tension but deliver strength, innovation, and better decisions. Take the DISC test here

Talent determines whether organizations grow or stagnate, yet many HR teams still rely on disparate tools, Excel spreadsheets, and subjective evaluations. Talent management system software brings coherence to talent processes and helps organizations make more informed decisions about their people, ensuring that performance, development, and career advancement are no longer evaluated in isolation from one another.

In short

  • Talent management system software helps organizations make well-informed decisions about employees.
  • A TMS brings performance, skills, development, and succession planning together in a single system.
  • Skills-based talent management only works when skills are clearly defined and used in a measurable way.
  • Without metrics, a TMS remains primarily a record-keeping system.
  • Manager adoption and data quality determine the outcome.

What is talent management system software?

Talent management system software, often abbreviated as TMS, is software that helps organizations track, develop, and deploy talent in a structured way. The system supports processes related to performance, skills, development, career advancement, and succession planning, ensuring that decisions about employees are made more consistently. A TMS is not a standalone HR application, but a platform that brings together multiple HR processes. By connecting these processes, it creates a single overview of talent within the organization, preventing information from becoming scattered across different systems.

Talent Management in Simple Terms

Talent management revolves around three interrelated questions: who demonstrates desired behavior and performance, who has room to grow further, and who can eventually take on a different or more demanding role. A TMS helps answer these questions by capturing data and combining it in a consistent manner.

What Does a Talent Management System Include?

Not every organization uses all components of a TMS at the same time, but the interconnection between components ensures that information from one process is used in another. Development agreements align with performance, and succession planning decisions are based on recorded data rather than isolated impressions.

Common components of TMS software

A talent management system typically includes modules for performance management-where goals and reviews are documented-as well as components for competencies and skills, which provide insight into what employees are capable of. In addition, many systems support learning and development to align professional growth with identified needs. Succession planning is also a common feature, as is support for internal promotion, feedback, and reports that provide an overview of trends and patterns.

Difference Between TMS, HRIS, and Performance Tools

The terms HRIS, performance tools, and TMS are often used interchangeably, even though they serve different purposes. An HRIS focuses primarily on personnel administration, such as data, contracts, and leave. Performance tools support discussions and goal-setting between employees and managers. A TMS combines information from these processes and supports decisions regarding development, career advancement, and succession planning.

Why Organizations Choose TMS Software

Organizations choose a TMS when standalone systems fail to provide sufficient visibility and talent processes become fragmented. Without cohesion, it is difficult to link performance, development, and succession planning, which often results in decisions being based on limited information.

Common Challenges

Without a TMS, there is often no up-to-date overview of skills, performance evaluations vary by manager, and succession planning is only discussed when an employee is about to leave. Additionally, training programs do not always align with performance, and information is scattered across multiple systems, making it difficult to identify patterns.

Skills-based talent management: More than just a trend

Skills-based talent management focuses on what employees can do, rather than just on job titles. This helps organizations adapt more flexibly to change and better support internal mobility.

What Makes Skills Useful in Practice

Skills only become useful when they are clearly defined and used consistently. Without clear definitions, you end up with a list that offers little guidance. A workable approach starts with a limited number of core skills per job family, which are linked to observable behaviors and used in performance reviews and development.

Performance Management in Modern TMS Software

More and more organizations are moving away from annual reviews and opting for shorter cycles with regular discussions. A TMS supports this way of working by providing structure for goals, agreements, and documentation, without taking over the conversation between manager and employee.

The basic principle of performance management

The system supports the conversation and assists with documentation, but it does not replace the conversation nor does it determine its content.

Succession planning and insight into potential

Succession planning is all about continuity and preventing unexpected vacancies in roles. Organizations want to know who can take over a role, both in the short and long term, so that risks remain manageable.

How succession planning works in a TMS

Within a TMS, positions are designated as critical, and the employees identified as potential successors are documented. By combining performance, skills, and other data, a more well-founded assessment is created than when decisions are based solely on experience or visibility.

Why Assessments and Feedback Are Used

Without metrics, talent management remains primarily a way to record information. Metrics help better substantiate decisions and provide greater insight into differences among employees.

Examples of talent information used

Organizations often use personality questionnaires to gain insight into behavioral preferences, tests that reveal learning ability, and feedback tools that examine behavior from multiple perspectives. Combining this information provides a broader picture than relying on a single source.

Implementation: Where Things Often Go Wrong

When implementing a TMS, technology rarely proves to be the biggest obstacle. Adoption by managers and the quality of the data recorded determine whether the system is actually used. When definitions are unclear or processes are designed to be too complex, usage declines and the system loses its purpose within the organization.

Factors That Support Implementation

Clear agreements on terminology, a design that aligns with managers’ work, and clear rules regarding data usage ensure that a TMS is used and maintained more effectively.

KPIs for tracking talent management

Using metrics provides insight into whether talent management contributes to the organization’s goals. Commonly used indicators include internal promotion, succession planning, time to readiness, and retention of employees in key roles.

When should you choose a talent management suite?

A TMS is suitable for organizations that want to systematically support talent decisions and consolidate processes related to development and succession planning. If HR operates primarily on an operational basis and processes are not yet established, it may be wiser to start with simpler tools first.

FAQ

How much does talent management system software cost?

Costs vary by vendor and the system’s configuration. A monthly fee per employee is often charged, supplemented by setup and implementation support costs.

How long does implementation take?

An implementation usually takes a few months, depending on the size of the organization and the selected features.

Is a TMS suitable for smaller organizations?

Smaller organizations can also use a TMS, provided the scope remains limited and the system aligns with existing workflows.

A happy employee is a good employee-every HR manager knows that. But how do you ensure your employees continue to enjoy their work? We’re sharing 5 helpful tips on workplace happiness during this Workplace Happiness Week. If you want a healthy and successful organization, you’d be wise to invest in your staff. After all, your people ultimately determine what you’re able to accomplish. And various studies show that happy, satisfied employees perform better. For example, researchers at the University of Warwick discovered a strong link between happiness and productivity in the workplace. Moreover, happy and motivated people take fewer sick days, cope better with stress, and stay with the same employer longer, as Professor Martijn Burger recently emphasized in the NRC newspaper . So it’s no surprise that more and more companies are actively working to increase their employees’ job satisfaction. As an employer, you obviously can’t completely control whether people are happy. But you can do a lot to contribute to your employees’ job satisfaction. These five tips will help you get off to a good start.  

Tip 1: Establish a clear vision

Employees spend a significant portion of their time at work. They therefore want to feel that the effort they put into their work is meaningful. Why does your organization do what it does? What goal are you pursuing? And what is the purpose of it all? As an employer, it’s important that you can provide clear answers to these questions. So formulate a clear vision-and, very importantly, communicate it. A shared goal motivates employees and establishes clear guidelines and expectations. Moreover, with such a narrative, you’ll attract employees who believe in you. Note: Your vision must align with reality-otherwise, you’ll lose your credibility. For example, if you’re a healthcare organization that says the client comes first, structure your operations so that employees don’t spend an unnecessary amount of time on administrative tasks and other peripheral matters.  

Tip 2: Actively Work on Your Company Culture

Colleagues and the atmosphere within a company are key determinants of employees’ job satisfaction. “Vitamin A,” is what wellness expert Hidde de Vries calls it in an interview with NRC. “People are social creatures. We need each other for our self-confidence, to feel good, and to produce the right brain chemicals,” he tells the newspaper. So think about the atmosphere you want to create, and tailor your policies accordingly. For example, when employees are given more freedom and autonomy to do their work the way they want, they experience greater job satisfaction. That can be a reason to be flexible with work hours and remote work. Also, plan regular team outings and other group activities to strengthen the bonds between colleagues. In addition, keep an eye on the workload. A consistently high workload is detrimental to job satisfaction. Take breaks seriously and send people who are working overtime home a little early. That said, too little work is also not good-it can lead to bore-out.  

Tip 3: Choose Your Managers Carefully

Various studies show that managers play a crucial role in workplace happiness. For example, the 2021 National Workplace Happiness Survey-a survey of 1,500 working Dutch people-revealed that managers can make or break employees’ workplace happiness. The authors of the Handbook on Job Satisfaction (2020) also conclude that managers play a decisive role. They must ensure that employees have enough autonomy, that the workload isn’t too high, that the atmosphere in the workplace is positive, and that the work remains challenging. It is therefore very important that your organization has capable managers and team leaders who are able to guide and coach their people. Managers with a directive or controlling style lead to lower job satisfaction among your staff. The same goes for managers who lead in a directive manner or are primarily focused on the process. Do you notice that your managers could use a little help? Training can help them further develop their leadership skills.  

Tip 4: Make sure employees feel appreciated

Appreciation is a major driver of happiness in the workplace. So let people know that you value them. Managers play a key role here as well. It’s important for them to give compliments regularly and to make room for everyone’s opinions and insights. There are many ways to show appreciation, by the way. For example, make sure employees don’t have to ask for a raise themselves-instead, take the initiative and offer one in a timely manner. Is someone home due to personal circumstances? Have some flowers delivered. And has an employee been working exceptionally hard lately? Surprise them with a personal thank-you card and a treat-such as brownies or cupcakes sent by mail. Generously filled holiday gift baskets (with a personal message from immediate supervisors) or a year-end bonus are also ways to show your appreciation. The same goes for good employee benefits: at some companies, for example, employees can claim reimbursement for their gym membership or haircuts. Or consider providing a nice lunch at the office. A daily shared moment like that immediately boosts the atmosphere!  

Tip 5: Make assessments part of your hiring process

In fact, job satisfaction begins even before someone starts working. Because if there’s no good fit between you and your new employee, nobody will be happy. People perform better when they’re in the right role. That’s why you can incorporate assessments into the hiring process. Nowadays, we’re doing this more and more online-and with great success! By having candidates take an assessment, you gain an objective picture of their personality and qualities. With that information, you can better assess whether someone is a good fit for your organization. Ultimately, this leads to people enjoying their work more. Moreover, the results of assessments help candidates get to know themselves better. They can use the test results to further their professional development. And that, in turn, contributes to their job satisfaction.

Since August 2017, teachers in primary (PO), secondary (VO), and vocational secondary education (MBO) have been required to meet legally established competency requirements. These requirements lay the foundation for professional quality in education. They serve not only as guidelines for those who wish to become teachers, but also as a compass for experienced teachers who want to continue their professional development. The focus is on three pillars: subject matter, subject-specific teaching methods, and pedagogical practice.

A Solid Foundation for Quality in Education

The more stringent requirements clarify what is expected of a teacher. They have been translated into seven specific competencies:
  • Interpersonal competence
  • Pedagogical competence
  • Subject-matter and instructional competence
  • Organizational competence
  • Competent in collaborating with colleagues
  • Competent in collaborating with the community
  • Competent in reflection and professional development
These competencies apply to both teachers in training and teachers who have been teaching for years. In the latter case, we refer to “competency maintenance”: maintaining and further developing professional standards.

Self-analysis as a starting point for development

For teachers who want to improve-or who notice that certain skills are lagging-it’s important to start with an honest self-analysis. Where are the strengths? What still needs attention? Only once you have clarity about your own profile can you develop in a targeted way. A competency assessment is a powerful tool for this. With the Entrepreneurship Competence Framework, also known as EntreComp for short, the European Commission provides citizens with tools for developing entrepreneurial skills. As a competency model, EntreComp is widely applicable-for example, for identifying and developing your own entrepreneurial skills.

European Commission Maps Out Entrepreneurial Skills

In 2016, the European Commission introduced the new competency model, EntreComp. EntreComp offers everyone the opportunity to assess their entrepreneurial skills. The European Commission’s goal is for citizens to feel motivated, through the insights gained, to further develop these skills. This makes the competency model applicable not only in the informal learning environment-where lifelong learning takes place-but also in professional contexts. EntreComp is well-suited for gaining insight into and developing your entrepreneurial skills.

Context of the EntreComp Competency Model

The EntreComp competency model is the result of a study commissioned by the European Commission and conducted by the Joint Research Center. In 2006, the European Commission set a goal of promoting the knowledge society. To this end, eight competencies were formulated. The EntreComp competency model gives concrete form to the pursuit of a “sense of initiative and entrepreneurship,” making it applicable within both formal and non-formal settings. With EntreComp, the Commission has introduced a widely applicable assessment tool in the field of entrepreneurial skills. The competency model is currently one of the most popular frameworks for understanding and developing entrepreneurial skills.

The EntreComp Competency Model

The model consists of three competency areas and fifteen competencies, each listing the most important aspects. The three competency areas are “ideas and opportunities,” “resources,” and “taking action.” What makes this model unique is that the boundaries between the different competency areas and competencies are not strictly defined. The competency areas and competencies are so intertwined that it is possible to establish new connections on your own. The model not only provides insight but also offers a path to self-development as an entrepreneur. The focus here is primarily on changing behavior and developing your ability to take action, rather than on acquiring theoretical knowledge.   [caption id="attachment_10865" align="aligncenter" width="635"] source: https://ec.europa.eu/ [/caption]  

Entrepreneurship-Oriented Learning

Entrepreneurial skills can be developed by taking actions aimed at creating value for others. This involves not only bringing ideas to life and recognizing opportunities, but also the ability to create value for others in both complex and less complex situations. The EntreComp competency model maps the progression of this development across four levels, from basic to expert. Each level is further divided into sub-levels.

Four Levels of Entrepreneurship

The bottom rung of the ladder is marked by the basic level. At the basic level, individuals are able to create value for others with some outside assistance. By applying these skills with increasing independence, individuals reach an advanced level. Subsequently, by repeatedly translating ideas into concrete actions, individuals reach an advanced level of entrepreneurship. The highest level-that of the expert-is reached when actions consistently lead to above-average results.

Application of the EntreComp Competency Model

The European Commission has set itself the goal of ensuring that everyone, regardless of their role in society, can use the competency model to develop entrepreneurial skills. This aligns with the concept of lifelong learning, in which skills are acquired not only through knowledge but also through experience. Developing entrepreneurial skills is key to the development of a knowledge-based society. However, it is also an excellent model to apply within a context explicitly focused on improving entrepreneurial skills within a specific professional group. A professional learning environment is indispensable for entrepreneurs who wish to reach the expert level.

Entrepreneurial Skills for Employees

Entrepreneurial skills are not only a key competency for entrepreneurs; salaried employees who develop these competencies are also of great value within a company. For example, in numerous roles, the ability to turn ideas into value and to recognize and seize opportunities are indispensable skills. The EntreComp competency model is therefore used by many employers to assess employees’ entrepreneurial skills and develop a path to further develop these competencies. The EntreComp competency model thus serves as a guideline within the business community for employee coaching programs.

Widely Applicable

EntreComp is not only useful for assessing current entrepreneurial skills. As we mentioned earlier, it is also an excellent model for determining the learning curve. Furthermore, the EntreComp competency model is used as a guideline in the development of various courses and programs in the field of entrepreneurship-oriented learning. These courses, programs, and coaching programs are now available at the secondary and higher education levels, in both formal and non-formal settings. EntreComp has thus proven to be a widely applicable reference model for the further development of a high-level knowledge society.

Essential Professional Knowledge

The EntreComp competency model focuses primarily on the entrepreneur’s actions. Subject-specific knowledge remains somewhat underemphasized in this context. Nevertheless, we must not forget that one does not become a successful entrepreneur through behavioral change alone. Identifying opportunities and developing ideas also requires a certain degree of knowledge development. The ability to develop this knowledge and the ability to turn thoughts into action are not equally accessible to everyone. Unfortunately, developing strong entrepreneurial qualities is therefore not within everyone’s reach.
