You can then use this knowledge to further improve your entrepreneurial qualities. The Big Fifty Personality Test maps out your personality profile. You’ll also receive an indication of opportunities to further develop various competencies. The online 360-Degree Feedback assessment provides a concrete picture of your skills, competencies, and other entrepreneurship-related traits. Insight is the first step toward progress.

Improving teamwork means ensuring that all team members communicate better with one another. Teams that work well together perform up to 35% better than teams where collaboration is difficult. This happens because people can pool their talents and reinforce each other’s strengths.

What will you learn in this article?

This article covers the key elements for better teamwork: • Establishing clear communication that prevents misunderstandings • Building trust among team members • Clearly defining roles and responsibilities • Resolving conflicts constructively • Setting team goals that motivate everyone

Why Collaboration Often Goes Wrong in Teams

Teams don’t fail because of a lack of talent, but because of poor collaboration. The biggest problem arises when team members work at cross-purposes instead of with each other. This often happens because no one has taken the time to lay a solid foundation. Fictional example: A marketing team at a software company worked for months on a product launch. Everyone did their best, but the campaign flopped. It turned out later that the graphic designer thought the product was aimed at young people, while the copywriter was writing for professionals. The project leader had assumed that everyone had the same target audience in mind. Situations like these cost time, money, and cause frustration. They arise because teams skip the fundamentals of collaboration and jump right into the work. The good news is that you can prevent this.

The Foundation of Everything

Good communication is the backbone of every successful team. Without clear communication, misunderstandings, missed deadlines, and unnecessary work arise. Effective team communication goes beyond just talking; it’s about understanding and being understood.

Establish clear communication rules

Start by establishing communication guidelines that apply to everyone. Decide which communication channels to use and when. Use email for formal matters, chat for quick questions, and face-to-face conversations for important decisions. This clarity prevents confusion about where to find information. Also agree on response times. No one expects an immediate reply to every email, but they do expect clarity on when a response will be provided. Responding to emails within 24 hours and to urgent messages within 2 hours works well for many teams.

Listening Is More Important Than Talking

Active listening means truly paying attention to what a team member is saying, without already thinking about your response. Ask probing questions such as, “Can you give an example of that?” This shows interest and provides greater clarity. Regularly summarize what you’ve heard: “What I understand is that you think we need more time for the analysis because the data isn’t complete yet. Is that right?” This helps prevent misunderstandings and makes the other person feel heard.

Building Trust Among Team Members

Trust doesn’t happen on its own-it grows through consistent actions and transparent communication. Teams with high levels of mutual trust feel comfortable admitting mistakes, asking for help, and giving each other honest feedback. This leads to faster decision-making and better results.

Transparency builds trust

Share information openly with your team, even when the news isn’t always positive. Don’t hide behind vague statements; instead, explain what’s happening and why. A team leader who says, “The budget is being cut by 20% because sales figures are lower than expected,” builds more trust than someone who simply says, “We need to cut costs.” Admit when you’ve made a mistake. This might sound vulnerable, but it backfires. Team members respect leaders and colleagues who acknowledge their mistakes and learn from them. It also gives others the space to admit their own mistakes.

Keeping promises builds credibility

Only make commitments you can keep. It’s better to set a realistic deadline than an overly optimistic one you won’t meet. If you can’t deliver what you promised, communicate this as early as possible along with an alternative plan. Don’t overlook small promises either. Saying you’ll send a document on Monday and not doing so until Wednesday undermines your reliability. Team members will start to doubt your word when it comes to more important matters.

Clearly Define Roles and Responsibilities

Unclear roles lead to overlap, missed tasks, and frustration. Everyone needs to know exactly what is expected of them and where their responsibilities begin and end. This clarity prevents conflicts and ensures that all tasks are addressed.

Create a RACI matrix for each project

A RACI matrix shows who is Responsible (executing), Accountable (ultimately responsible), Consulted (consulted), and Informed (informed) for each task. This may sound formal, but it works exceptionally well for teams struggling with unclear responsibilities.
Task Responsible Accountable Consulted Informed
Create a content calendar Marketing Associate Marketing Manager Sales Manager Executive Management
Social media posts Content creator Marketing Associate - Marketing Manager
Campaign Results Data analyst Marketing Manager Marketing Associate Executive Management
This table prevents discussions about who does what and ensures that no one is left out.

Discuss overlapping responsibilities

Of course, some tasks fall between two roles. Discuss these situations openly with your team and establish clear agreements. Who takes the lead when a customer has a complaint that involves both sales and customer service? These conversations prevent conflicts down the line. Regularly review whether the division of roles still fits the current situation. Teams evolve and tasks shift. What made sense three months ago might not work anymore.

Resolving Conflicts Constructively

Conflicts are a natural part of teamwork and aren’t always a bad thing. They can lead to better ideas and stronger solutions. The problem arises when conflicts aren’t addressed or are resolved in a destructive way.

Address conflicts immediately

Don’t ignore conflicts in the hope that they’ll go away on their own. Minor irritations can escalate into major problems if they aren’t discussed. Speak with those involved individually and work together to find a solution that works for everyone. Focus on the behavior and the situation, not on the person. Say, “I’ve noticed that deadlines are regularly missed,” instead of, “You’re always late.” This makes the conversation less personal and increases the likelihood of a constructive solution.

Look for win-win solutions

The best conflict resolutions ensure that all parties are better off than before. This requires creativity and a willingness to look beyond the original positions. Ask, “What do you need to resolve this problem?” instead of insisting on one specific solution. A developer and a designer regularly had disagreements about the user interface. The developer wanted simple solutions that could be implemented quickly, while the designer aimed for visually appealing designs. The solution was to sit down together for an hour each week and align priorities before work began.

Shared Goals That Motivate the Team

Teams perform better when everyone is working toward the same goal. These goals must be specific, measurable, and relevant to all team members. Vague objectives such as “performing better” don’t motivate anyone.

SMART Goals for Teams

Formulate team goals according to the SMART criteria: Specific, Measurable, Acceptable, Realistic, and Time-bound. Instead of “generate more revenue,” use: “Increase monthly revenue from €50,000 to €60,000 within 6 months by acquiring new customers.” Involve all team members in setting goals. People are more motivated to achieve goals they’ve helped create. Ask for input and adjust goals based on feedback.

Celebrate successes together

Recognize the achievements of the team and individual members. This doesn’t have to involve big celebrations-sometimes a brief mention in the team meeting is enough. People want to feel appreciated for their contributions. Make successes visible to the entire team. A simple dashboard or a weekly update shows everyone how the team is progressing toward its goals. This transparency keeps motivation high.

Regular Evaluation and Improvement

Improving collaboration isn’t a one-time effort, but an ongoing process. Teams that regularly reflect on their work methods and are willing to make adjustments perform better than teams that cling to old habits.

Organize monthly retrospectives

Schedule a short retrospective each month where the team reflects on their collaboration. Discuss what went well, what could be improved, and what concrete steps you’ll take. Keep these meetings short-one hour is usually enough. Ask three simple questions: What should we keep doing? What should we stop doing? What should we start doing? These questions lead to concrete areas for improvement without endless discussions.

Track progress

Track how collaboration is improving using concrete metrics. These could include: the number of missed deadlines, time spent in meetings, or customer satisfaction scores. Numbers make improvement tangible and show whether your approach is working. Also, regularly ask team members for feedback on collaboration. A short survey or individual conversations provide valuable insights you might otherwise miss.

Frequently Asked Questions About Team Collaboration

How long does it take for collaboration to improve? You’ll often see initial improvements within 2-4 weeks after implementing new guidelines. Significant changes in team dynamics usually take 3-6 months. What if a team member isn’t willing to cooperate on improving teamwork? Talk to this person one-on-one to understand what’s going on. Sometimes there are underlying concerns that need to be addressed first before someone is open to change. Can collaboration improve in remote teams? Yes, remote teams can collaborate exceptionally well with the right tools and guidelines. However, it’s important to pay extra attention to communication and creating informal opportunities for interaction. How do you prevent improvements from fading away? Make new ways of working part of your standard processes. Regular evaluations and adjustments help maintain progress and build on it further. Improving collaboration in your team starts today. The quality of your service is reflected in every task your employees perform. Year-end reviews are the ideal time to look back and look ahead together. These reviews go beyond mere evaluation-they provide an opportunity for genuine dialogue about performance, ambitions, and well-being within the organization. A well-prepared year-end review helps determine the success of your business. It provides insight into employee performance and lays the foundation for future growth. But how can you turn this annual ritual into a valuable experience for both parties?

Conducting Effective Year-End Reviews

Many organizations traditionally evaluate their employees in December or January. This evaluation typically consists of a performance review, possibly supplemented by a formal assessment. The results can lead to important decisions regarding promotions, job changes, or development paths. Modern year-end reviews, however, go beyond simply looking back. They focus on development, growth, and mutual expectations. Proper preparation makes the difference between a mere formality and a valuable opportunity for growth. These five practical tips will help you transform year-end reviews into constructive dialogues that move both parties forward.

1. Start with self-reflection

A successful conversation starts with you. First, analyze your own performance as a manager before evaluating your employees. What successes have you achieved? Where did things not go as smoothly? This self-reflection helps you approach the conversation with an open mind and makes you more receptive to feedback from your employees. Take specific notes on your own strengths and areas for improvement. This preparation allows you to be authentic and vulnerable during the conversation, which enriches and deepens the dialogue.

2. Implement continuous 360-degree feedback

Don’t wait until the year-end review to share feedback. Foster a culture in which employees regularly seek and provide feedback-not only to you, but also to their colleagues. This 360-degree feedback approach ensures timely course corrections and prevents surprises during the year-end review. Continuous feedback makes the year-end review a natural continuation of previous conversations. Employees can adjust their work behavior along the way and grow throughout the year, rather than only after the annual review.
Discussion Topic Estimated Duration Focus
Opening & check-in 5-10 minutes Set the tone, align expectations
Reviewing performance 15-20 minutes Results, successes, learning moments
Development & growth 15-20 minutes Competencies, skills, ambitions
Goals for the coming year 10-15 minutes SMART goals, expectations
Agreements & Closing Remarks 5-10 minutes Specific next steps, planning

3. Support criticism with concrete examples

Vague criticism is demotivating. When discussing areas for improvement, illustrate them with specific situations and behaviors. Explain why certain behaviors impact the team or the organization. This specificity helps employees understand the feedback and actually act on it. Use the SBI method (Situation-Behavior-Impact) to clearly structure your feedback. This prevents misunderstandings and gives employees practical tools for improvement.

4. Build on previous agreements

Every year-end review has a context. Refer to reports from previous reviews and discuss progress on agreements made. This continuity demonstrates that you take agreements seriously and fosters a sense of accountability on both sides. Prepare by:
  • Reviewing previous meeting minutes
  • Taking stock of agreements made
  • Gathering concrete examples of progress
  • Identifying any obstacles

5. Foster a constructive dialogue

A successful year-end review is not a monologue but a dialogue. Start by acknowledging successes and strengths before moving on to areas for development. This positive approach fosters openness and trust. Ask open-ended questions that encourage reflection: “What are you most proud of this year?” and “What support do you need to achieve your goals?” This approach fosters ownership and engagement in one’s own development.

From Evaluation to Development

Modern year-end reviews are shifting from one-sided evaluations to collaborative development. They serve as a moment of connection in which the manager and employee jointly explore growth and potential. By carefully preparing for these conversations and approaching them with the right mindset, you can transform them from mandatory evaluations into valuable opportunities for growth. Invest in the quality of these conversations. They determine not only your employees’ motivation and performance, but also the culture and success of your entire organization. A good year-end review is an investment in the future of both the employee and the company.

For most companies, online assessments have become an indispensable part of the hiring process or a tool to support employee or team development. They can provide many valuable insights with a high degree of predictive accuracy. A careful approach yields the best results. What are the key considerations and success factors in this regard?

Why conduct an assessment?

An (online) assessment allows you to evaluate current employees or job candidates for traits that determine their success within the organization or their professional development. This may involve, for example, assessing motivations, competencies, intelligence, behavior, or personality traits. An assessment provides an objective picture of these factors and is valuable, for example, for follow-up discussions about the strengths and areas for development of employees or teams. This fosters employee growth and offers opportunities to engage and retain them or to work on, for example, job satisfaction or sustainable employability. In addition to supporting employee development or team-building efforts, the insights gained from assessments are, of course, valuable for hiring new staff. After all, recruiting, selecting, and onboarding a new employee is costly. That’s why you want to know as much as possible in advance about the likelihood of success.

Prevent “Bad Hires”

According to estimates, a “bad hire” costs at least 30 percent of the annual salary. And these failed matches occur regularly. At least three-quarters of organizations acknowledge this. According to reports, there are various underlying causes for this. For example, during a job interview, the focus was primarily on whether the candidate was a “nice person” rather than on their competencies, motivation, or driving factors (32% cite this as the cause). Or the person did not yet possess all the necessary skills, but it was assumed that he or she could learn them quickly (35%). And that is not always the case. Or perhaps the person’s skills were considered, but not their attitude (29%). Or worse yet: there were already warning signs, but they were simply ignored (25%). This is also a pitfall in an increasingly tight labor market. An assessment can prevent this and, moreover, offer many more benefits.

Benefits of Online Assessments

Assessments can be conducted in person, but these days they’re mostly held online. These online assessments (or e-assessments) save companies (and candidates!) a tremendous amount of time and money. It aligns well with the current culture of increased remote work and can significantly contribute to a positive “candidate experience,” serving as an introduction to your organization and helping to manage expectations. The use of objective assessment tools with a validated, high predictive value makes it possible to pre-screen (large groups of) applicants and increase their chances of success in the role. This also enables remote (pre)selection. You then interview only the most suitable candidates, saving a significant amount of time and money.

Convenience and time savings

Many types of tests and questionnaires are now readily available online and can therefore be completed at home or in another setting. This can also be a controlled environment when necessary. An online assessment can usually be administered more quickly, which can significantly shorten the turnaround time of a recruitment process. Furthermore, online assessments no longer require specialized experts, as was often the case in the past with offline, on-site assessments. As a result, assessments were used rather sparingly. Fortunately, these days the process is much more accessible and therefore more widely used. The results are also immediately available, making it easier to compare candidates’ performance. This can also help objectify the assessment of candidates. It prevents incorrect decisions caused by unconscious “biases” during the recruitment process. Consequently, it can also contribute to competency-based matching and to greater diversity and inclusivity in the workplace. Of course, an online portal can be available 24/7. This makes testing much easier anytime and anywhere. Online assessments are also ideal for generating conversation topics for candidates coming in for interviews. As a result, interviews can often delve deeper more quickly and in a targeted manner. This, too, yields more valuable insights about the candidates.

Success Factors for Online Assessments

An online assessment can include various components. Exactly which ones are used depends, of course, on an organization’s approach and its priorities. If an organization uses assessments frequently, a fixed base platform with multiple types of tests on a single online portal is recommended. We offer this with hrmforce for a broad suite of online assessments. This is useful if, for example, you want to use a Big Fifty personality test or a Motivator Test one time, while another time you need more insight into how quickly a person understands problems, forms an opinion, or is able to learn new things (Ability Scan). In addition to such assessments, an online intake can also be used to immediately clarify topics for an interview round. A prerequisite for using online assessments is, of course, that employees or candidates have access to a device that allows them to work online, but that’s rarely a problem these days. It is also quite possible these days to remotely verify that the person taking a test is indeed the person expected to be taking it. With certain tests, there is also a risk that participants will deliberately give incorrect answers to “do better” on the test-or to create an impression that makes them seem like a better fit for the organization. This can be effectively addressed by including smart verification questions in the test or by incorporating specific discussion topics into follow-up interviews.

Reliability of Online Assessments

Are online assessments just as reliable as traditional on-site assessments? A great deal of research has been conducted on this topic over the past 25 years. Conclusion: the value of an assessment does not depend on whether or not it is conducted online. The quality of the tests themselves is, of course, a determining factor. In addition, the context in which a test is taken can have an impact. If a candidate comes to take an assessment on-site but arrives completely stressed out due to traffic and has little time to adjust, this can negatively affect the test. And if someone takes a test remotely but experiences an unstable connection or noise from children at home, that will also have a negative impact. A test with a clear structure in a quiet testing environment always yields the best and most reliable results. A clear structure gives candidates confidence in an accurate result, which benefits the assessment results-including their reliability and the overall picture. Of course, hrmforce’s online assessments already take this into account.

Frequently Asked Questions About Online Assessments:

  • How can you ensure that online assessments are fair and unbiased in a diverse workplace?
    • It is helpful to regularly validate assessments and check them for cultural and language-related biases. Involving diverse panels during development and evaluation can also contribute to fairness.
 
  • What measures can be taken to ensure candidates’ confidentiality and data privacy during online assessments?
    • The use of encrypted platforms, access restrictions, and regular audits of security protocols are important steps to protect candidates’ privacy.
 
  • How can the results of online assessments be effectively used to promote employee development?
    • Results can be linked to personalized development plans, supplemented with targeted feedback sessions and training tailored to employees’ specific needs, as identified in the assessments.

Have you just taken a DISC test and are you now looking at a report with colors, graphs, and behavioral descriptions? If so, there’s one thing you want to know above all else: What does this really say about me? In this article, you’ll learn step by step how to interpret a DISC report, what high and low scores usually mean, how to translate your profile into workplace behavior, and which misconceptions you should avoid.

In short

  • A DISC report shows which behaviors you naturally tend to exhibit in your communication, pace, and approach to collaboration.
  • The letters D, I, S, and C aren’t about talent, IQ, or personal suitability, but about behavioral preferences.
  • It’s best to read your report as a whole. No single score tells the whole story-it’s the pattern that matters.
  • High scores often indicate what comes naturally. Lower scores, on the other hand, show what comes less naturally but is still possible.
  • Would you like to understand the basics of the four colors first? Then be sure to read our page explaining DISC colors.

What exactly is a DISC report?

A DISC report is the result of a behavioral analysis. The report shows which behaviors you typically display first when interacting with others, under pressure, when collaborating, and when achieving goals. So DISC doesn’t look at who you are deep down, but at observable behavior. That makes the model useful for work, communication, feedback, and collaboration. Haven’t taken the test yet, or would you like to receive a report that clearly explains what your profile means? Then you can take our DISC test right away.

Step 1. Look at the big picture first, not just a single score

Many people immediately make the mistake of focusing only on their highest color. That’s too simplistic. A DISC report works best when you look at the entire profile. Perhaps you score high on D and also fairly high on I. In that case, you often have a different behavioral pattern than someone with high D and high C. So your report isn’t just about your primary color, but about the combination of colors, the relative distances between them, and the strength of certain preferences.

Step 2. Understand what the four DISC colors mean

Before you read your own report, you need to know the basic language of DISC. In short, each color represents a different behavioral orientation:

D. Dominance

Focused on pace, results, making decisions, taking on challenges, and following through.

I. Influence

Focused on enthusiasm, connection, persuasion, energy, visibility, and bringing people along.

S. Steadiness

Focused on calm, collaboration, patience, reliability, support, and a steady rhythm.

C. Conscientiousness

Focused on thoroughness, analysis, structure, facts, agreements, and precision.

Want to dive deeper into this? Then be sure to read our comprehensive page on the meaning of DISC colors.

Step 3. See what high scores usually indicate

A high score usually means that certain behaviors feel quite natural to you. That doesn’t mean you’re like that all day long, but it does mean that this style often comes to the fore quickly, especially at work, in communication, or under pressure.
  • High D. You make decisions more quickly, enjoy a fast pace, and tend to be direct in your communication.
  • High I. You’re more likely to reach out to others, talk more easily, bring energy to situations, and often win others over to your ideas.
  • High S. You tend to exude calm, are patient, loyal, and a pleasure to work with in stable collaborations.
  • High C. You observe carefully, ask probing questions more readily, and want to clarify matters first.
Do you see two higher colors close together in your profile? This often results in a mixed profile. You might see this, for example, in someone who is both people-oriented and meticulous, or who thinks on their feet while also being strongly results-driven.

Step 4. Pay close attention to low scores as well

Low scores are often underestimated, even though they contain a great deal of valuable information. A lower score usually doesn’t mean you can’t do something. More often than not, it means this behavior comes less naturally, requires more energy, or isn’t your first instinct. For example, a lower D score might mean you’re less inclined to seek confrontation. A lower I score could indicate a more reserved communication style. A lower S-score is more common among people who get impatient with slowness or excessive repetition. A lower C-score may mean that you tend to be more pragmatic and don’t get bogged down in details for as long. It’s precisely these lower scores that help you understand why you’re immediately on the same page with one colleague but tend to miss each other’s mark with another.

Practical tip: Always read your report with this question in mind: “Which behaviors come easily to me, and which ones require a conscious effort to adjust?”

Step 5. Translate your profile into real-world behavior

A DISC report only becomes truly useful when you link it to specific situations. So don’t just ask yourself what your color is, but more importantly, how that manifests in your workday. Consider questions such as:
  • How do I react to pressure or deadlines?
  • How do I make decisions?
  • How do I give feedback?
  • How do I handle rules and agreements?
  • Where do I encounter friction when collaborating?
Someone with a more dominant style will often make decisions more quickly. Someone with a higher S or C score, on the other hand, tends to first consider support, risks, or due diligence. Neither is inherently better. The key is to learn to recognize your natural style and when it’s wise to adapt.

Step 6. See how your style comes across to others

This is one of the most valuable parts of a DISC report. It’s not just about your intention, but also about your impact. Perhaps you mean to be clear, while someone else perceives you as brusque. Maybe you see yourself as meticulous, while others interpret that as slow or critical. That’s why it’s wise to read your report from a collaborative perspective as well. How do others perceive your pace, tone, need for structure, or way of persuading? This helps not only in teams but also in conversations with candidates, clients, and managers. Want to better understand how colors complement each other-or, conversely, how they might clash? Then check out our page on which DISC colors go well together.

Step 7. Consider the context. You’re more than your DISC profile

A report shows behavioral preferences, not a fixed label. You may exhibit different behaviors at work than you do at home. Your role can also have a significant impact. A team leader often learns to use different behaviors than someone in a specialized role. That’s why you should never read a DISC report as a box you’re stuck in forever. The smartest way to use DISC is not to think, “That’s just the way I am,” but rather, “This is my natural starting point, and I know where I can make adjustments.”

Common Misinterpretations of a DISC Report

1. My dominant color represents my entire personality

No. Your profile shows a pattern. The combination of colors and the context make all the difference.

2. A low score means I’m bad at that

No. More often than not, it means this behavior comes less naturally. You can certainly demonstrate it when the situation calls for it.

3. DISC determines who is suitable for a position

Not on its own. DISC can help in discussions about behavior, collaboration, and role expectations, but you shouldn’t use it in isolation from experience, context, and job requirements. You can read more about this in “Using DISC in Recruitment and Selection.”

4. People with the same color are the same

No. Two people with high D scores can come across as completely different due to their varying secondary scores, work experience, and environment.

How can you use a DISC report effectively in the workplace or during the selection process?

A DISC report is particularly effective as a starting point for a conversation. You use it to clarify expectations, improve communication, and discuss together what naturally energizes someone. In the selection process, this can help you ask more targeted questions-not to pigeonhole someone, but to make their behavior more concrete. If you’re working with candidates or teams, it’s wise to always discuss a report in the context of real-life situations. So don’t just ask about the color-ask for examples. How does someone handle deadlines? How does someone respond to feedback? How does someone collaborate with someone who works at a different pace or has a different style?

Summary

The best way to read a DISC report is in seven steps. First, look at the big picture. Next, understand the four colors. Then, review your high and low scores. Translate those into observable behavior, pay attention to how you come across to others, and always take context into account. This way, a report becomes not a label, but a practical tool for self-insight, collaboration, and selection.

Discrimination in the labor market-whether conscious or unconscious-remains a persistent problem. Although there is an increasing focus on equal opportunity, statistics show that many job applicants are still treated unequally. In 2023, the government passed the Equal Opportunity in Recruitment and Selection Oversight Act. Since then, employers have been legally required to have policies in place to combat discriminatory practices. Questionnaires and objective tests can help make the selection process fairer. In this article, you’ll learn how this works and what benefits it brings.

Labor Market Discrimination in Numbers

According to the SER advisory report from 2023, job applicants with an immigrant background still have a significantly lower chance of receiving an interview invitation, even if they have the same resume as someone without an immigrant background. Recent research by the Ministry of Social Affairs and Employment shows that over 30% of job applicants with a non-Western background experience discrimination when looking for work. Research by RTL Nieuws and the Verwey-Jonker Institute (2023) again showed that people with Moroccan, Turkish, or Surinamese backgrounds, in particular, are less likely to be invited for a job interview. When combined with age, gender, and work history, this leads to exclusion, even if it is not always intentional.

What does the law say?

Article 1 of the Constitution prohibits discrimination. This is further elaborated in, among other laws, the General Equal Treatment Act (AWGB). The Equal Opportunity in Recruitment and Selection Supervision Act has been in effect since 2023. This law requires employers to have a procedure in place that explains how discrimination is prevented. Small employers must be able to explain verbally how they ensure equal opportunities; larger companies must document this in writing. The Dutch Labor Inspectorate monitors compliance and can impose sanctions. The measures are intended to change structural behavior, not just address individual incidents.

Conscious and Unconscious Discrimination

Discrimination is by no means always intentional. A job posting that calls for a “young, energetic colleague” excludes older applicants-even if age isn’t explicitly mentioned. Or consider asking for “accent-free Dutch,” which unintentionally excludes people with an immigrant background. According to the Netherlands Institute for Human Rights, employment and job application procedures are the most commonly reported areas of discrimination. Preventing this requires both awareness and action.

What can employers do?

There are three key steps employers can take to promote equal opportunities:
  • Create an inclusive work environment . As an organization, make it clear that discrimination will not be tolerated. Establish a code of conduct, appoint a confidential advisor, and ensure that managers lead by example.
 
  • Identify and address issues Be alert to signs of discrimination within the team. Take reports seriously and provide feedback on how they are being addressed. Only then will employees feel safe and heard.
 
  • Objective recruitment and selection Use standardized tests, screening questions, or online assessments during the hiring process. This prevents “gut feelings” from playing a role. Consider personality tests, motivation questionnaires, or cognitive assessments-all without names, ages, or photos.
 

Online Tests as a Tool

A good tool for making recruitment and selection more objective is the early use of online tests. At hrmforce, for example, you can use:
  • Big Fifty personality test—insight into behavioral preferences
  • Ability Scan—cognitive skills (abstract reasoning, numerical reasoning)
  • Motivation Test, what drives the candidate?
  • Leadership Test, potential for leadership roles
Based on predefined profiles (competency profiles, cultural fit), the system can automatically calculate how well a candidate fits. This prevents subjective judgments and ensures a fairer process.

Blind Applications: Do They Work?

In recent years, various municipalities have experimented with anonymous job applications. The results have been mixed. Some cities, such as The Hague, saw positive effects. Other municipalities, such as Utrecht and Nijmegen, discontinued the practice due to limited results or the feeling that the interaction had become impersonal. According to Professor Robert Dur (Erasmus University), the evidence from the Netherlands and abroad is mixed, but there are certainly situations in which anonymization helps-especially when it comes to the initial screening based on resumes. A combination of anonymous applications and objective testing appears to be the most effective in practice.

Fair selection within your organization?

Do you want to actively combat discrimination in your recruitment and selection process and be able to objectively justify why you do or do not invite someone for an interview? If so, there are various tools that can help you-without compromising on quality or speed. Contact us for a no-obligation introductory meeting. Our consultants would be happy to work with you to develop a fairer and more effective selection process.

The seven teaching competencies-also known as SBL competencies-were formulated by the Foundation for Professional Quality in Teaching (SBL for short) and incorporated into the Education Professions Act (BIO Act). By clearly defining these competencies, it becomes easier to measure and further develop them. This provides schools with a high-quality tool for recruiting, selecting, and helping their teachers develop. Hrmforce therefore uses these SBL competencies as the basis for its education-related assessments. This enables schools to efficiently and effectively recruit and select teachers who meet the established competency profile. Click here for more information about our assessment options in education.  

What has changed?

The main changes have been substantive improvements, making the competency requirements now unambiguous, concrete, and more easily assessable. The seven competencies are grouped under the main themes: subject-specific, subject-specific teaching, and pedagogical. This has increased their clarity. The competency requirements focus on student learning and the core of the teaching profession.

The SBL competencies are:

  1. Interpersonal Competence
  2. Pedagogically Competent
  3. Subject-Specific and Didactic Competence
  4. Organizational Competence
  5. Competent in Collaborating with Colleagues
  6. Competent in Collaborating with the Community
  7. Competent in Reflection and Professional Development
 

1. Interpersonal Competence

Creating a trusting atmosphere by interacting with students in a positive and open manner. Behaviors that may be associated with this:
  • treats students with respect
  • knows his or her boundaries
  • uses humor in situations and to resolve conflicts
  • showing personal commitment to students
 

2. Pedagogically competent

Provides students with guidance and structure in a safe work environment so they can develop socially, emotionally, and morally. Behaviors that may be associated with pedagogical competence:
  • encourages desirable behavior in students
  • teaches students to treat one another with respect
  • Encourages students to think critically about their views and to express them
  • values students’ contributions
 

3. Subject-matter and pedagogical competence

Helping students acquire the cultural and subject-specific knowledge necessary to function fully in society. Behaviors that may be associated with subject-specific and pedagogical competence:
  • can deliver the lesson material flawlessly
  • uses play as a learning tool
  • explains the lesson material clearly and concisely
  • clearly explains the learning objectives of an activity
 

4. Organizational Competence

Ensuring a well-organized, orderly, and task-oriented atmosphere in the learning environment. Behaviors that may be associated with organizational competence:

  • improvises in a professional manner
  • sets clear priorities
  • is able to maintain order
 

5. Competent in Collaborating with Colleagues

Making a professional contribution to a positive pedagogical and didactic environment, to effective collaboration among colleagues, and to effective school organization. Behaviors that may be associated with this:
  • asks colleagues for help
  • offers help to colleagues
  • exchanges information with colleagues on their own initiative
  • makes a constructive contribution to various forms of consultation
 

6. Competent in Collaborating with the Community

Ensuring effective communication and coordination with parents and other stakeholders involved in students’ education and development. Behaviors that may be associated with this:
  • actively seeks contact with parents and other stakeholders
  • explains his or her approach to parents and other stakeholders
  • Builds relationships with other educational institutions
  • adopts a constructive and open attitude in interactions with parents and other stakeholders
 

7. Competent in Reflection and Development

Regularly reflecting on and developing personal and professional competence. Behaviors that may be associated with the Reflection and Development competency:

The Employee Code of Conduct is one of the most important sections of your Employee Handbook. We have drafted a code of conduct to help you communicate your expectations to your employees in a clear and tactful manner. Please note that this template is not a legal document and may not take into account all relevant local and national laws. Therefore, ask your attorney to review the final policy document or handbook.

Code of Conduct for Employees

As an employee, you are responsible for behaving appropriately while at work. Here is an overview of our expectations. We cannot cover every possible scenario, but we trust that you will always use your best judgment. Please contact your manager or HR manager if you encounter any difficulties or have questions.

Dress Code

Our company’s official dress code is [Business / Business Casual / Smart Casual / Casual.] This includes [pants / shoes (loafers) / blouses / boots.] However, an employee’s position may also provide guidance regarding their attire. If you regularly meet with clients or prospects, please adopt a more formal dress style. We expect you to be well-groomed when you come to work and to avoid wearing unprofessional clothing (such as workout clothes). As long as you comply with our guidelines above, we have no specific expectations regarding the type of clothing and accessories you wear. We also allow various styles of grooming, clothing, and accessories related to religious beliefs, ethnicity, or a disability.

Cybersecurity and Digital Devices

This section covers all digital matters at work. We would like to establish a set of guidelines for the use of computers, phones, internet connections, and social media to ensure security and protect our assets.

Internet Use

Our business internet connection is primarily intended for business use. However, you may also use our connection occasionally for personal purposes, as long as it does not interfere with your responsibilities. We do expect you to temporarily stop any personal activities that slow down our internet connection (such as uploading photos) if we ask you to do so. You must not use our internet connection to:
  • Download or upload obscene, offensive, or illegal material.
  • Send confidential information to unauthorized recipients
  • Invasion of another person’s privacy and gaining access to sensitive information.
  • Download or upload illegal movies, music, material, or software.
  • Visit potentially dangerous websites that could compromise the security of our network and computers.
  • Engaging in unauthorized or illegal activities, such as hacking, fraud, and buying or selling illegal goods.

Cell Phones

We allow the use of cell phones at work, but we also want to ensure that these devices do not distract you from your work or cause a disturbance in our workplace. We therefore ask that you follow a few simple rules:
  • Use your cell phone in a way that benefits your work (business calls, productivity apps, calendars).
  • Keep personal calls brief and use an empty conference room or common area to make those calls so you don’t disturb your coworkers.
  • Avoid playing games on your phone or excessive texting.
  • Do not use your phone, for any reason, while driving a company vehicle.
  • Do not use your phone to record confidential information.
  • Do not download or upload inappropriate, illegal, or obscene material using our business internet connection.
  • Do not use your phone in areas where cell phone use is explicitly prohibited (for example, in laboratories).

Work Email

Email is essential to our work. You should therefore use your work email primarily for work-related purposes. We permit the use of your work email for certain types of personal communication.
  • Work-related use.
    • You may use your work email application without restrictions for work-related purposes. For example, you may subscribe to newsletters and online services that can help you perform your job or support your professional growth.
  • Personal use.
    • You may use your email application for personal reasons as long as you do so securely, do not send spam, and do not disclose confidential information. For example, you may send emails to friends and family members, and download e-books, manuals, and other safe documents for personal use.

Our General Expectations

Regardless of how you use your work email application, we expect you to avoid the following:
  • Signing up for illegal, untrustworthy, disrespectful, or suspicious websites and services.
  • Sending unauthorized marketing messages or emails.
  • Signing up for a competitor’s services, unless authorized.
  • Sending offensive or discriminatory messages and communications.
  • Spamming other people’s email inboxes, including those of your colleagues.
  • As a general rule: use strong passwords and be on the lookout for emails containing malware or phishing attempts. If you’re unsure whether an email you’ve received is safe, please contact our [Security Specialists.]

Social Media

We would like to provide you with practical advice to avoid careless use of social media in our workplaces. To that end, we focus on two types of social media use: the use of personal social media at work, and representing our company through social media.

Using Personal Social Media at Work

Access to your personal social media accounts is permitted at work, but we do expect you to act responsibly and in accordance with our policies, and to ensure that you remain productive. Specifically, we ask that you:
  • Self-discipline. Don’t let your social media platforms distract you from your work.
  • Make sure others know that your posts on your personal accounts are not made on behalf of our company. For example, use a disclaimer such as “the opinions expressed are my own.”
  • Avoid sharing intellectual property (such as trademarks) or confidential information. Consult with your manager or PR representative first before sharing company news that has not been officially announced.
  • Avoid defamatory, offensive, or derogatory comments. You may temporarily set aside our company’s anti-harassment policy if you wish to inform colleagues, customers, or partners of the existence of such posts for informational purposes.

Representing Our Company on Social Media

If you use our social media accounts or speak on behalf of our company, we expect you to protect our company’s image and reputation. Specifically, we ask that you:
  • Be respectful, polite, and patient.
  • Discuss matters outside your area of expertise as little as possible.
  • Follow our policies regarding confidentiality and data protection, and comply with the law regarding copyrights, trademarks, plagiarism, and fair use.
  • Consult with our [PR/Marketing Department] before sharing any important message with significant impact.
  • Do not delete or ignore comments without good reason.
  • Correct or remove potentially misleading or incorrect posts as soon as possible.

Conflict of Interest

When a conflict of interest arises, your personal goals are no longer aligned with your responsibilities to us. For example, if you own stock in one of our competitors, this constitutes a conflict of interest. You may also face ethical issues. Accepting bribes, for example, may provide you with financial gain, but it is illegal and violates our company’s code of ethical conduct. If we discover such behavior, you will lose your job and may face legal consequences. A conflict of interest is therefore a serious issue for all of us. We expect you to be vigilant and to identify circumstances that could cause a conflict of interest-both for yourself and for those around you. Follow our policy and always act in the best interests of our company. Do not let your personal or financial interests conflict with your work. If you encounter an ethical dilemma, discuss it with your manager or HR manager. We will always try to resolve the matter with you.

Relationships Among Employees

We want to ensure that relationships among employees are appropriate and harmonious. In this regard, we would like to draw your attention to our guidelines and ask that you always conduct yourself professionally.

Forming Friendships

Forming friendships refers to dating or becoming friends with your coworkers. In this policy, we define “dating” as mutual romantic and sexual relationships. Relationships that do not occur with mutual consent constitute sexual assault, which we explicitly prohibit.

Dating Colleagues

If you are dating a coworker, we expect you to remain professional at all times and keep personal discussions outside of our work environment.

Dating Managers

To prevent allegations of favoritism, abuse of authority, and sexual harassment, supervisors may not date their direct reports. This restriction applies to any manager in relation to a direct report. Even if you work as a contracted manager, you are not permitted to hire your partner for your team. You may refer them to a position on other teams or in other departments where you do not have managerial authority or responsibility for hiring staff.

Friendships at Work

Employees who work together are, of course, welcome to form friendships with one another, both at work and outside of work. We encourage these types of relationships among colleagues because they can be helpful in communication and collaboration. However, we do expect you to focus on your work and keep personal disputes out of the workplace.

Employment of Family Members

Anyone hired, transferred, or promoted by our company is selected solely on the basis of their skills, character, and work ethic. However, we do not tolerate nepotism, favoritism, or conflicts of interest and will therefore impose certain restrictions regarding the hiring of employees’ family members. For our company, “family member” is defined as anyone who is a relative by blood or marriage up to the third degree of an employee. This includes: parents, grandparents, parents-in-law, spouses, domestic partners, children, grandchildren, brothers, sisters, uncles, aunts, nephews, nieces, stepparents, stepchildren, and adopted children. As employees, family members are permitted to work for our company. These are the only restrictions:
  • [There must be no supervisory-subordinate working relationship between family members.]
  • [You may not be transferred, promoted, or hired by a family member if there is a direct chain of command.]
  • [You may not serve on a hiring committee where a family member is being considered for a position.]
  • If you find yourself in a manager-subordinate relationship after both of you have joined our company, we may need to [transfer one of you].

Visitors to the Workplace

If you wish to invite a visitor to our offices, please first request permission from our [HR Manager / Security Officer / Department Manager]. Also, notify our [reception / front office] of your visitor’s arrival. Visitors must sign in and provide identification. They will receive visitor badges and will be asked to return them to the [reception / front office] once their visit is complete. If you host visitors at the office, you also have responsibilities. You must:
  • Always keep an eye on your visitors (especially if they are minors).
  • Keep your visitors away from dangerous machinery, chemicals, confidential documents, or sensitive equipment.
  • Prevent your visitors from trying to proselytize your colleagues, asking for donations, or requesting that they participate in activities while on our premises.
Those delivering orders, mail, or packages for employees must not go beyond the reception area or the gate of our building. If you are expecting a delivery, [front office staff / security personnel] will let you know when you can pick it up.

Solicitation or Distribution

Solicitation is defined as any form of asking for money, support, or participation in connection with products, groups, organizations, or matters unrelated to our company (for example, missionary work and requests for signatures on petitions). Distribution is defined as the distribution of literature or materials for commercial or political purposes. We do not permit solicitation or distribution at our workplaces by non-employees. As an employee, you may only ask your coworkers for something if you:
  • Want help from coworkers in organizing events for another employee (for example, in connection with adoption, the birth of a child, a promotion, or retirement).
  • Are seeking support for a cause, a charity, or a fundraiser that is sponsored, funded, organized, or authorized by our company.
  • Want to invite coworkers to participate in employee activities for an authorized non-business purpose (e.g., recreation, volunteer work).
  • Want to ask colleagues to participate in work-related activities or groups that are protected by law (e.g., labor unions).
  • In all cases, however, we ask that you refrain from disturbing your colleagues or distracting them from their work.

Among all the leadership styles that exist-and their many hybrid forms-organizational leadership has been gaining significant ground in recent years. This is especially true among managers who have several years of experience and want to continue developing their skills. This can create a more pleasant work environment for organizations, teams, and individual employees, one in which they can perform better. Good self-awareness and a Leadership Operating System (LOS) make this leadership style particularly powerful.

Challenges in Leadership Development

Companies and the (work) environment in which they operate have become increasingly complex over the years. This is reflected in the areas of focus that managers at various organizational levels must address. These include operational processes, innovation, team development, networking, and, for example, sustainability or fostering individual career development. Given all these areas of focus and the critical importance of effective leadership, leadership development is becoming increasingly vital. After all, as a manager, you want to be sure you’re always making the right decisions. This is also reflected in the many leadership styles that exist. A modern manager often needs to be able to switch between them. At one moment, an authoritative approach may be needed, while the next moment calls for a more coaching-oriented or connecting style of leadership. This can be overwhelming-after all, when exactly do you choose which role to adopt? And don’t we sometimes make things too complex in organizations? The rise of organizational leadership is making the field a lot clearer again.

What is organizing leadership?

Organizational leadership is a management approach in which leaders help set strategic organizational goals while motivating teams and individual employees to successfully carry out tasks to achieve those goals. The “organizational leader” is strongly focused on the organization’s strategy and objectives, but also pays close attention to the specific skills and qualities that teams need in their work environment. This is quite a different approach from that of the more traditional functional manager. Compared to traditional management styles, organizational leadership is more people-oriented, aiming to achieve not only good results but also emotional well-being. In this way, it plays an important role in developing modern and healthy companies with engaged employees.

Characteristics of Organizing Leadership

Organizing leadership is important for modern companies because it helps ensure that work processes run smoothly. Coupled with its human-centered focus, this means, above all, taking a close look at the strengths, weaknesses, and areas for development of employees within the organization. Assessing competencies and areas for development is extremely valuable in this regard. In addition, organizing leadership skills have proven to be a powerful way to motivate employees by aligning them with a shared goal and through inclusive leadership. It also promotes performance and success by fostering a positive work environment with a strong focus on employee morale and motivation. These are many of the elements that modern organizations and their employees are seeking today. Key characteristics include:
  • Goal-oriented approach based on objectives and strategy
  • Leading teams with a strong focus on individual needs.
  • A strong focus on employee well-being.
  • Emphasis on (interdisciplinary) collaboration.
  • Focus on effective communication.
  • A culture of improvement and development.
  • Results-oriented work.
It is crucial to take a people-centered approach. Because to achieve strategic organizational goals, you must see the bigger picture, but also understand what steps are needed to bring about the desired changes.

Self-awareness as a major driver

Increasing self-awareness is a key driver for fostering organizational leadership. This applies to managers, but certainly also to other employees within the organization. It directly addresses important aspects such as a focus on development and individual needs, strengthening collaboration, and the importance of effective communication. The Big 50 personality test offers valuable insights in this regard. It is the most widely used (and researched) personality theory, and for most organizations, the Big 50 competencies serve as a perfect starting point for taking a more competency-based approach to the development of employees and managers. These insights are valuable for translating a personality profile into competencies (that can be further developed). To leverage this for organizational leadership, we at hrmforce have further expanded the personality test with the leadership report for organizational leadership. In this way, the Big 50 personality test continues to evolve to meet new needs.

Leadership Operating System (LOS)

In addition to greater self-awareness across different levels of the organization, a clear Leadership Operating System (LOS) can also significantly increase and accelerate the impact of organizational leadership. This is the framework of discussions, shared protocols, and communication and decision-making flows through which leaders steer the organization in the right direction. They own the system and determine the pace at which they “move forward.” They make the decisions and ensure clear communication, but above all, they create space for feedback and new ideas from within the organization. Many organizations crave this clarity and the ability to make clear choices in our increasingly complex world with all its challenges. Organizational leadership aligns with this approach and is reinforced by the LOS.

LOS: Benefits and Skills

A well-designed LOS reduces bureaucracy, increases decisiveness, improves communication, and accelerates goal-oriented actions. In this regard, organizing leadership and the LOS fit together just as a car actually needs a good (highway) road. The vision behind the Leadership Operating System shows how, as leaders reach higher levels, they do fewer things that directly lead to results and, indirectly, do more by guiding and supporting others to achieve the established objectives. This is a logical development in itself, but in the LOS vision, it is not only about having the right core competencies but, above all, about creating the right environment. Key skills for a LOS:
  • Developing leadership potential in others.
  • Communicating the organizational vision (including inspiring others to share the vision).
  • Identifying future innovations and opportunities.
  • Thinking strategically, broadly, and holistically.
  • Understanding the business environment.
In addition, these “soft” skills are also of great value:
  • Effective communication (especially listening).
  • Relationship-building and team-building.
  • Decision-making and problem-solving skills.
  • Integrity and ethics.
You can find more background information on the LOS in the book of the same name, *Leadership Operating System*.

Due to the COVID-19 crisis, remote recruitment has become increasingly common. And it’s here to stay, because digital recruitment offers all kinds of advantages. But how do you properly assess the person on the other side of the screen? In other words: how do you find the best candidate remotely? Those with office jobs have grown accustomed to working from home in recent years. But that doesn’t apply to all sectors: in healthcare, education, and the security industry, for example, working from home is often not an option. Healthcare professionals are needed in hospitals, nursing homes, and in the community; teachers are needed in the classroom; and security guards are needed at the locations where they’re hired. Although these professionals’ day-to-day work usually cannot be done remotely, recruiting new staff digitally is certainly possible. During the COVID-19 crisis, many organizations have already experimented extensively with this approach. And with success, because remote recruiting offers many advantages-even in these critical sectors.

Advantages

What are the benefits of digital recruitment? For starters, the recruitment process is much more efficient. Job interviews often involve at least three people-a manager or team leader, a recruiter, and, of course, the candidate. It’s easier to schedule a time when not everyone has to be in the same location. In addition, a job interview via Zoom or Teams saves all participants travel time. The interview itself is also often shorter and more to the point. As an employer, this allows you to interview more candidates in less time. A second advantage of remote recruitment is that you’re casting a wider net. With an online selection process, you also give candidates who live farther away the chance to apply. What’s more, you increase your chances of finding the right candidate. After all, as an HR manager, you know how difficult it is to find staff. That’s especially helpful in today’s tight labor market!

Fairer Assessments

Admittedly, digital job interviews often feel a bit more businesslike. The informal chit-chat before and after the official interview is shorter, simply because you’re not walking down the hall together or waiting for the elevator. But there are ways to address this. For example, start the conversation by telling the candidate a little about yourself, and take the time to put them at ease. You can explain how the interview will generally proceed. This way, the candidate will have a better idea of what to expect, which will make them feel more confident. A more “business-like” video call also has its advantages. More and more companies and organizations are using competency-based hiring: they assess candidates based on the skills they’re looking for in a role, rather than on the impression a candidate makes. This is easier with digital interviews, precisely because there’s less nonverbal communication. For example, only a small part of a person’s clothing is visible, and any personal chemistry you might have plays a lesser role. Prejudices-whether conscious or unconscious-therefore get in the way less during the selection process. That makes such a process fairer and more objective. Whether someone is a good fit for your organization depends on that person’s skills and competencies as well as your organizational culture. How do you, as professionals, typically work together, and does the candidate’s personality align with that? In digital recruitment, it’s important to try to make this as explicit as possible. You can also literally give candidates a sense of what it’s like to work for you. For example, with a short video about your company or organization in which colleagues talk about what they think of working there, what their day looks like, and what they believe are the defining characteristics of the organization’s culture.

Proper Preparation

Remote recruitment requires proper preparation from both parties, emphasizes recruitment expert Aaltje Vincent on a Dutch government website. Test your internet connection in advance and make sure you’re in a quiet place where people won’t just walk by or come in. Turn off your email program and other applications so the interview isn’t interrupted by distracting noises. And make sure you have a quiet background: a white wall is better than a cluttered bookshelf. Also, help candidates get started by emailing them in advance about the digital process. There’s a good chance they’ve never applied for a job this way before. So explain step-by-step how they can log in to the video meeting. Also give candidates the opportunity to test the technology beforehand. And tell them what to do if the connection drops-for example, provide the phone number of one of the participants so they can call someone. Some of these tips may sound a bit basic, but good preparation really is half the battle.

Collecting Objective Data

Want to screen candidates remotely even more effectively? Start the hiring process with a digital assessment. By having candidates complete such an assessment first, you can narrow down the field. You can then have more targeted conversations with the people who have the right competencies to work within your organization. A major advantage of assessments is that they provide objective data about a candidate. For example, you can measure how someone scores in terms of leadership qualities. In addition, assessments lead to greater diversity in the workplace, according to the daily newspaper NRC. “There’s no worse way to select someone than based on a resume and a job interview,” a recruitment specialist told the newspaper. “That tells you something about what someone has done, for how long, and for whom, but nothing about how well they performed their tasks or under what circumstances. Let alone whether it predicts how someone will perform a future assignment.”

Positive Candidate Experience

Assessments don’t just benefit you as an employer. They also contribute to a positive candidate experience. You’re signaling to a candidate that you genuinely want to get to know them and are willing to invest in that process. Have you found the right candidate? Then it’s time to meet in person. Your new employee can get to know you and your colleagues. And by then, you’ll be certain that this person isn’t just a good fit for your company-you’ll have concrete proof that it’s a great match. Digital assessments can be administered at various locations throughout the Netherlands. Candidates receive a warm welcome and personalized attention, so they feel completely at ease. Curious about the possibilities? Check out the Lamark or hrmforce websites and book an assessment right away.

This week’s HRMForce update takes a closer look at the “360-degree feedback” questionnaire. This questionnaire, which gathers feedback from others, is one of the four most commonly used tools on our portal, along with those assessing personality, intelligence, and motivators. Although the 360-degree feedback tool isn’t new, we’ve recently introduced customization options. Organizations can now customize all text within the questionnaire themselves, including introductions, explanations, emails, and closing messages. Many HR professionals are familiar with this scenario: a candidate makes a strong impression during the interview but performs differently than expected after being hired. An assessment during the hiring process helps you gain insight into a candidate’s potential, behavior, and capacity for development before hiring, so your selection is based on data rather than gut feeling.

In short

  • A pre-hire assessment predicts job performance better than an interview alone
  • The combination of ability, personality, and motivation provides the most reliable picture
  • Assessments measure potential, not just experience
  • Objective selection reduces mismatches and early turnover
  • Proper use requires interpretation and discussion, not just scores

 

What is a pre-employment assessment?

A job application assessment is a structured evaluation of traits that, taken together, indicate a candidate’s likelihood of success in a role. It’s not about what someone has done, but about what they are likely to demonstrate in terms of behavior, performance, and development. At its core, an assessment measures three dimensions:
  • cognitive ability
  • personality traits
  • motivation and drivers
Together, these layers form the foundation of workplace behavior. A resume describes the past. An assessment looks to the future. If you’d like to see how this works in practice, check out the page on online assessments .

Why is an assessment more reliable than a job interview?

Interviews are prone to bias. Sympathy, self-confidence, and communication style strongly influence judgment-often unconsciously. An assessment:
  • objectively compares candidates
  • looks beyond background or networks
  • highlights patterns in thinking and behavior
This results in a more realistic prediction of how a candidate will perform in practice.

What types of assessments are used in the hiring process?

Various types of assessments are conducted.

What does an aptitude test measure during a job application?

An aptitude test measures the ability to process new information, make connections, and solve problems. This ability determines how quickly someone learns and how they tackle complex tasks. Especially for positions with:
  • changing responsibilities
  • analytical challenges
  • independent decision-making
cognitive ability is a strong predictor of success. Important to know: It’s not about knowledge, but about thinking skills. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Xby8NLaqJEE

What does a personality assessment measure?

A personality assessment identifies behavioral tendencies. It shows how someone tends to act under normal circumstances and under pressure. Examples of what it reveals:
  • how someone collaborates
  • how someone handles responsibility
  • how someone responds to change
  • how someone makes decisions
The assessment does not judge right or wrong. It shows what likely comes naturally and what requires effort. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=lc7vN_e36Yc&t=7s

What does a motivation questionnaire measure?

Motivation determines why someone wants to exhibit certain behaviors. Two people with the same profile may perform differently due to differences in their motivations. A motivation questionnaire provides insight into:
  • what gives someone energy
  • when someone stays engaged
  • what demotivates someone
This helps predict whether someone is likely to commit to a role or organization over the long term. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tf8VEEDfruY

When should you use an assessment during the hiring process?

The right timing determines the value of the tool. In practice, there are three logical points:

1. After an initial screening

You use the assessment to objectively compare several suitable candidates.

2. Before the in-depth interview

The results provide input for targeted questions. You test assumptions rather than making them.

3. When you’re torn between candidates

The assessment helps reveal differences that don’t come to light during interviews. Important: Never use an assessment on its own. Its strength lies in combining it with the interview.

What does an assessment reveal-and what doesn’t it reveal?

An assessment tells you a lot, but not everything.

What an assessment does

  • provide insight into potential
  • highlight development potential
  • identify risks

What an assessment does not do

  • guarantee behavior
  • replace experience
  • Take the full context into account
That is why the conversation remains essential. The assessment guides the conversation, not the other way around.

How do you prevent misinterpretation of assessment results?

A common mistake is reading scores literally. This leads to hasty conclusions and unjustified rejections. Proper interpretation requires:
  • an understanding of norm groups
  • insight into the relationships between factors
  • a conversation with the candidate
A score is not a judgment. It is a hypothesis that you test through dialogue. For example, a lower score on a competency does not mean that someone is unable to demonstrate that behavior. It says something about how naturally that behavior comes to them.

How does an assessment contribute to objective selection?

Objective selection means evaluating candidates based on job-relevant criteria, not on personal preference. An assessment supports this by:
  • standardized measurement tools
  • equal starting points for every candidate
  • transparent decision-making
This reduces the risk of unconscious bias and strengthens the rationale behind decisions communicated to management and the candidate.

What does this mean for turnover and performance?

Mismatch is one of the main causes of early departure. Often, this mismatch arises not from a lack of ability, but from differences in expectations, work style, or motivation. By making more accurate predictions in advance:
  • the likelihood of a sustainable placement increases
  • the quality of onboarding improves
  • the risk of attrition within the first year decreases
Assessment data helps you not only select candidates but also provide targeted guidance after they start.

How do assessments fit within legal and privacy regulations?

Clear rules apply in the Netherlands. Key principles:
  • only assess what is job-relevant
  • Be transparent with the candidate
  • Do not retain data longer than necessary
Candidates must know:
  • why they are taking an assessment
  • what happens to the results
  • who has access to the results
Proper use strengthens trust in the selection process.

Frequently Asked Questions About Job Application Assessments

What exactly does a job application assessment measure? It measures potential based on ability, personality, and motivation-not just experience. How reliable are online assessments? When properly standardized and interpreted, they have high predictive value. Can you reject someone based on an assessment? Yes, provided the assessment is job-relevant and forms part of a broader decision. How long does an assessment take on average? That varies depending on the assessment’s structure. Often between 30 and 75 minutes. What if a candidate doesn’t recognize themselves in the results? Then that serves as a topic for discussion. The dialogue is part of the interpretation. Are assessments also suitable for rare profiles? Especially then. They help identify potential that isn’t evident on the resume. Can you share assessment results with the candidate? Yes. Many organizations do this during or after the interview.

In conclusion: How to Use Assessments Effectively

If you want to use assessments effectively in the hiring process, follow these steps:
  1. Determine in advance what success in the role means
  2. Choose tools that align with that
  3. Combine the results with a structured interview
  4. Use scores as a starting point for dialogue
  5. Incorporate assessment data even after the candidate starts work
This way, an assessment becomes not just a selection tool in and of itself, but a resource for better decisions and sustainable growth. If you want to quickly see which tools are right for your situation, check out the assessment overview.
