Conducting competency-based interviews and discussions with candidates or current employees is of great value to the success of organizations. This makes competency management tangible by clarifying which skills people already possess and which they can still develop. This enables targeted selection, coaching, and development discussions with staff. Above all, this requires clear competency-based language and a systematic approach to conducting interviews.  

Not Just for Hiring Interviews

In many organizations, competencies have now become the primary factor in hiring, helping to develop, and coaching employees. They form the basis of HRM systems and play a key role in employee recruitment, career progression, and turnover. Furthermore, managing and developing based on competencies helps organizations work in a more results-oriented manner, aligned with organizational goals. Consequently, HR professionals and managers today also want to conduct competency-based selection interviews, performance reviews, or coaching sessions, for example. When it comes to competency-based conversations, Recruitment & Selection is often the first thing that comes to mind. In this context, selection interviews using structured interviews provide insight into candidates’ competencies. But competency-based conversations are also extremely valuable when modernizing the conversation cycle with truly valuable performance reviews and coaching sessions aimed at employee development.  

A Unified Competency Language

An important tool for conducting effective competency-based conversations is a consistent set of competency terminology within the organization. This ensures that everyone speaks the same “language,” which prevents misunderstandings. A competency language clearly defines which definitions you use for the competencies-and the behaviors associated with them. Differences may exist between organizations in this regard; they may indeed use their own, distinct language. An organization can develop its own competency language or adopt one, as off-the-shelf options are also available. For example, users of HRMForce’s HRM software can simply use their own terminology and link it to the tools, but there is also a competency framework available that includes a comprehensive competency handbook. This framework encompasses approximately 50 competencies (based on the Big50) that make behavior measurable and discussable. For each competency, a definition is provided along with examples of behaviors at four levels (beginner, operational, tactical, and strategic). It also includes selection questions, development tips, and coaching advice. By describing competencies in concrete terms, it becomes easier to discuss competencies within your organization, for both managers and employees. There is also less confusion about the behaviors associated with specific competencies. This improves the ability to guide behavior. You can integrate your own competency language into your HR tools for, for example, Recruitment & Selection, the performance cycle, management development, and the training and development of employees. Watch a video explanation of both scenarios here: for organizations with or without an existing competency framework.  

Asking Questions in a Structured Manner

To work in a structured and as objective a manner as possible, the STARR method is often used (more on this later). This creates a systematic approach to interviewing. In this method, a candidate or participant is asked to describe specific behaviors from the (recent) past to substantiate his or her competencies. Numerous scientific studies have already shown that this approach has a higher predictive value than asking how someone thinks they will behave in a certain situation in the future. With this approach, you ask someone about various situations in the workplace and let them describe how they acted, what the outcome was, and what they learned. This provides insight into qualities such as results-orientation, adaptability, creativity, business acumen, flexibility, or innovative thinking. It all depends on what is important for your organization, the position in question, and the future.  

Big50 Competency Interview

To conduct competency-based interviews and discussions, you can use the many competency-based questionnaires available online for this purpose (such as this one). You can link the questions to the competency profiles that are important for your organization and roles. This allows you to have meaningful conversations with candidates or employees, but you can also take it a step further-for example, by incorporating the characteristics from the Big50 personality test into the discussion. This is certainly useful for career development or identifying high potentials. After all, an employee or manager can, in principle, develop any competency, but some skills are more difficult to develop than others. The more a competency is determined by attitude or personality traits, the harder it is to develop. Knowledge and skills, therefore, are easier to develop. Using scores from the Big50, you can focus specifically on competencies using the STARR technique. hrmforce also offers an interview guide for this purpose. The Big50 is valuable for translating a personality profile into competencies (that can be further developed). For each competency, an indication is provided of the extent to which an employee can develop that competency. This is based on personality and on the five key personality factors influencing behavior in work situations (Neuroticism, Extraversion, Openness, Conscientiousness, and Agreeableness).  

STARR as an Interview Guide

It is not always easy to remain objective when conducting selection or development interviews. The STARR method enables high-quality interviews that also provide as objective a picture as possible of a potential or current employee. This also makes it easier to compare different individuals. Many HR professionals use STARR as a tool and a type of interview guide to assess people’s experience and knowledge. STARR stands for Situation (what is the context), Task (what was the task), Action (what actions were taken), and Result (what was the outcome), often with an additional R for Reflection. It is important to ask follow-up questions on these points during the interview to gain a clear picture of the situation and how a candidate or employee would respond.  

Competency Profiles and Types of Competencies

A major advantage of the current focus on competencies is that these characteristics are objectively observable and assessable. This makes it easy to evaluate recognizable abilities and behaviors without resorting to in-depth psychological interpretations of behavior. Furthermore, this focus is practical because it links competencies to relevant and recognizable tasks or problem situations in the workplace. In principle, there are an infinite number of competencies. To keep them manageable, an organization selects the most important competencies for its own competency profiles, tailored to the various positions or roles within the organization. A competency profile often consists of six to eight competencies divided into four types (core competencies at the organizational level, departmental competencies, leadership competencies, and position- or role-specific competencies). For most organizations, the Big50 competencies are a perfect starting point.

With the growing tightness in the labor market and higher employee turnover at companies, employee retention has become a priority for organizations. It is incredibly important to an organization’s success, and turnover is costly: on average, 20% of a position’s annual salary. In addition to well-known key factors for retention-such as job satisfaction, development opportunities, and recognition—the personal needs of individual employees are particularly decisive in keeping them engaged. Various assessments help prevent employee turnover and keep employees engaged longer while increasing their job satisfaction.

Top Priority

With employee turnover reaching historically high levels, the focus on employee retention is growing. Having-and retaining-sufficient staff is becoming increasingly important for the success of organizations. Those who can recruit and retain the right people are already a significant step ahead of their competitors in this tight labor market. Research by TNO also shows that a good balance between technology, sustainable employability, and employee development leads to a 25% improvement in performance and a 35% increase in motivation within an organization. In addition, higher employee engagement results in an average reduction in employee turnover of 25% to 65%.

Costs of Employee Turnover

Employee turnover also costs organizations a great deal of money due to replacement costs and the loss of expertise. Replacing an employee costs an average of 20% of their annual salary. For positions requiring specialized skills, this cost can be significantly higher. When calculated for the healthcare sector, the average cost per departing employee is €41,000. This figure includes only recruitment, onboarding, and temporary loss of productivity.

Gaining Insight

If you want to retain employees for longer, you need to know what motivates them and what they need-as well as how engaged they are with your organization. A number of general, basic factors for job satisfaction and employee retention are well-known, but there can be significant differences depending on the organization, industry, and individual employee. For example, while a sense of purpose (including for gifted individuals) and meaningful work may play a key role in healthcare or education, in other sectors or organizations, the focus might be more on autonomy or recognition and appreciation. Retaining staff starts with understanding the factors that are most important to your employees. Currently, expected turnover-and which employees are at high risk of leaving (and why)—remains a major “black hole” for many organizations because their motivations and needs are often not made transparent.

Key Metrics

While organizations currently invest a great deal of time and money in attracting the right people, they should actually be paying more attention to retaining talent in the long term. Ideally, right from the moment new employees join the organization, thought should be given to the best ways to keep people with the organization for as long as possible. To gain a better understanding of turnover risks and identify concrete action steps to promote greater job satisfaction and employee retention, various measurement tools are available. Such as: ✅ Engagement Scan Measures how engaged employees are to identify the risks of turnover early on. This is part of the Motivator Test at hrmforce. ✅ Motivation and Drive Analysis The Motivational Test mentioned above also reveals what employees truly value in their work. What role do salary, personal recognition, and, for example, development opportunities play? ✅ Personality Analysis A personality test such as the Big50 Personality Test helps to better understand what energizes people and what drains them. Valuable for greater self-insight and job satisfaction, as well as for promoting employee retention and personal growth. ✅Employee Retention Indicator This is a specific analysis that can predict which employees are at an increased risk of leaving. Various hrmforce assessments can be used individually or in combination to gain a complete picture of the factors that influence employee turnover. This can also be done anonymously.

From Measurement to Action

With these insights, an organization can take steps to improve employee retention. This allows you to identify risks early on and intervene promptly. Furthermore, you can then have data-driven discussions within the organization and make targeted investments in retaining key talent. A proactive approach to retaining employees usually consists of a mix of strategies, naturally tailored to the needs of the employees in your own organization. This can start with a warm welcome and proper onboarding of new employees, while for many employees, development opportunities and a good work-life balance are important. For older employees, a slightly different role or approach may be needed to retain them and continue to make the most of their skills. Therefore, in addition to generic options, take a close look at the needs of individual employees.

Note: Recognition and Appreciation

In addition to individual and organization-specific retention factors, recent studies also reveal interesting trends to consider in advance when it comes to employee retention. One key area of focus, for example, is the recognition and personal appreciation that employees experience. An analysis of nearly 3,500 employees in 2024 revealed that employees who receive a high level of recognition are as much as 45% less likely to leave within two years (research by ). These employees are also 65% less likely to actively look for another job. This underscores the importance of targeted and sincere appreciation in retaining talent.

Other Factors

Furthermore, development opportunities, meaningful work, clear goals, and a safe and supportive work environment are among the frequently cited factors. Of course, competitive benefits can also play a role. Think of hybrid work arrangements, flexible work hours, or extra days off. These can be valuable tools for promoting job satisfaction and reducing turnover. Those who want to gain more insight into truly personal and organization-specific factors are best advised to start with assessments in the form of personal evaluations.

There are various personality tests in use. In particular, tests that are based, to a greater or lesser extent, on Dr. Carl Jung’s personality theory are gaining increasing popularity among managers and executives. Why are personality tests so popular? What does Jung’s personality theory entail? And how can you implement personality tests within your company? In this article, we’ll discuss all these aspects of personality testing.

Why use a personality test?

More and more companies are administering personality tests as part of their hiring process. Personality tests are designed to reveal the true character of a potential employee. After all, during a job interview, someone might present themselves as better than they really are. A personality test can reveal whether someone is actually suited for the position and whether they’re a good fit for the company. After all, a good match can reduce employee turnover and increase productivity.
Advantages of personality tests Possible disadvantages
Objective insights into candidate profiles Risk of labeling and bias
Better match between the role and the candidate’s personality Snapshot; personality can change
Enhanced team dynamics and collaboration Not always scientifically substantiated
Lower costs due to reduced employee turnover May limit diversity in teams

Jung’s theory of personality

Jung introduced his personality theory in his book *Psychological Types*. He bases this theory on four psychological functions: thinking and feeling (rational functions) and sensation and intuition (irrational functions). In addition, he distinguishes two fundamental life attitudes: introversion and extraversion. According to Jung, every person has a dominant life attitude and a primary function that define them as a specific personality type.

Jung’s Four Psychological Functions

Jung categorized the human psyche based on four fundamental functions that determine how we process information and make decisions:
Function Type Characteristics
Thinking Rational Logic, analysis, objective assessment
Feeling Rational Values, emotions, subjective assessment
Perception Irrational Sensory perception, concrete information
Intuition Irrational Possibilities, patterns, subconscious insights

The 8 Jungian personality types:

  1. The extroverted thinking type
  2. The Introverted Thinking Type
  3. The Extraverted Feeling Type
  4. The Introverted Feeling Type
  5. The Extraverted Sensing Type
  6. The Introverted Sensing Type
  7. The extroverted intuitive type
  8. The Introverted Intuitive Type

Practical Recognition of the 8 Jung Types

Each personality type has specific characteristics that are recognizable in everyday life and in the workplace:
Personality Type Core Characteristics Suitable for roles
Extraverted Thinking Type Practical, goal-oriented, organized Management, consulting, project management
Introverted Thinking Type Theoretical, reflective, in-depth Research, analysis, strategic planning
Extroverted Feeling Type Social, harmonious, empathetic HR, sales, customer service
Introverted Feeling Type Value-driven, loyal, caring Healthcare, nonprofit, coaching
Extraverted Sensing Type Action-oriented, flexible, hands-on Sales, marketing, event management
Introverted Sensing Type Practical, reliable, detail-oriented Administration, accounting, technology
Extroverted, intuitive type Innovative, inspiring, visionary Entrepreneurship, creative industries
Introverted Intuitive type Creative, independent, forward-thinking Design, writing, strategic consulting

Definitions

To understand personality theory, it is important to define the terms mentioned as Jung intended them.

Introvert versus Extrovert

According to Jung, an introvert focuses on their inner world of experience, whereas an extrovert’s outlook on life is more focused on the outside world.

The Thinking Type versus the Feeling Type

The thinking type acts based on reason, while the feeling type acts from the heart.

The Sensing Type versus the Intuitive Type

The sensing type is guided by external sensory stimuli, while the intuitive type is guided by indefinable feelings from within.

Common Misunderstandings About Jung’s Concepts

Jung’s terminology is often misinterpreted in modern personality tests. Here are the key differences between Jung’s original intent and contemporary interpretations:
Important: Jung’s introversion and extraversion are not about being shy or social, but about where a person draws their energy from and where they direct it. An introverted person can be very social, but draws energy from inner reflection.

Dominant life stance supported by a primary function

As mentioned above, the different life attitudes and functions can be viewed as opposites. According to Jung, one life attitude is always dominant. In addition, there is a primary function, secondary functions, and a lower, less developed function. Take, for example, the introverted thinking type. For this type, introversion is the dominant life stance, thinking is the primary function, sensation and intuition are the secondary functions, and feeling is the lower, underdeveloped function.

Jung’s Function Hierarchy System

Jung developed a complex system in which each person has a unique hierarchy of functions:
Function Level Role in Personality Degree of Development
Dominant Function Strongest point, natural preference Highly developed
Auxiliary function Supports the dominant function Moderately developed
Tertiary function Used less consciously Limitedly developed
Inferior function Weakest point, source of stress Underdeveloped

What does Jung think of personality tests?

Jung introduced his personality theory as a model for categorizing different individuals for the purpose of providing psychotherapy. It was never his intention to use his model to label people. If he knew that his theory was being used to categorize people based on simple questionnaires, he would not have agreed with that. Although he speaks of opposites in his theory, he did not believe that people always fall at the extreme left or right of the spectrum. Rather, the goal of psychotherapy is to find a harmonious balance between the various attitudes and functions.

Jung’s Warnings About the Use of His Theory

Carl Jung warned on several occasions against misinterpreting his work:
“It would be a great mistake to think that there are only as many psychological types as I have described. There are as many different types as there are people.”: Carl Jung

Is a personality test based on Jung’s theory right for your company?

There are various personality tests based, to a greater or lesser extent, on Jung’s ideas. You can choose from the Myers-Briggs Type Indicator, the Management Team Roles Indicator, the Type Dynamics Indicator, the Jungian Type Indicator, Insights Discovery, and the Golden Personality Type Profiler. The drawback of these tests is that they are based on a theory not intended for selecting employees based on their personality. The results are often snapshots that are useful for gaining some insight into the personality of (potential) employees, but they lack a scientific foundation. With such personality tests, you miss the mark when it comes to the purpose of administering a personality test.

Overview of Popular Jung-Based Tests

These tests are popular in corporate settings, but each has its own advantages and disadvantages:
Test Focus Scope of Application Scientific Basis
Myers-Briggs (MBTI) 16 personality types Team building, career counseling Limited
Insights Discovery Color Psychology Communication, Sales Moderate
DISC Assessment Behavioral Styles Leadership Development Moderate
Jungian Type Indicator Original Jungian Theory Psychotherapy, coaching Theoretical

The Big Five Personality Test: Highly Recommended

If you’d like to incorporate a personality test into your recruitment process for potential employees, it’s best to choose a professional and scientifically valid test such as the Big Five Personality Test. The Big Five Personality Test uses five dimensions to assess a person’s personality, namely:
  1. Extraversion/Introversion
  2. Agreeableness
  3. Conscientiousness
  4. Emotional Stability/Neuroticism
  5. Openness to Experience

Why the Big Five Is Superior to Jung-Based Tests

The scientific basis of the Big Five makes it a more reliable tool for personnel selection:
Aspect Jung-based tests Big Five
Scientific validation Limited research Extensively validated
Predictive value Low to moderate High for work performance
Cultural validity Western context Validated worldwide
Test-retest reliability Variable Highly consistent

Practical implementation of personality tests

For organizations looking to implement personality tests, these are the key considerations:
Step-by-step implementation plan:
Step 1: Define clear objectives for using the test Step 2: Choose a scientifically validated test such as the Big Five Step 3: Train HR staff to interpret results correctly Step 4: Integrate the test as part of a broader selection process Step 5: Regularly evaluate effectiveness and make adjustments as needed

Frequently Asked Questions

Can personality tests lead to discrimination? Yes, this risk exists. Tests can unintentionally disadvantage certain groups. That’s why it’s essential to use only validated tests and to combine the results with other selection criteria.
How often does a person’s personality change? Research shows that personality is relatively stable but can change due to life events and conscious development. Tests therefore provide a snapshot in time, not a lifelong prediction.
Can employers require personality tests? This depends on local legislation. In many countries, this is permitted, provided the test is relevant to the position and forms part of a fair selection process.
What is the difference between Jung’s types and modern assessments? Jung developed his theory for therapeutic purposes, not for personnel selection. Modern assessments such as the Big Five have been specifically developed and validated for organizational contexts.
Can Jung-based tests be useful for team development? These tests can offer valuable insights for team building and awareness, but use them as a supplement and not as the basis for important HR decisions.

Conclusion

Implementing a personality test in the selection process for potential employees can be an effective method for recruiting people who are a good fit for a position and within the company. A good match can reduce employee turnover and increase productivity.

Key Recommendations:

Opt for science: Use the Big Five Personality Test instead of Jung-based tests for HR decisions Combine methods: Use personality tests as part of a broader selection process Invest in training: Ensure HR staff know how to interpret results correctly Stay critical: Regularly evaluate the effectiveness of your assessment strategy
It is better to choose a scientifically validated test such as the Big Five Personality Test rather than a test based on Jung’s personality theory.

[caption id="attachment_22144" align="aligncenter" width="732"] Source: Elcovs[/caption] Giving a colleague feedback on their work style can be nerve-wracking and difficult. But it’s also an important part of professional collaboration. Fortunately, it doesn’t have to feel so “daunting” if you follow a few basic principles. That way, your feedback is more likely to be acted upon and can greatly contribute to personal growth, better team dynamics, and a positive work environment.

Why do we find it difficult to give feedback to colleagues?

Many people find it difficult to give feedback to others, especially in the workplace. Several factors can play a role here-from power dynamics or past disagreements to your own perspective on the situation. The work environment itself or the timing may also not be suitable for engaging in dialogue. Ideally, giving feedback isn’t a one-way street, but a dialogue that also involves listening. Remote collaboration can also make it more complicated to give each other feedback in a constructive way.

Defensive Triggers

One of the biggest barriers is that people are naturally inclined to react defensively to feedback, even when it’s well-intentioned. This certainly plays a role in the workplace, which often feels less safe than a conversation at the dining room table at home. According to Harvard Law School, people mainly go on the defensive because of three triggers:
  • Truth triggers: the feedback doesn’t align with your own perception or goals.
  • Relationship triggers: The recipient has issues with the person giving the feedback.
  • Identity triggers: the feedback affects a person’s self-esteem.
When people react defensively, there’s a greater chance that feedback won’t be taken seriously or may even backfire. It can even lead to conflict .

How can you give constructive feedback to colleagues?

To give a colleague constructive feedback in the right way and to facilitate this effectively within organizations, there are several key considerations. Pay particular attention to these ten points.

1. Create a safe environment

Before giving feedback, it’s important to create an environment where your colleague feels safe and valued. Choose a quiet moment when you can have the conversation together. This prevents your colleague from feeling attacked and promotes openness and honesty.

2. Focus on behavior, not personality

Over the past few decades, a great deal of scientific research has been conducted on giving feedback in the workplace. A key conclusion is that feedback is only effective when it’s focused on the task level (what someone should do). Avoid personal feedback (don’t say, “You’re unqualified”) and focus on the behavior and the task (“You could try…”). In other words: focus on the issue, not the person.

3. Be specific and clear

Be careful with overly general comments, such as: “You’re not doing well.” Be concrete and provide specific examples of behavior or situations that could be improved. For example: “During yesterday’s meeting, I noticed that you interrupted others several times. This made it difficult for others to make their point.”

4. Use “I” statements

By giving feedback in the “I” form, you prevent a colleague from feeling attacked. For example, say: “I noticed that the report wasn’t turned in on time, which affected my schedule,” instead of: “You always turn in your work late.” So keep it task-oriented and personal.

5. Make feedback a routine

Giving and receiving feedback can feel awkward at first. But together, you can make it a positive part of your work culture. By scheduling regular feedback sessions, giving and receiving feedback becomes the norm. This reduces stress and fosters collaboration on continuous improvement. Giving feedback no longer has to be “formal.” Organizations where feedback is regular, informal, and two-way perform better. Feedback must be embedded in the organizational culture, not just in annual performance reviews.

6. Consider 360-degree feedback (recommended)

Organizations that want to make constructive feedback a permanent part of their culture can use the 360-degree feedback methodology and the accompanying 360-degree feedback questionnaire or assessment. This is a powerful tool for better leveraging employees’ potential and improving their performance. In this process, employees’ performance is evaluated by multiple people with whom they interact-such as their manager and colleagues, or sometimes even customers or suppliers. This provides a broader perspective and aligns well with remote collaboration. This feedback method is extremely valuable for managers and employees because it provides a clear and accessible overview of individual performance. Together, they can review the results and identify valuable areas for development.

7. Avoid the “sandwich method”

To get off to a positive start and provide constructive feedback, it can be effective to first compliment someone, which conveys appreciation. But be careful not to sandwich areas for improvement between compliments-this can dilute the message. This is also known as the “sandwich method,” where the feedback is wrapped like a filling between two compliments (slices of bread). Be honest and direct, but remain respectful. This ensures clarity and prevents confusion.

8. Follow a feedback method

There are various conversation methods for giving others constructive feedback that is structured, effective, and respectful. Here are some well-known approaches:
  • Situation-Behavior-Impact: Describe the situation, the specific behavior, and its impact to your colleague. ​
  • I-I-You: Start with your own observation, share your feelings, and then ask for your colleague’s response. ​
  • 4 G’s: Behavior-Feeling-Consequence-Desired Outcome: Describe the behavior, your own feelings about it, the consequence, and what you’d like to see in the future. ​
Choose the approach that works best for you.

9. Listen actively and encourage dialogue

Ideally, feedback is not a one-way street. Give your colleague the space to respond and share his or her perspective. This promotes mutual understanding and can lead to joint solutions.

10. Show commitment and offer support

Giving feedback is only the first step. Offer your colleague support to help bring about the desired changes. This can be done in various ways, depending on their development needs. If relevant, it’s a good idea to schedule a follow-up meeting right during the conversation to discuss progress. This also demonstrates your commitment and provides an opportunity to offer further support. Bonus tip: podcast on giving and receiving feedback

Many companies want to modernize the performance review cycle with their employees. Traditional performance reviews, in particular, have become a “rut” and have proven ineffective for personal growth and team development. These reviews should be more flexible, simpler, and more tailored to individual needs. The desire and the will are there, but actually implementing the changes is often put off “for a little while.” This is mainly because HR, managers, and employees lack the right tool. A comprehensive online development environment offers a solution.

The old approach is pointless and demotivating

The old performance review and appraisal meetings no longer work. Numerous studies in recent years have already shown that the traditional “performance and appraisal” cycle is demotivating and even counterproductive. The Vrije Universiteit in Amsterdam conducted seven years of research on this topic. Key conclusion: both employees and managers find traditional performance reviews pointless-a waste of time and money. They also find them demotivating and unfair. The latter is because many other factors also play a role in the evaluation. In his book *Het Nieuwe Belonen* (*The New Way of Rewarding*), researcher Kilian Wawoe therefore advocates for the abolition of the “performance review.” And he advocates for a better, more modern cycle of conversations: more effective, fairer, smoother, with two-way dialogue, and-ideally-more continuous communication between manager and employee.

A Source of Frustration in the Modern Workplace

Many companies do want to make the transition, but they often keep putting it off “for just one more year.” After all, how do you actually make the transition? And they often still view the lack of the right tools as a “barrier.” So, just to be safe, they prefer to stick with the old system “for a little while longer” because it’s transparent and everyone is familiar with it. Much to the frustration of both employees and managers. Because the old performance review cycle-which has been around for decades-is truly no longer sustainable, says development expert and educational specialist Annet van Duren. “The traditional performance review cycle is actually always a disappointment. Employees experience it more as a judgmental review and return to work demotivated.” She also advocates for a modern performance review cycle based on development-oriented conversations. The old, traditional approach is also no longer suited to today’s faster-paced and more flexible work environment. Often, goals are set in January so that by December, an employee’s performance can be evaluated to see if they’ve met them. This approach fails to take into account the challenges and complexity of the work. As a result, the goals are often already outdated by February or March.

More Frequent, Brief Check-ins

In a modern review cycle free from the old routine of mandatory performance reviews, employees can also take on a greater role-both within the evaluation system and in steering their own development, as expert Jacco van den Berg advocates in his book *Het Nieuwe Beoordelen*. “Let them contribute ideas about their own development. When setting goals, you can ask what contribution they themselves think they’ll make during the upcoming performance period.” This can happen, for example, during a planning meeting at the start of the year, but also at other times. The author also advocates for more frequent performance review opportunities. “A continuous dialogue is better. Don’t just go through that mandatory ritual once a year; instead, have regular, short, and impactful conversations in which you look ahead. It’s, of course, very strange that an employee only finds out after six months or a year that something isn’t going well. If you have more frequent brief conversations about someone’s role, they can improve more quickly.” As part of modernizing the performance evaluation and feedback cycle, many organizations are focusing on more ongoing coaching of employees, with motivational and goal-oriented feedback to support their development. So not because of a performance review required by “the boss,” but driven by intrinsic motivation: because employees want it themselves and also see its value firsthand.

A Single Flexible Development Platform

This desired, more contemporary approach does, however, require a new “development system” that effectively facilitates the intended simplicity, flexibility, and personalized customization. Ideally, a single platform where all actions, documents, performance data, and reports are clearly consolidated. And, if possible, with an online dashboard that provides (real-time) insight into the performance of employees and the organization. Modern online tools make this possible, such as Hrmforce Development. This serves as a single, comprehensive, and efficient solution for facilitating individual and team development and (team) performance. It offers a complete set of tools for HRM, managers, and employees, enabling them to design a customized development process. Users utilize this to manage (mid-year) evaluations and other meetings, and, for example, to work with competency models. They can use it to generate individual development plans, analyze strengths and weaknesses, or organize 90- or 360-degree feedback, for example. With such a comprehensive environment, the “lack of a technical tool” no longer needs to be an obstacle.

Breaking New Ground

With this approach, organizations can truly explore new avenues with their performance cycle and appraisal interviews. It also opens new doors for the organization, employees, and managers. It then becomes primarily a matter of choosing how to implement the new approach. This can be done in phases by starting simple. Over time, additional features can be added. This, of course, depends on your organizational goals and developments. You can also go quite “far” with this. A great example is the IT company Computest. This self-managing organization, with about a hundred employees, moved away from traditional performance reviews. Here, colleagues within the various teams began evaluating one another. The organization conducted its own research into how its employees best give and receive feedback from one another. During one-on-one meetings, people tended to get nervous more quickly and would often become defensive when receiving negative feedback. “A conversation with a colleague gives you more breathing room to say what you really think. We also focus on what’s going well and what we appreciate about each other-something you don’t usually do on a daily basis,” explained Computest founder Hartger Ruijs.

Involving Clients in Employee Evaluations

Those who want to take it a step further can also give customers a role in evaluating employees, as is often done in 360-degree feedback. The Brabant-based engineering firm Coenradie went one step further and linked employee performance directly to customer satisfaction. At this firm, fifty employees around the world provide measurement solutions across various sectors. Measuring their own customer satisfaction ensures that service delivery can be continuously optimized. The results are shared internally, but in a casual manner and based on team performance. The findings are displayed internally in real time and uncensored on the homepage of the intranet. If a customer wishes, this can be done with the sender present. Employees can respond to the feedback internally. And if necessary, they contact the customer directly. This increases customer satisfaction, and employees receive a bonus every time a customer gives a rating of 10. And that’s happening more and more often. “The average customer rating also increases over time. We now know how satisfied customers are with each project-and why. If necessary, we can take immediate action, and customers appreciate that,” says Director Wouter Coenradie. Of course, as an organization, you don’t have to go that far. Above all, a modern feedback cycle must be supported by a platform that facilitates the desired flexibility and customization around the conversations-especially as these increasingly take the form of shorter coaching sessions.

Many organizations use the Big Five personality model to gain a clear understanding of their employees’ personality traits. For example, this is done during the recruitment and selection of candidates, but also in talent and team development or when coaching current staff. This model has been practically translated into competencies in the well-known Big Five personality test, but its foundation consists of five main dimensions. But what do abstract concepts such as “extraversion,” “neuroticism,” and “conscientiousness” actually mean in practice?

The Core of the Big 5 Personality Traits

The Big Five personality model is one of the most widely accepted and scientifically grounded psychological models. Its foundations were laid as early as the 1930s. It wasn’t until the 1980s and 1990s that it was fully developed and gained widespread acceptance. At the heart of the model are five main dimensions:
  1. Openness to Experience
  2. Conscientiousness
  3. Extraversion
  4. Agreeableness
  5. Neuroticism
The traits measured in a personality test are reflected in the test results on a scale. A “high or low” score isn’t positive or negative, but indicates a different personality type. This is a valuable indicator to consider in the personal and professional development of employees.

What do these traits mean in practice?

In this article, we’ll take a closer look at the five fundamental traits with practical examples of how you might encounter them in everyday life. Each example will feature someone who scores “higher” and someone who scores “lower.”

1. Openness to Experience

This trait describes the extent to which someone is open to change and new experiences . It also reflects the extent to which someone has a variety of interests. People who score high are often imaginative, curious , and appreciate art and innovation . People with a low score tend to be more practical, value traditions, and prefer predictability. Example: Lisa is a fashion designer who enjoys experimenting with new techniques and styles. She travels regularly to find inspiration for her work. Her colleague Mark prefers routine and feels most comfortable in familiar situations and structures. He prefers reading nonfiction books over fiction and likes to choose vacation destinations he already knows.

2. Conscientiousness

This refers to the extent to which someone is organized , goal-oriented , and reliable . People who score high on this trait are often meticulous , disciplined , and plan ahead. Those with a low score, on the other hand, are often more spontaneous and less structured in their approach. Example: Project manager Emma likes to follow her work schedule meticulously. She creates detailed plans and keeps her to-do lists neatly organized. Her colleague Tom, on the other hand, is a last-minute worker who regularly procrastinates and often doesn’t start working on his projects until later. He needs those deadlines to perform well. https://nl.pinterest.com/pin/711428072366234320/

3. Extraversion

This describes how sociable and energetic a person is. Extroverts draw energy from social interactions and are often talkative and assertive . Introverts feel more comfortable in a quieter environment and gain energy from solitary activities and introspection. Example: Things are always lively around account manager David. He loves to network, makes friends easily, and feels most at ease in a large group. His colleague Sophie is the opposite. She prefers to work in silence and would rather read a good book than attend a busy social gathering.

4. Friendliness

This isn’t such an abstract concept, but it does mean more than just being “nice.” It indicates how accommodating , empathetic , and helpful someone is. People with a high score are often seen as warm , caring, and cooperative . People with a low score tend to be more competitive or may be more critical or skeptical. Example: Anna is always willing to help others. She often offers to support her coworkers and believes it’s important for everyone to feel appreciated. Her coworker Michael, on the other hand, is primarily focused on his own success and considers it less important to take others’ feelings into account.

5. Neuroticism

This trait refers to a person’s emotional stability . People who score high experience stress, anxiety, and negative emotions more frequently. Those with a low score are generally calm, resilient, and emotionally stable. Example: Peter often worries about his work and overthinks minor details. He tends to find stressful situations overwhelming. His colleague Shirley usually remains calm, even in challenging circumstances. She handles setbacks well.

Conclusion and Further Information

The Big Five personality traits are a valuable guide for better understanding human behavior and individual differences. The model helps people better understand themselves and others and interact more effectively with others. In a Big50 Personality Test report, a person’s personality profile is translated into competencies (as a combination of knowledge, skills, and behavior). This is important for gaining insight into and managing personality traits and an individual’s skills. For each competency, an indication is provided of the extent to which an employee can develop that competency, based on their personality. The Big50 Personality Test is valuable for using objective data in employee development. It is the most widely used and researched personality theory for this purpose. Management Team Development Needs

The composition and functioning of an executive or management team (MT) directly influence the success of organizations. This influence can be positive or negative. After all, important decisions are naturally made at this team and organizational level. And this is where the impact on the entire organization begins. By first assessing the development needs of MT members through short online tests, they can receive targeted learning support. And as recent research from Harvard shows, even a small learning intervention can actually make a big difference.

Essential, yet underestimated

“As the executive team fares, so does the organization,” goes an old organizational adage. This speaks volumes about the importance of having the right composition for this team-especially now that more and more is expected of management, including in the area of modern leadership. In addition to the great importance of team development for the entire organization-now a top priority at many organizations-the appreciation for the value of team development at the “top” is also growing. And yet, this is still regularly overlooked with relative ease. At the root of this lies a deceptive pitfall: the assumption that simply bringing together a good group of managers automatically results in a well-functioning management team. Unfortunately, it’s not that simple. Many international studies show that management teams too often consist of people who possess only some of the required personal qualities (and often the same ones). And that’s not even mentioning the level of collaboration that team members establish with one another. And that, too, has a direct impact on the entire organization.

Management or TEAM?

When there is a group of “good leaders for each business unit,” but their collective performance falls short, this can lead to slow decision-making, “endless discussions,” energy “draining away” during meetings, or, for example, poor collaboration in execution. The challenge, therefore, is to ensure a true management TEAM. This begins even before the actual team is formed. After all, what should the team look like? What qualities and competencies are needed? These are important considerations that you can address in a targeted manner, for example, following brief online assessments. And once the team has been formed, ongoing maintenance and development are also necessary. Just as the organization continues to evolve, so do the demands placed on management team members. Common pitfalls include members not viewing their team role as a formal position or failing to develop (quickly) enough, even when organizational changes demand it. In practice, it often happens that management team members remain primarily focused on the division or department they lead. The MT is then seen as something that’s “on top of” their other responsibilities. Or, once at the top, members may invest less in their own development. Yet it is precisely at this stage that additional skills are needed compared to their previous role. And especially during periods of growth or organizational change, it is important to continue developing leadership competencies.

Where do you start with development?

But where do you start when it comes to maintaining and developing an MT? Team development always proceeds in phases. A goal-oriented approach first requires an understanding of the full range of desired qualities. This applies to personal qualities as well as the extent to which team members complement one another. Next, you can use short online assessments for each team member to identify which qualities are already present and which could be further developed. A brief 15-minute assessment can often go a long way toward boosting self-awareness and self-insight in this area. This allows you to select the right development tools in a targeted manner-such as training, e-learning courses, or coaching.

Measuring and Testing in Practice

Fortunately, using team development and personal development in a targeted way is now easily accessible thanks to the various online tests and assessments available. Take Hrmforce Analytics, for example, which provides organizations with detailed insights into the talents, pitfalls, and performance of employees or teams. To do this, it integrates data from multiple sources and channels. With this growing insight, you can, for example, identify success factors and competencies, monitor the development of teams or team members, and increase their self-awareness. In addition to this comprehensive analysis tool, you can also use very short tests to measure specific traits or competencies. Take, for example, the Communication Styles test, which is widely used in team development. After an assessment lasting about 15 minutes, it immediately becomes clear which communication style(s) a participant prefers (out of a total of 8 communication styles). You can also do this with, for example, the Conflict Styles Test, which analyzes individual behavior in conflict situations and provides insight into the extent to which certain conflict styles are valuable. This test also takes a participant about 15 minutes to complete. And, of course, there are many other short or more comprehensive test formats available.

Goal-Oriented Growth

After the assessment, development goals-depending on the results-may focus on collaboration, communication, leadership skills, or, for example, personal leadership. In addition to increasing self-awareness, the results can also provide a better understanding of the entire management team or of other colleagues. After all, what is that other management team member’s natural leadership style? And which of their qualities can you effectively leverage in your collaboration? And who would be the best person to bounce ideas off of regarding that new, challenging project, to complement your own strengths? These can be extremely valuable questions and insights.

New Insights for Team Development

Insights into team performance-including at the executive team level-are also growing. In scientific research on team performance based on “serious gaming” using an escape room (by Friesland Boeit), team performance was examined at the competency level, with a strong focus on leadership. “In today’s rapidly changing world and economy, leadership and collaboration are currently crucial areas of focus,” says leadership expert Jelle Dijkstra (lecturer in Personal Leadership & Innovation at NHL University of Applied Sciences), who was involved in the study. But these often still turn out to be the weak points. “Organizations are going to ‘work differently’ and ‘collaborate differently,’ but how exactly? That question often remains unanswered.” And to measure is to know. This provides tools for a targeted and efficient approach. Another notable conclusion from years of research in the escape room is that the most successful teams have two leaders: a dominant leader and a social leader. “They must be able to take turns and switch flexibly between different leadership styles, depending on their team, the environment, and the task,” says Dijkstra.

Small interventions: big impact

Another interesting finding is that small (targeted) interventions for managers can make a big difference. For example, even a short training session can help them make significant strides, as confirmed by recent research from Harvard Business School. This specific study focused primarily on communication styles and examined how managers can improve them to foster high-quality collaboration. The researchers found that just five minutes of training in receptive communication techniques can already have a significant effect. There is often much to be gained in this area. “Leaders tend to dominate conversations: they don’t listen well and shut out others’ ideas,” says researcher Francesca Gino (Professor of Business Administration). “As a result, the other members of the team are often too anxious or simply too bored and distant to actively contribute their own ideas.” She also outlines five key elements for fostering greater receptiveness. Of course, whether this theme is actually relevant to a specific executive or management team must first be determined through assessments. But let the conclusion of this Harvard study serve as encouragement to start by testing it as a starting point for the development of a management team. Once you know where the major needs lie, self-awareness and a little developmental support are enough to take significant steps forward for the entire organization.

The performance review is a crucial moment in an employee’s development cycle. It provides an opportunity to make timely adjustments, celebrate successes, and remove obstacles. A well-conducted performance review motivates, inspires, and leads to better performance. This article offers practical tips for effective performance reviews that truly add value.

What is a performance review?

A progress review is a structured dialogue between a manager and an employee about progress toward agreed-upon goals. It differs from a performance review in that the focus is on development and course correction, not on a final assessment. These meetings take place several times a year and serve as the link between planning meetings and the year-end evaluation.
Type of meeting Frequency Focus Duration
Planning meeting Annual Setting Goals 60-90 min
Progress Meeting Quarterly Development & Course Correction 30-45 min
Check-in Monthly Brief update 15-20 min
Performance Review Annual Evaluation & Appraisal 60 min

1. Create an equal dialogue

Successful progress reviews are characterized by mutual respect and openness. Position the conversation as a joint exploration of possibilities, not as a one-sided evaluation. Practical tips for creating an equal dialogue:
  • Start with an open-ended question: “How do you feel about your progress?”
  • Actively ask for feedback on your role as a manager
  • Discuss obstacles without immediately proposing solutions
  • Agree jointly on next steps

2. Maintain an effective frequency of conversations

Annual reviews fall short in our dynamic work environment. Modern organizations maintain a continuous dialogue with formal checkpoints.

Recommended meeting cycle:

  • Weekly: Brief operational coordination (5-10 min)
  • Monthly: Check-in on well-being and priorities (15-20 min)
  • Quarterly: Formal progress review (30-45 min)
  • Annually: Planning and performance review (60-90 min)
This frequency prevents surprises and allows for timely course corrections. Employees feel heard and can proactively ask for support.

3. Focus on strengths and talents

Research shows that focusing on strengths leads to up to 6 times higher engagement. Therefore, spend at least 60% of the meeting time discussing what’s going well. Practical approach:
  • Always start with successes and positive developments
  • Analyze together what made these successes possible
  • Explore how strengths can be leveraged to address challenges
  • Celebrate milestones achieved, no matter how small

4. Structure the conversation effectively

A good structure ensures both depth and efficiency. Use this framework:
Phase Content Sample Questions
Opening (5 min) Set the tone, share the agenda "How are you?" "What would you like to discuss?"
Review (10 min) Results, successes, challenges "What are you proud of?" "What went differently than expected?"
Analysis (15 min) Delving deeper into progress "What helped you?" "What obstacles are you facing?"
Looking Ahead (10 min) Plans, priorities, support "What do you need?" "How can I better support you?"
Wrap-up (5 min) Agreements, next steps "What are you taking away from this?" "When will we talk again?"
 

5. Make progress measurable and visible

Vague objectives lead to vague conversations. Use SMART goals and visualize progress for concrete, motivating conversations. Tools for visualizing progress:
  • Development matrices by competency
  • Progress bars for projects
  • 360-degree feedback results
  • Personal growth curves

6. Digitize for efficiency and insight

Modern HR software transforms performance reviews from an administrative burden into a strategic tool. Digital tools provide real-time insights and streamline the entire process.

Benefits of digitization:

  • Automatic reminders for meetings
  • Centralized storage of appointments and notes
  • Trend analyses across multiple periods
  • Integration with development goals and KPIs
  • Self-service for employees

Common pitfalls (and how to avoid them)

Pitfall Solution
Meetings get postponed when things get busy Block out specific times in calendars
Focus is on problems Always start with successes
No specific follow-up actions End with SMART agreements
One-way communication Ask 70% open-ended questions
Lack of preparation Use preparation forms

By investing in frequent, structured, and collaborative reviews, you create a culture of continuous development. hrmforce Development supports this process with smart digital tools. From automated review scheduling to real-time dashboards-everything you need to make performance reviews effective and efficient. In this day and age, when more and more of the HR department’s tasks are being taken over by online tools, you may be wondering what value HRM adds to your company. In the worst-case scenario, you might even be wondering whether HRM still has a future and whether this department will be eliminated in the foreseeable future. HRM certainly still has a future, although the department’s focus will need to shift in order to continue providing added value. In this article, we’ll explore the role of HR within organizations.

The Current Role of HR Management

In most companies, HRM is seen as the first point of contact for questions regarding personnel matters. Over the past few decades, it has therefore specialized in recruitment and selection, employment contracts, terms of employment, and absenteeism policies. As a result, employees often only interact with this department when matters regarding compensation and other terms of employment need to be addressed, when requesting time off, or in cases of sick leave. The focus of HRM is thus primarily on administrative tasks, even though there are-or could be-various tasks of value to your organization that fall under HRM’s purview.

A Future for HR?

HRM is increasingly using online tools to carry out its (administrative) tasks. Not only are the administrative tasks related to personnel management being digitized, but the informational role of management is also becoming increasingly digitized. For example, employees can often use an online platform to find answers to their questions. This development is a cause for concern for some managers. In a world that is becoming increasingly digitized, is there still a place for HRM?

Shifting Focus

To continue providing added value to your organization, HRM will need to shift its focus. The use of online tools also frees up more time and resources to make this shift possible. The new HRM focuses more on employees, as these individuals largely determine the success of your organization. It is the role of HRM to ensure that employees are satisfied, productive, and feel a strong connection to the organization. Loyal employees who are happy in their roles are more productive than employees who are unhappy and feel a disconnect between themselves and their employer. To successfully take on this task, however, HRM will also need to work on its own image within your company.

Eliminating Unnecessary Tasks

Over the years, many HR departments have taken on tasks that actually belong to someone else-in most cases, the immediate supervisor. Often, the cause lies with the manager, who has no affinity for certain aspects of their responsibilities, such as managing conflicts or absenteeism. In some cases, HR has actively taken on certain tasks to increase or emphasize its value within the organization. It is advisable for HRM to set clear boundaries within its scope of responsibilities. The most important tasks should be strategic workforce planning, sustainable employability, and talent management.

Strategic Workforce Planning

One of the most important tasks of HRM in the future is conducting strategic workforce planning. After all, it is not just a matter of ensuring that the current workforce is appropriate in terms of both quality and quantity; rather, it is HRM’s task to anticipate future changes. By keeping an eye on the organization’s business plan and recent developments, this department ensures proper and appropriate staffing. In this way, HRM actively contributes to the effectiveness-and thus the success-of your organization.

Sustainable Employability

Sustainable employability focuses primarily on aligning with the wishes and expectations of employees, enabling them to continue working for your organization longer and with enthusiasm. It is important to identify the wishes and expectations of employees. Assessing these wishes and expectations has been a positive trend in recent years, but many HR managers lack the time or resources to actually translate the findings into concrete changes. However, by adjusting employment conditions, tailoring job responsibilities, or offering training, satisfaction increases and fewer employees leave prematurely.

Talent Management

In line with sustainable employability, talent management should be one of the core tasks of HRM. The goal of having employees who feel happy within the organization and experience a certain degree of loyalty begins with making a good match when hiring new employees. It is therefore essential to first conduct a thorough analysis of the ideal candidate for an open position. Placing the right person in the right role increases satisfaction and productivity. The greatest successes are achieved when HRM attracts employees with specific talents that are valuable to your organization. In addition, HRM must remain attentive to the talents of current staff and capitalize on them as much as possible.

Building the Image

Focusing on aspects of HRM beyond mere administrative tasks will radically transform the role of HR within an organization. To be successful, however, management will also need to work on its own image. Among employees, HRM often has a reputation for acting solely in the organization’s best interests. As a result, employees have the impression that management acts primarily in the organization’s best interest. It is therefore important that HRM understands what is happening on the shop floor and operates at the same level. Management does not stand above the staff but strives to work with them to achieve good business results.

Collaboration with Other Departments

HRM can only be a good strategic partner within an organization when it collaborates with other departments. It must not only be aware of what is happening on the work floor but must also understand all aspects of the business. By collaborating with other departments, key tasks can be carried out in a way that effectively builds toward a workforce that is appropriate in terms of both quality and quantity. Only then will HRM remain a key partner on the path to success and continue to add value to your organization in the future.

Conducting a Performance Review

It’s common for employees to be taken by surprise during a performance review. Suddenly, it becomes clear that the employer is dissatisfied. Only then does the employee learn what the objectives were and what was expected. You can prevent this by holding a planning meeting at the beginning of each year. During a planning meeting, the employee and manager discuss plans for the coming year together. They make concrete agreements and set clear goals. This meeting marks the beginning of a cycle that also includes the evaluation meeting and the performance review. Together, they form the development meeting. Talent development is becoming increasingly important. Standing still means falling behind. Here are 5 tips for a successful planning meeting.

1. Start from a position of equality

Having a good conversation isn’t always easy. People often don’t listen to each other very well and are too quick to judge. In a planning meeting, there may seem to be an imbalance-the manager is higher up in the hierarchy. However, modern organizations are increasingly moving away from old hierarchical structures. The meeting should therefore take place on an equal footing. Listen carefully to what employees have to say. Compare this with your own objectives and adjust course where necessary.

2. Be clear about the purpose and value of the meeting

Just because you consider planning meetings important doesn’t mean your employees feel the same way. Therefore, make it clear in advance why a development meeting is important for:
  • The organization
  • The employee themselves
Explain why your organization values talent development. Describe how employees can take ownership of their own development. Also explain the difference between a planning meeting and a performance review. The purpose of this specific meeting must be clear. In planning meetings, you articulate expectations and set goals. These objectives should be the result of a two-way conversation. Both parties contribute their expectations, ideas, and wishes. The goals must be specific. A goal such as “show more initiative” is too vague. The employee can interpret it in many ways, and it’s difficult to measure.

3. Set SMART goals

When you formulate goals, you must be able to monitor them. Make them “SMART”:
  • Specific: Is the objective concrete enough?
  • Measurable: Can you measure the result?
  • Acceptable: Do both parties agree on it?
  • Realistic: Is the goal achievable?
  • Time-bound: When does it need to be completed?
For an even more comprehensive approach, you can opt for SMART ER :
  • Ecological: Does the goal align with the employee’s experience and capabilities?
  • Relevant: Is the goal valuable to the organization?
Schedule the meeting well in advance so that both parties can prepare thoroughly.

4. Focus on the positive

It’s easy to focus on what’s going wrong during development discussions. But talent development is actually about highlighting the employee’s strengths. By emphasizing the positive, you build the employee’s confidence and encourage further growth. Build on what’s already going well. As a manager, ask yourself: “How can I make sure you feel even more comfortable in your role?” And: “How can you make the most of your strengths?” For the employee, the question is: “How can I get the best out of myself and make a meaningful contribution to the organization?” This positive approach works for both sides and yields the best results.

5. Schedule a follow-up meeting

The employer bases the discussion on the goals the company has set. The employees’ individual goals stem from these. Be careful not to set the bar too high. Take the employee’s competencies into account. Put all agreements in writing and submit them to the employee for approval. Afterward, it’s important that you stick to the agreements made. Use a planning form to document everything. Also schedule a follow-up meeting in the form of a performance review right away.

Conclusion

An initial meeting at the start of the year is essential for every organization. By setting goals together and clarifying expectations, you’ll have a more motivated workforce. They’ll know exactly what’s expected of them. A planning meeting is the ideal preparation for the subsequent performance review.
