Feedback Without Follow-Up: Why It Often Backfires

Many organizations invest heavily in gathering feedback-think 360-degree feedback, employee satisfaction surveys, and performance reviews. This shows that they’re paying attention to what’s happening on the job. However, the real value doesn’t lie in collecting feedback. It lies in what happens afterward. And that’s precisely where things often go wrong in practice.

Why feedback without follow-up leads to frustration

When employees share their opinions, they don’t just expect to be heard. They also want to see what happens with their input. If that feedback doesn’t come, doubts arise:
  • Has my feedback even been read?
  • Is anything being done about this?
  • Is there any point in doing this again?
Employees who feel that their voice matters often feel more engaged in their work. The reverse is also true. When input disappears without visible follow-up, engagement often decreases. That means feedback without follow-up isn’t neutral. In fact, it can backfire. If you want to learn more about how feedback works, check out the 4Gs of feedback here. Or explore sample feedback questions right away.

The psychological mechanism behind feedback

This effect can be easily explained through the lens of motivation psychology. People become more motivated when they feel they have an influence on their environment, sense that their contribution matters, and realize they are being taken seriously. When employees give feedback, it directly addresses those basic needs. They voice their opinions, contribute ideas, and invest in improvement. But if nothing comes of it, the opposite often happens:
  • The sense of influence declines because nothing visibly changes
  • The sense of contribution decreases because input seems pointless
  • The sense of connection declines because there is no response
The result is predictable: less engagement and less willingness to provide input in the future.
Start with effective 360-degree feedback

What Often Happens in Practice

In many organizations, things don’t necessarily go wrong because of a lack of willingness. The problem often lies in how feedback processes are structured. You often see three recurring patterns.

1. Feedback is collected but not shared

There’s a survey or evaluation. The results are discussed internally, but employees hear little more about them afterward.

2. Actions remain invisible

Changes are implemented, but they aren’t linked to the original feedback. As a result, employees don’t recognize that their input has led to any results.

3. Everything is prioritized, so nothing really changes

A lot of input comes in. Without clear choices and prioritization, it often remains at the level of intentions and scattered ideas. It is precisely that last step-making visible what happens with feedback-that largely determines how much trust employees have in leadership and the organization.

The tipping point: from listening to demonstrating

The true value of feedback only emerges when employees recognize what happens to their input. That doesn’t mean you have to solve everything. It does mean you need to be transparent about the decisions you make. Organizations that take a strong approach to this often do three things differently.

1. They close the feedback loop

Every piece of feedback receives a visible follow-up. For example:
  • What did we gather?
  • What are we going to do?
  • What aren’t we doing, and why?
That feedback makes a big difference. Employees then see that their input doesn’t just disappear into a drawer.

2. They make actions concrete

No vague statements like “we’ll get started on this,” but clear decisions. For example:
  • Which team will take on the task
  • What change will be implemented
  • By when it will happen
The more concrete the follow-up, the more credible the message.
See how to make feedback concrete

3. They communicate continuously

Don’t just send one update after a survey-provide feedback more frequently. For example, by highlighting small improvements, sharing successes, and explaining the decisions that were made. This way, feedback becomes part of daily practice rather than a one-off event.

Even “no” is valuable

A common mistake is that organizations only communicate when they’re going to make a change. But explaining exactly why something isn’t changing is just as important. This shows:
  • Feedback has been taken seriously
  • That decisions have been carefully considered
  • There is transparency regarding decisions
Without that explanation, people quickly get the impression that feedback has been ignored-even though it may very well have been discussed internally.

What this means for HR and leadership

HR and managers have a clear role to play here. Not only in organizing feedback sessions, but especially in making follow-up actions visible. This requires:
  • Well-defined processes for follow-up
  • Clear ownership of actions
  • Clear communication with teams
Perhaps, above all, it calls for a different way of looking at things. Don’t measure just for the sake of measuring; measure to improve. And then make visible what that delivers in practice.

Practical steps to get started today

If you want feedback to truly make a difference in your organization, you can start right away:
  1. Link each survey to a fixed feedback session
  2. Identify one to three concrete actions per theme
  3. Assign an owner to each action
  4. Communicate what’s happening within two to four weeks
  5. Continue to provide updates throughout the process
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=EFufGPHxbXI&t=21s&pp=ygURaHJtZm9yY2UgZmVlZGJhY2s%3D
Get started right away with 360-degree feedback

In conclusion

Seeking feedback sends a strong signal. It shows that you’re willing to listen. But without visible follow-up, that signal quickly turns into noise. So the question isn’t just whether you’re collecting enough feedback. The real question is whether employees can see what happens with their input. Only then does feedback become more than a fleeting moment. Then it becomes a driving force for improvement.

You’ve probably been there. A meeting gets bogged down, even though everyone shares the same goal. By understanding communication styles, you can reduce misunderstandings, conduct feedback sessions more effectively, and make team agreements that really stick.

In short

  • Communication styles are preferred patterns in how someone speaks, listens, makes decisions, and reacts under pressure.
  • Miscommunication often arises from differences in interpretation, not from bad intentions.
  • Under stress, people are more likely to revert to their preferred style. This increases friction within teams.
  • Assessments can help you identify communication styles. This aids in recruitment, onboarding, and development.
  • The greatest benefits come from establishing agreements on language, pace, level of detail, and forms of feedback.

What do we mean by communication styles in the workplace?

Communication styles describe how someone processes and conveys information. You can see it in word choice, pace, level of detail, and the way someone expresses tension or resistance. So it’s not just about “how you talk,” but also about how you listen, how you ask questions, and how you support or, conversely, hinder decisions. In teams, communication styles are particularly noticeable in three situations: during coordination, when giving feedback, and during conflict. In calm times, differences seem minor. As soon as the pressure rises, those differences become more pronounced. That’s exactly why this topic comes up so often in HR when it comes to turnover, collaboration issues, and leadership challenges. If you want to link communication styles directly to measurable data and HR processes, take a look at how online assessments can help.

Which communication styles do you see most often in teams?

Many organizations use a four-style framework because it provides quick recognition. Think of it as a practical guide, not a label. People do switch styles, but they do have preferences.

1. Direct and task-oriented

This style communicates concisely, concretely, and with a focus on progress. You’ll hear lots of statements and few detours. In meetings, they focus on decisions, deadlines, and tasks. In feedback, they’re clear and sometimes direct. Collaboration goes smoothly when everyone wants to move things along. Friction arises when others first need context or buy-in.

2. Analytical and structured

This style demands facts, substantiation, and logical steps. You’ll often see questions, checklists, and scenarios. In discussions, they want to address risks upfront. In feedback, they use examples and nuances. Friction arises when others expect speed, while they first want “accurate” input.

3. Relational and supportive

This style pays attention to atmosphere, timing, and support. They gauge the mood, listen carefully, and build bridges. In feedback, they often opt for gentler phrasing and questions. Friction arises when directness is perceived as harsh, or when the team wants to move quickly while they prefer a calmer approach to the interaction.

4. Expressive and Persuasive

This style communicates energetically, associatively, and through storytelling. They create momentum, inspire enthusiasm, and make topics open for discussion. In feedback, they use a lot of emotional language and examples. Friction arises when others feel details are missing, or when structure is needed and the conversation becomes disjointed. Would you like to see how this translates to HR applications, including recruitment and development? On the assessment overview, you can see which scans and questionnaires are suitable for these purposes.

Why do communication styles clash so quickly-even among smart professionals?

Miscommunication is rarely about intellect. It’s about assumptions. People fill in the gaps with their own preferences. A direct person thinks, “I’m being clear.” A relational person hears, “I’m being criticized.” An analytical person thinks, “I want to weigh this carefully.” A task-oriented colleague hears, “He’s holding me back.” There’s a second factor at play: stress. Under pressure, people fall back on their preferred style. Direct becomes more direct. Analytical becomes more cautious. Relational becomes more conflict-averse. Expressive becomes more verbose. That pattern is predictable, and that’s precisely why you can make agreements about it. If you want to make that predictable behavior visible in advance to teams or leadership, an approach using online assessments as a starting point for the discussion can help.

How can you identify communication styles in 10 minutes during a meeting?

You don’t need to test anyone to spot the first signs. Pay attention to four observation points: pace, level of detail, phrasing of questions, and response to resistance.
  • Pace: Does someone speak quickly and wrap things up, or do they build their argument step by step?
  • Level of detail: Does someone stay at a high level, or do they want numbers, examples, and definitions?
  • Question format: Does someone ask a lot of “what are we going to do” questions, or “why” and “what if” questions?
  • Resistance: Does the person become more forceful, quieter, more cautious, or, on the contrary, even more persuasive?
Use this as a starting point. It helps you focus conversations not on personality, but on behavior in a given situation. This makes the conversation safer and more concrete. If you want to incorporate this into a team agreement or leadership framework, be sure to review the assessment overview to determine which assessment aligns with your goal.

How do you use communication styles in recruitment without falling into “typecasting”?

In recruitment, you don’t want to assume “the right style,” but rather increase the likelihood of success. You do this by linking communication style to context. What does the role require? Many stakeholders? Then you’ll often benefit from coordination and influence. Many incidents and operational pressure? Then clear, rapid communication helps. High risk and compliance requirements? Then structure and attention to detail help. Practical approach in interviews:
  • Ask for a recent example of friction in collaboration. What happened, in their own words?
  • Ask what someone does when there’s no time for consultation. What do they say, word for word?
  • Ask how someone gives feedback to a colleague who reacts defensively.
Combine this with assessment data. That way, you can predict behavior rather than just hope for the best. This provides an immediate benefit: fewer mismatches after hiring and faster onboarding. If you want to combine the selection process with an online track, online assessments are a logical next step.

What role do communication styles play in feedback and annual reviews?

Many annual reviews fail not because of content, but because of form. The message doesn’t get through because the style clashes with the recipient. A direct conversation can be enlightening for one person, while for another it feels like rejection. A relational feedback session can feel safe for one person, while for another it feels vague. Therefore, establish guidelines on three levels:
  • Language: Speak in terms of behavior and examples, not labels.
  • Structure: Start with the goal, then an example, then the desired change, then the agreement.
  • Timing: Choose the right moment and channel. Some people want immediate feedback, while others prefer context first.
With a shared language about communication styles, you’ll have fewer discussions about “tone” and more focus on results. Do you want to link feedback to development actions and metrics? Review the assessment overview and choose a path that fits your feedback cycle.

Which approach works in teams? A practical framework that HR can implement right away

Use the TTDV framework: Pace, Language, Detail, Form. This is a quick method for addressing differences without making anyone feel attacked.

Pace

Agree on how quickly decisions are made. Establish a rhythm. First, assess the situation; then, make a decision. Teams without an agreed-upon pace become frustrated. One person finds it too slow; another finds it too rushed.

Language

Agree on a framework. We’ll describe behavior and its effect. For example: “When you said X, Y happened, and I need Z.” This prevents discussions about intent.

Detail

Define what “enough information” means. Analytical styles want the details; task-oriented styles want the essentials. Establish when to use which level of detail.

Format

Choose the best format for each topic. One-on-one for sensitive feedback. In a team setting for process agreements. In writing for decisions. Verbally for tensions you want to resolve immediately. If you want to embed this framework with measurable insights, you can gather team or individual data through online assessments and then translate that into agreements during a team session.

How do you link communication styles to assessment data?

The framework is most effective when you don’t view communication styles in isolation, but link them to underlying preferences. Consider decision-making behavior, stress responses, the need for structure, and social approach. This allows you to be much more specific in reports and conversations. For HR, this means:
  • You receive a prediction of behavior in challenging situations.
  • You’ll receive coaching tools tailored to the individual.
  • You can better assemble teams based on roles and collaboration.
Practical example: A team has many analytical and task-oriented styles. This can lead to quick decision-making, but also to more direct feedback. If you add relational styles to the mix, alignment often improves, though the pace may sometimes slow down. With data, you can make agreements about this in advance instead of putting out fires afterward. If you want to set up this process with a clear roadmap, start with the assessment overview and choose the assessment that fits your needs.

FAQ on Communication Styles

What exactly are communication styles? Communication styles are preferred patterns in how someone speaks, listens, persuades, and reacts under pressure. It’s behavior you can observe in terms of pace, level of detail, and the form of feedback. Can you measure communication styles with a test? Yes, provided you measure behavior and underlying preferences. This allows you to identify differences and translate them into workplace agreements and development actions. The best-known test is the DISC test . Are communication styles the same as personality? No. Personality describes broader traits . Communication style is how those traits play out in interaction. The same person can communicate differently in a different role or context. Why does communication deteriorate as pressure increases? Because people fall back on their preferred behaviors. Direct communication becomes more concise, analytical communication becomes more cautious, relational communication becomes quieter, and expressive communication becomes more verbose. This is predictable, which is why you can make agreements about it. How do you prevent friction between a direct and a relational communication style? Make agreements about language and timing. The direct style addresses behavior and goals. The relational style checks how the message is received and what context is needed. It’s best to schedule difficult feedback one-on-one. What’s a quick team exercise to open up a discussion about communication styles? Use TTDV. Discuss Pace, Language, Detail, and Form. Have everyone name one preference for each component and establish team agreements based on those. If you want to back this up with data, you can start with online assessments . Does this also help with onboarding? Yes. New colleagues settle in faster when you make it clear how the team communicates. Include communication guidelines in the onboarding plan and link them to the first feedback sessions.

In conclusion: 5 steps you can take this week

  1. Choose one team or department where misunderstandings frequently occur. Summarize the problem in one sentence.
  2. Use the TTDV framework in a short session and establish 4 concrete team agreements.
  3. Adjust your feedback format: Goal, Example, Effect, Agreement. Stick to observable behavior.
  4. Specify when to provide feedback in writing and when to do so verbally. This prevents endless threads and confusion.
  5. Support your approach with metrics. Start with the assessment overview and choose a path that fits your selection or development goals.

Identifying the as-yet-unknown talents of new and existing employees is becoming increasingly important for employers. This is not only due to the tight labor market, but also because talent development and sustainable employability are becoming increasingly important for the success and growth of organizations. Motivational and personality tests are particularly valuable for quickly identifying untapped talents.

Talent Development: The Cornerstone of Priorities

Hybrid work and the tight labor market are currently the most important trends HR professionals are taking into account. The top two priorities are, without a doubt: sustainable employability and strategic workforce planning. In both cases, talent development is the crucial linchpin. This begins with recognizing talent so it can then be further developed, ideally aligned with your organization’s strategic goals and developments. Several factors underlie these priorities, but it’s not entirely surprising that the rapidly increasing labor shortages are now the “burning platform” driving many employers to take extra action. After all, labor market shortages-partly due to an aging population-were predicted years ago, but they are now being felt quite acutely in an increasing number of sectors. This is certainly not limited to Schiphol Airport; it’s also evident in shopping districts where stores and restaurants are forced to close more often. Trains are running less frequently, school classes are being sent home more often, and plans for the energy transition are being postponed out of necessity due to a shortage of installers. And it wasn’t just in the Netherlands that unemployment fell to a historic low in 2022; across the entire eurozone, unemployment had never been lower. As a result, it’s difficult to fill these shortages with workers from other countries. And so we must, above all, work smarter by innovating and by making better use of the (hidden) talents that are already available.

The Importance of Motivational and Personality Tests

In practice, this means that for employers, HR professionals, and managers, it’s becoming increasingly important to identify and utilize the talents of (existing) staff. And certainly also to identify and retain people with key talents. As well as to effectively facilitate their talent development. But how do you recognize employees’ hidden talents? For measuring talents, there is, for example, the Competency Check. However, a person’s personality and motivation also prove to be decisive factors for ultimate success. To this end, hrmforce offers tools such as the Motivation Test and the Personality Test (Big50). We’ll discuss these in more detail shortly. In addition to the great importance of a person’s motivations and personality, there is another key reason to pay close attention to these factors in talent development. This is also crucial for investing wisely in the right people. Wise managers are eager to help employees recognize and utilize their talents and qualities. After all, this leads to greater job satisfaction, more motivated employees, and better results for your organization. The formula is well-known, but by no means always a given. Sometimes investments are made in assessments and training without employees actually changing their work practices. For example, studies show that 45% of investments in learning and development do not lead to application in the workplace (“scrap learning”). By investing in (newly discovered) talents among highly motivated individuals with compatible personality traits, the likelihood of success is significantly greater. This greatly increases the return on development investments. In this way, investments in talent development can truly contribute to your organization’s success. This does not mean, however, that people will be “left behind.” Above all, it ensures that development programs are better aligned with each employee’s talents.

Focus on Talents Also Lacking in Staff-Shortage Sectors

Despite the growing focus on talent development in recent years, employees often still experience significant shortcomings in this area, even in sectors that have long struggled with major shortages. Take healthcare, for example-and nurses in particular. According to recent research, they often say they feel “right at home” in their jobs-primarily due to the work atmosphere, collaboration within their team, and the satisfaction that comes from helping patients. But it is precisely in the area of talent development that progress often stalls. Only 56% of nurses in home care, nursing homes, and long-term care facilities feel their professional development receives sufficient attention (among hospital nurses, this figure is slightly higher: 67%). These are striking figures in a sector where every bit of talent should count. A major bottleneck is that talents are often not actively identified and therefore remain hidden. Yet you must first recognize talents before anyone can develop them further. In doing so, pay particular attention to employees’ motivation and personality traits. That may sound complicated, but it’s actually very simple.

Personality and Motivation Tests in Practice

The Big Fifty (Big50) personality test is valuable for working with objective data. This is the most widely used (and researched) personality theory for this purpose. After an online test lasting about 20 minutes (150 questions), you’ll know much more about an employee’s existing competencies. This is valuable for translating a personality profile into competencies (that can be further developed). For each competency, an indication is also provided of the extent to which an employee can develop that competency. This is based on their personality and on the five key personality factors influencing behavior in work situations (Neuroticism, Extraversion, Openness, Conscientiousness, and Agreeableness). In addition, the Motivation Test is valuable for understanding what increases and decreases a person’s motivation. After all, motivations are the primary factors that determine why someone does something and why some employees are less motivated than others. This is closely tied to a person’s personal motivations. While for one person “meaningful work” or personal development may be the most important motivators, for another, salary or, for example, interaction with colleagues may be the primary factors. And that makes quite a difference when it comes to talent development. There are many other motivations worth mentioning as well. This online test also takes about 20 minutes and provides valuable insights into a person’s motivators and demotivators. Organizations that have these insights can make significant strides in talent development-especially when the focus on exploring and recognizing (hidden) talents is linked to a modern performance review cycle that includes personal development discussions.

New Steps in Exploring and Developing Talent

There is a strong need to place greater emphasis on talent development. This is because structural shortages and mismatches in the labor market are continuing to grow. We must take this into account for the coming decades, because even-and this is different from before-in times of economic headwinds with reorganizations, far more sectors than ever are still struggling with major shortages. Consulting firm Berenschot therefore also advocates for innovative solutions in which talent management plays a key role. According to the firm, this does require a different leadership style-one that is more facilitative-and a culture in which all talents are deliberately harnessed. “For organizations, the first priority is to determine what talent they truly need, taking into account their mission, strategy, and continuity,” says a performance specialist at Berenschot. “Especially given the realization that talent is truly the key success factor for the coming decade.” And we wholeheartedly agree.

ENFP is a way to understand behavior. It reveals people’s behavioral preferences. Especially in the workplace-when working in teams-it’s helpful to know each other’s communication preferences.

In short

  • ENFP describes preferences, not fixed work behaviors
  • Use ENFP primarily for coaching and team discussions, not for hiring
  • ENFP behavior varies significantly depending on context, role, and workload
  • Avoid stereotyping by also measuring behavior, motivation, and thinking style
  • Make development concrete with goals, examples, and assessment points

What does the ENFP personality type mean according to the MBTI?

ENFP is a type from the Myers-Briggs model. The letters stand for:
  • Extravert
  • -iNtuition
  • Feeling
  • Perceiving
The model describes preferences in information processing and decision-making-in other words, what someone is more likely to choose when given the option. Source: NinjAthlete This sounds familiar in HR conversations. Still, it’s wise to clarify one nuance right away. A preference is different from the behavior you see every day. Someone may have a preference for variety and yet plan meticulously, because the role requires it, because they’ve learned to do so, or because the environment demands it. If you want to use the MBTI, use it as a tool for reflection. If you want to predict whether someone will perform well in a role, you need assessment tools that measure behavior on scales and compare it to normative groups. That distinction determines whether you use it for inspiration or for decision-making. You can read more about the data-driven use of online questionnaires at hrmforce.com/online-assessments.

How do you recognize ENFP behavior in the workplace?

ENFP preferences are often evident in situations involving a lot of interaction, new stimuli, and room for ideas. Think of the initial phase of a project, a kick-off meeting with stakeholders, or building buy-in within a team. Common behaviors that managers identify in practice:
  • Quickly comes up with options, perspectives, and alternatives
  • Makes connections easily and seeks collaboration
  • Brings energy to meetings and group sessions
  • Seeks meaning in work and goals
  • May be less detail-oriented during long implementation phases
Pay attention to what you actually observe. Don’t say “ENFPs are chaotic,” but instead describe specific behaviors such as “deadlines get pushed back” or “agreements aren’t always followed through on.” This makes the conversation concrete and honest.

Why ENFP Is Not Suitable for Recruitment and Evaluation

In recruitment, you want answers to questions such as: Does this profile fit the job, its complexity, and the context? The MBTI-and therefore ENFP-works with categories. You get a type, but you lack a scale that shows the degree to which someone exhibits certain behaviors. Furthermore, you cannot reliably compare MBTI results with job levels or norm groups. This makes it difficult to base selection recommendations on them. In performance evaluation, another factor comes into play. A label can act as a stigma, causing managers to interpret behavior differently than it actually is. In practical terms, this leads to two risks. The first risk is a false match. Someone may seem sociable and energetic, but turns out to require a great deal of calm and precision in the role. The second risk is a false mismatch. Someone is labeled “unsuitable,” even though their behavior and results are perfectly fine.

When ENFP Is Valuable in HR

ENFP can be valuable when used to facilitate dialogue. It helps employees articulate what energizes them, what distracts them, and where tension arises. This is particularly effective in coaching, team development, and leadership development. Examples of HR situations where ENFP language can help:
  • An onboarding conversation. What do you need to settle into your role?
  • A development discussion. What do you want to gain more control over?
  • A team session. Where do misunderstandings arise in collaboration?
  • A career discussion. What kind of work environment suits you?
The value lies not in the type itself, but in the questions you ask afterward. This shifts the focus from “who are you” to “what do you do in situations that matter.”

What are common pitfalls for ENFP profiles?

ENFP profiles are often associated with enthusiasm, connection, and creativity. That may be true, but HR also sees recurring pitfalls, especially when there’s high work pressure or a lack of structure. Pitfalls you can observe in behavior:
  • Starting many initiatives at once, causing a loss of focus
  • Making plans but following through less consistently
  • Finds repetition difficult, especially without a sense of purpose
  • Reacts strongly to feedback from others
  • Takes on too much out of enthusiasm
As HR, you can address this directly with clear agreements: Who monitors the scope? Who conducts reviews? When is something “done”? That works better than talking in terms of labels. Source: Hitostat

ENFP and leadership. When does it work, and when doesn’t it?

ENFP preferences can align well with leadership that revolves around connection, direction, and momentum. Think of teams that need to drive change, or departments that need to restore collaboration. At the same time, leadership also requires consistency. You have to stick to decisions, monitor priorities, and have difficult conversations. That’s often the difference between “inspiring” and “directive.” A practical check for HR and managers: observe behavior in three situations. How someone responds to resistance. How someone responds to setbacks. How someone handles routine tasks. That’s where you’ll see if their leadership remains stable.

What approach helps HR translate ENFP into results?

Use a simple framework that you can apply in every conversation. It prevents vagueness and keeps the focus on behavior.

Framework. Context. Behavior. Effect. Agreements

  1. Context: Describe the situation. When did it happen, with whom, and what was the pressure?
  2. Behavior: What exactly did you do? What did you say, and how did you act?
  3. Effect: What was the impact on planning, the team, and the results?
  4. Agreements: What will you do differently next time? What will you agree on with your manager or team?
This framework helps you make the conversation concrete. It also prevents “ENFP” from becoming an excuse. You focus on behavior that you can repeat, measure, and discuss.

How do you link ENFP to hrmforce without resorting to labeling?

If you use ENFP as a starting point in coaching or team discussions, you can then follow up with assessment data from HRMForce. This shifts the focus from recognition to substantiation. For example, you can combine personality data with motivators and cognitive abilities to see what someone is likely to demonstrate in a role and where there is potential for development. In the HR cycle, this works as follows in practice. You start with a conversation about preferences and collaboration. Then you purposefully administer a personality assessment or 360° feedback to reveal behavior in real-world situations. For more complex roles, you add a competency test, such as the Ability Scan. This way, you use ENFP as a framework while basing your decisions on measurable outcomes. This helps with selection, promotion, and development, and it makes your feedback cycle more consistent.

How do you avoid stereotyping when someone says “ENFP”?

The quickest way is to immediately return to specific examples. Ask about a recent situation in which that behavior was evident. Also ask about a situation in which the opposite behavior was evident. This demonstrates that behavior varies and isn’t confined to a single label. Then use the same structure in every conversation: What was the context? What was the behavior? What was the effect? What agreement do you reach? This makes the process feel fair and ensures you’re focused on results.

Which roles typically suit ENFP preferences, and which ones don’t?

It’s not about “being able to or not,” but about what gives someone energy and where risks arise. ENFP preferences often align with roles involving a lot of interaction, variety, and room for ideas, such as account management, internal communications, change management roles, project initiation, and stakeholder management. Roles involving prolonged detail-oriented work, strict compliance, and little variety can feel more taxing, especially if someone feels they have little room to maneuver. Think of management positions, lengthy administrative processes, or highly repetitive work. That doesn’t mean it’s impossible. It means you’ll need additional agreements regarding structure, priorities, and follow-up.

FAQ on the ENFP Personality Type in HR

What does ENFP say about job performance? ENFP reflects preferences, not performance. Job performance also depends on skills, experience, motivation, role clarity, and the work environment. Can you use ENFP in job interviews? It’s best not to use ENFP as a selection criterion. At most, use it as a conversation starter, and base decisions on assessments that make behavior and potential measurable. Why do people identify so strongly with ENFP? Many MBTI descriptions are broadly and positively worded. People quickly identify with them, especially if they align with how they like to see themselves or how they want to work. Is ENFP the same as extraversion? No. Extraversion is just one preference within the type. ENFP also encompasses how someone processes information and makes choices, but it remains a typology. Can someone change types? When retested, some people change their MBTI type. This primarily shows that the model works with preferences and that context and timing have an influence. How do you discuss ENFP in a development conversation? By discussing situations in which certain behaviors were evident. Link this to goals and agree on follow-up, priorities, and collaboration. What’s a smart way to combine this with HRMForce? Use ENFP as a starting point for reflection, and then implement a personality assessment, 360° feedback, or competency test to make behavior and potential measurable. That’s when development becomes concrete.

Here’s how to use ENFP wisely as an HR professional

ENFP provides a framework for understanding preferences, but it isn’t a basis for making definitive HR decisions. When used wisely, it actually helps open up the conversation and then allows for the targeted use of data.
  1. Use ENFP as a conversation starter in coaching and team sessions
  2. Always ask for specific examples and situations
  3. Agree on focus, priorities, and follow-up
  4. Measure behavior and potential using assessments based on scales
  5. Document the results and discuss them as part of your feedback cycle

Which leadership style suits you best?

Does perfect leadership even exist? And if so, how can you tell? Is the ideal leader characterized by a specific leadership style, or is it a blend of styles that makes someone the right person to lead? In this article, we’ll explore these questions.  

Good leadership is essential for an organization

One of the buzzwords in many organizations today is leadership development. After all, every organization benefits from strong leadership that fosters greater productivity and efficiency, harmony, and a positive work environment. But there is much more that distinguishes a good leader from a bad one. Good leaders dare to think ahead and do not let themselves be swayed by the issues of the day. They are highly capable of communicating a vision and know how to inspire and motivate others with it. In addition, they are skilled at listening-or rather, at encouraging employees to come up with their own ideas and learn new skills so they can reach their full potential. In this way, they contribute to the development and progress of an organization. Furthermore, good leaders understand better than anyone the art of guiding others and maintaining an overview to stay on the right course.  

Command-and-control is a thing of the past

Incidentally, this kind of guidance is becoming less and less like that of a traditional ship’s captain. Today’s world calls for new forms of leadership. Modern leaders must possess very different qualities than traditional leaders. For decades, many organizations were led according to the principle of “command and control.” This approach was based on William Edwards Deming’s quality cycle. However, his famous Plan, Do, Check, Act framework has shown its limitations. Although it made an important contribution to organizational efficiency and was an excellent tool for managing processes, it left little room for flexibility and change. Today, it is precisely important for companies and institutions to be dynamic and able to adapt to rapidly successive changes in the market and society. New leadership means different relationships between management and employees, a different communication style, and more room for initiatives from the front lines.  

Which leadership style is the most effective?

According to Daniel Goleman, an American psychologist, author, and science journalist, there are six different types of leaders. In the overview below, these different leadership styles are ranked from most effective to least effective.

  1. Authoritative

    This is a leader who articulates a vision and knows how to convey it in a way that motivates employees. This type of leader is like a messiah who, together with his “followers,” achieves goals and delivers results. Such leaders are extremely effective, but few and far between. Former Apple CEO Steve Jobs is a good example.

  2. Coaching

    This type of leader aims to bring out the best in their team. They encourage people to reflect on themselves and, above all, to further develop their strengths. This leader believes in their people but is also dependent on them. Of course, the staff must be open to self-development.

  3. Affiliative

    Leaders who adopt this style have a strong bond with their employees. They have frequent conversations with them and give people freedom in how they carry out their work. The leader is a true team builder who knows how to foster a sense of unity. This type of leader can also have a revitalizing effect on an organization where the atmosphere isn’t all that great.

  4. Democratic

    This leader values the opinions of their employees and gives them a certain degree of influence over how things are run. This often leads to satisfaction. People feel taken seriously and believe their opinions matter. Whether this style is successful ultimately depends on whether the leader is able to make timely decisions.

  5. Authoritarian

    This style primarily represents the “Leader 1.0.” Decisions are made from the top down. There is little room for initiative or new ideas. This isn’t particularly motivating and is less effective today. Although there may always be situations where an authoritative approach is desirable.

  6. Exemplary

    This is the type of leader who strikes fear into his staff. By working extremely hard himself, he sets the tone. There’s always room for improvement, and anyone who can’t keep up with the pace had better get out. This often turns out to be a rather ineffective way of leading.
Interview with Daniel Goleman. Source: Key Step Media  

Combining Different Styles

Every person is unique, and a mix of different traits makes a person who they are. The same applies to a leader. Often, it’s a combination of styles that makes someone the leader they are. In fact, it’s essential for a leader to be able to apply different styles depending on the situation. Some leadership styles are naturally part of one’s personality. A “born leader” will experience them as second nature. However, not everyone is born a leader. Anyone who wants to lead must first know themselves and ask what qualities make them a leader-which leadership style best matches their personality, and which style(s) should or should not be used in certain situations.

Performance management links your organization’s strategic goals to the performance of individual employees and teams. This essential process makes organizations more efficient by making optimal use of all available resources-human, financial, and material. It goes beyond mere evaluation; it creates a continuous cycle of planning, executing, monitoring, and improving.

The Structure of Effective Performance Management

Managers and employees collaborate on objectives that are directly aligned with the organizational strategy. This collaborative approach establishes clear expectations that later serve as a benchmark for performance. A well-designed performance management system enables timely course corrections and ensures continuous improvement in organizational performance. A structured performance review helps organizations systematically evaluate and improve. Results are measured against predefined goals. When deviations occur, you analyze the causes and take targeted measures. This cyclical approach ensures the constant optimization of processes and performance.

The four pillars of performance review:

  1. Performance planning: Defining expectations, standards, and performance metrics
  2. Performance management:
    • Providing coaching and training to employees
    • Establishing processes that facilitate performance
    • Creating a positive work environment
    • Providing the necessary resources, time, and support
  3. Performance assessment: Objectively evaluating performance
  4. Performance recognition: Valuing and rewarding contributions

The phases within the evaluation cycle:

  1. Planning and setting agreements
Start by jointly determining measurement criteria such as objectives, KPIs, and required competencies. Seek consensus on these criteria through discussion. Clearly document all agreements in a form signed by both parties. This commitment forms the basis for the entire assessment process, both for individual employees and for teams.
  1. Managing and supporting performance
Employees carry out the agreed-upon tasks while line managers provide active support. This support ranges from coaching and guidance to removing obstacles and providing resources. Managers monitor progress, provide interim feedback, and adjust the approach as needed. Their role is primarily to facilitate, motivate, and inspire.
  1. Objectively Evaluating Performance
Evaluate performance based on concrete results and measurable criteria. Share the burden of proof regarding achieved results transparently with employees. Give employees room for self-evaluation and their own input in the evaluation process. This bottom-up approach fosters ownership and leads to innovative insights for the organization.
  1. Valuing and rewarding performance
Personal growth is the strongest motivator for employees. Therefore, explicitly acknowledge achievements and celebrate successes. This recognition goes beyond mere financial rewards-it also includes development opportunities, new challenges, and public recognition. Make recognition an integral part of your organizational culture.
Performance Phase Activities Frequency
Setting Goals Formulating SMART goals, defining KPIs Annual + quarterly review
Monitoring Tracking progress, providing feedback Monthly/weekly
Coaching One-on-one meetings, discuss development Every two weeks
Evaluate Formal evaluation, 360-degree feedback Semiannually/annually

Modern performance management: from annual to continuous

The traditional annual performance review is no longer sufficient in today’s dynamic work environment. Organizations need real-time insight into performance to be able to make quick adjustments. Continuous performance management is therefore increasingly replacing the annual cycle. This means more frequent check-ins, immediate feedback, and flexible goal setting.

KPIs: the key to success

Key Performance Indicators (KPIs) serve as your organization’s compass. They go beyond just financial results and encompass all factors that contribute to success. Identifying the right KPIs requires analysis and insight. Look at processes that take longer than planned, survey customer satisfaction, and analyze where employees excel. Together, these pieces of the puzzle form a complete picture of organizational performance.

Clarity fosters engagement

Clear KPIs give employees focus and direction. When they understand which factors contribute to success, they can channel their energy toward them. This transparency regarding expectations and objectives makes performance measurable and evaluations objective. Roles are defined based on results, not just tasks.

Getting the right person in the right place. For many recruiters, this is a challenge-but often a difficult one as well. It sometimes feels like looking for a needle in a haystack. Moreover, the entire hiring process can cause a great deal of stress when the right candidate needs to be found in a short amount of time. 9 tips for recruitment.

1. Develop a clear strategy

To get the right person in the right place, it’s wise to establish a strategy in advance. What qualifications should the ideal candidate have? Are you looking for a “junior” or “senior” employee? Should the candidate possess very specific knowledge, or be more versatile? How strict are the requirements? It’s worth taking the time to thoroughly analyze the role for each job opening and translate that into specific job requirements. Do you need to fill multiple positions? If so, rank them from highest to lowest priority.

2. Create a timeline

Is there a strict deadline for filling the position? Is a new project about to start for which the new employee is absolutely essential? If so, a timeline is crucial to ensure that the right candidate is found and hired on time. Such a timeline can be created based on existing data and allows for meticulous planning. How long did it take in the past for similar candidates to be hired?

3. Collaborate with other teams

By collaborating with the teams that will be working with the new colleague, you’ll significantly increase the chances of finding the right match. When a significant portion of communication takes place online, it’s important that everyone involved has access to a robust ATS (Applicant Tracking System) that allows you to effectively manage the recruitment process.

4. Take advantage of the benefits of an ATS

With the help of an Applicant Tracking System (ATS), recruiters can keep a close eye on exactly which positions each candidate has applied for, what stage of the application process they’re in, and what the findings are so far. Such a tracking system offers numerous possibilities for streamlining the application process down to the last detail.

5. Make it easy to apply

The easier it is for candidates to apply, the more people will do so. Also, make sure applicants can apply via computer, tablet, or smartphone. Send all candidates a notification when their application is received and explain the next steps in the process.

6. Ask the same questions during interviews

Give all candidates equal opportunities-that is, ask the same questions in the same order and ensure that the same colleagues are always involved in the interview.

7. Be consistent

Consistency is the key to an effective recruitment process. This means evaluating every candidate in the same way. That way, you can easily compare candidates and determine who is the best fit for the organization.

8. Collect data

To make the right decision, it can be extremely helpful to have gathered all kinds of data from previous recruitment processes. This allows you to avoid problems that occurred in the past and work more effectively.

9. Avoid biases

Bias has no place in the hiring process. This applies to every step of the application process. Bias can be prevented by involving multiple people from diverse backgrounds in the interviews. Additionally, rely on the facts and don’t let your personal feelings influence your judgment.

Many organizations and HR professionals are looking for ways to modernize their performance review cycle, transforming it into a more powerful tool with performance reviews that are truly valuable. Especially for employee development. This means placing greater emphasis on development discussions and coaching. But how do you do that? Key stepping stones include a more open dialogue, effective follow-up on outcomes, and an objective agenda for the discussions-for example, using 360-degree feedback.

The traditional approach falls short

The need to modernize the entire appraisal cycle with valuable progress or development discussions is a hot topic in industry publications. It sometimes also leads to heated discussions among HR professionals in various HR groups on LinkedIn. The traditional approach also costs a lot of time and money and often fails to deliver what it sets out to achieve, as a seven-year study at VU University Amsterdam has already shown. Researcher and HRM lecturer Kilian Wawoe advocates for a more modern approach with a greater focus on development through continuous, motivational coaching.

From Talking to Having a Meaningful Conversation

For many HR professionals, employers, and employees, the performance review is still synonymous with “evaluating performance.” And how do you move from simply “having a conversation” to a truly meaningful conversation about someone’s development? Managers often find this challenging. Key strategies for this include: thorough preparation, striving for genuine conversations as an open dialogue, establishing concrete agreements, and ensuring follow-up on these conversations-especially by making adjustments where necessary. All these steps actually require a single underlying foundation: objective data and feedback to start the dialogue and continue tracking development. This also makes it possible to move away from the traditional approach with three isolated moments per year (setting goals, discussing progress, and the performance review). After all, an annual bouquet of flowers on your wedding anniversary doesn’t make for a good marriage. Those who let go of that can allow the conversation cycle to evolve into a more accessible, continuous development dialogue between managers and employees-ideally featuring more frequent, brief check-ins that are primarily coaching in nature.

360-Degree Feedback

There are various ways to make the performance review cycle more objective. Utilizing 360-degree feedback can already be a major step in this direction. After all, constructive feedback is essential for employee development. Feedback from employees themselves and from relevant people in their professional environment-such as managers, colleagues, (internal) clients, or other relevant parties-often turns out to be the “missing link” needed to improve the employee review cycle. For an entrepreneur or manager alone, it’s often difficult to evaluate employees, especially if, for example, you don’t see them all the time. And this is happening more and more often. In such cases, it makes sense to involve others who are closer to the employees and have their own perspective. Fortunately, this can be done in a simple and accessible way these days, for example, with hrmforce’s 360-degree feedback questionnaire. By drawing more broadly on employees’ work environment, performance and development opportunities are identified in a constructive and accessible way. The “360 degrees” represent the various perspectives from which feedback is received on, for example, skills, abilities, personality, and motivation. This provides a solid foundation for dialogue between employees and managers, as well as for progress discussions regarding development and related needs.

Focus on personality? Big50!

During a personal development program, an employee’s personality can, of course, also play an important role. In such cases, a personality test like the Big Fifty (Big50) can be valuable for conducting discussions based on objective data. This is the most widely used (and researched) personality theory. The Big50 is valuable for translating a personality profile into competencies (to be further developed). For each competency, an indication is provided of the extent to which an employee can develop that competency. This is based on their personality and on the five key personality factors that influence behavior in work situations (Neuroticism, Extraversion, Openness, Conscientiousness, and Agreeableness).

Consistency through honest conversations

The Development Module from hrmforce (which includes various digital review cycles) is valuable for effectively documenting concrete agreements and goals from reviews and for monitoring progress. This also contributes to the objectivity and continuity of the review cycle. Once the continuity and foundation for effective conversations are in place, the focus should then shift primarily to the conversations and interactions between the employee and the manager. Above all, this should be an open and honest dialogue in a safe conversational environment. In some organizations, a performance review is still primarily a one-way communication from the employer or manager. Being willing to listen and opening up to an open dialogue can provide them with highly valuable insights into the development of employees, teams, or the entire organization-including, for example, what is needed to achieve specific goals. In addition to openness in the dialogue, honesty is also crucial. Don’t beat around the bush-address issues directly and constructively. After all, not every employee is performing up to par. And sometimes someone has much more potential than they show. Or perhaps someone is setting the bar too high. During a performance review, an employee must also receive clarity and be told whether they are performing well, meeting their goals, and demonstrating effective behavior-especially if that is not the case. And in those discussions as well, measurable, objective data helps elevate the conversation directly to the appropriate level.

More tips for a modern performance review cycle

Anyone who wants to prioritize talents, people, and their development must be able to flexibly tailor the development cycle accordingly. In this way, a one-sided process driven by the organization or a manager evolves into a more collaborative process involving coaching and development discussions. In this process, the manager and employee jointly set the goals and determine the course of action. They are also jointly responsible for these. The following are important steps in this process:

  1. Start the dialogue

Start a conversation with employees about their talents, competencies, and ambitions. Where does someone want to be in three years? And how can the organization help them get there? Feedback questionnaires can provide support in this process.

  1. Short-term performance agreements

In addition to the open dialogue about talent and (personal) development, performance agreements are a key requirement for making a modern performance review cycle focused and concrete. Don’t just look at the long term; also set performance agreements for the short term, such as once a quarter.

  1. From Judging to Developing

When evaluating performance agreements, the development discussion must remain the guiding principle. Avoid turning the discussion into a new performance review or even a “judgmental” conversation. Discuss what is going well, what could be improved, and what is needed to achieve the set goals. Look beyond KPIs and engage in a broad discussion about an employee’s results, competencies, and behavior. This quickly shifts the focus to development and targeted support in this area.

  1. Organizational Tools

In addition to supporting employees, teams and the entire organization also need tools to ensure a modern review cycle in which the intended dialogue between employees and managers can be conducted effectively. Assess your organization’s needs to determine which tools are necessary. For example, what added value could 360-degree feedback or other modern feedback questionnaires bring to the coaching dialogue?

“Employers, take good care of your people.” The appeal by headhunter and columnist Aylin Bilic in NRC this spring sounded almost like a cry for help. The job market is perhaps tighter than ever, and it doesn’t look like that’s going to change anytime soon. That means that, as an employer, you need to pull out all the stops to keep your staff on board. Developing your staff benefits you as an employer. By giving people the opportunity to grow and broaden their horizons, they remain motivated to continue working for you. Frank Verduijn, a labor market advisor at the UWV, emphasized last month in a report by the NOS that providing sufficient opportunities for growth and challenges helps retain people within your organization. You can find all kinds of helpful tips online for encouraging employees to continue learning and developing. But did you know that using assessments is also an effective approach? An assessment is a psychological evaluation that measures a person’s intelligence, personality, motivations, and behavior. You gain insight into what an employee is capable of and what makes him or her tick. But did you know that assessments also offer significant benefits to your organization? Here are six reasons why assessments contribute to the development of your employees-as well as that of your educational institution, healthcare facility, or security company.  

1. To measure is to know

When you begin working on your staff’s development, it’s important to know where you stand right now. What talents do your employees have? In which directions can they continue to develop, and what aligns with their personalities? An assessment allows you to measure all of these factors. Although there are many different types of assessments, they can be broadly categorized into two types:
  • Selection assessments. These are used when recruiting new staff.
  • Development assessments. These assessments are designed to provide guidance on how an employee can advance within the organization.
Of course, the second “type” of assessment is the most relevant here. You can think of such an assessment as a baseline measurement. It gives you a clear picture of your employees’ strengths and potential. With that data in hand, you can create development plans based not on gut feeling but on numbers. That’s much more reliable.  

2. The Right Person in the Right Place

Every person has their own talents. That also means that not every employee will thrive in every role. Therefore, place your people in positions where their competencies are put to good use. An assessment helps you determine which roles someone is suited for. As an employer, this requires you to know which competencies and skills are needed for the various roles within your company. What must employees be able to do, at a minimum? Also prioritize the job requirements: which qualities are absolutely essential, and which skills could someone develop over time? Create a list-as specific as possible-of the requirements you want to assess.  

3. Assessments Keep the Dialogue Going

More and more organizations are moving away from the traditional performance review. They’re opting for a modern cycle of conversations , in which learning and development play a key role. These conversations aren’t about how you think your employee is performing. The focus is on where you both want to go: what are your employee’s aspirations, and how do they align with the organization’s mission and strategy? The results of an assessment can serve as a guide for such a conversation. Moreover, they provide a useful incentive when reflection and coaching sessions are easily overlooked amid the daily hustle and bustle. Plan ahead, and set aside time throughout the year for dialogue about an employee’s development. During the conversation, also set specific learning goals. For example, have employees write a personal development plan (PDP) in which they articulate what they want to achieve in the coming period.  

4. Help your employees get to know themselves better

For employees, an assessment is a good way to get to know themselves better. The questions asked during the tests encourage them to reflect on who they are and how they function-both at work and beyond. What character traits define them? What values do they consider important, and how do those values manifest in their work? What about their motivation, and under what circumstances do they prefer to perform their tasks? Assessments prompt candidates to consider these kinds of questions. As a result, they become more self-aware. And self-awareness has many benefits. People who know themselves well can empathize with others more easily, collaborate better, and learn more from their mistakes. All of this helps you continue to enjoy your work.  

5. You can build mutual trust

Taking an assessment can also be nerve-wracking for employees. After all, why does their employer actually want to “test” them? And what will happen with the results? Employees who are further along in their careers and have been through multiple reorganizations, in particular, may be more critical than enthusiastic. As an employer, it’s important to be mindful of these uncertainties. Be open and transparent: explain why you’re asking your staff to take an assessment. Also be aware that you can never force people to participate in an assessment. Furthermore, employees have the right to review the results themselves first. If you handle this carefully, assessments can actually be a good way to build mutual trust. In essence, you’re saying, “I want you to be in the right role with us. Shall we continue working on that together?” That’s how you express your trust. And employees who feel that their employer trusts them are more energetic, more engaged, and take fewer sick days, according to various studies, including one by the Harvard Business Review.  

6. Current and former employees become ambassadors

Sometimes, based on an assessment, you have to conclude that there’s no longer a suitable role for an employee within your organization. That’s unfortunate, but at the same time, it’s good to know: a dysfunctional employee isn’t helpful to anyone. You and your employee can use the insights gained from the assessment to work together to explore good opportunities for him or her outside your organization. If someone ultimately leaves your company well-supported and satisfied, there’s a good chance they’ll recommend you to others in their network in the future-whether those are clients or potential new colleagues. You couldn’t ask for a better ambassador! Tip: Of course, you can also incorporate assessments into your new hiring process. That way, you can be sure you’re bringing in the right candidate.

A bilateral meeting is a private conversation between a manager and an employee. If it’s a productive conversation, topics will come up during this “one-on-one” that are rarely, if ever, discussed in a staff meeting. The bilateral meeting is an excellent opportunity to discuss issues, development, and competencies in a personal setting.

What does “bilateral” mean?

“Bilateral meeting”—it’s a mouthful and sounds, at the very least, somewhat pompous. In reality, it simply means a conversation between two people. The word “bilateral,” which originally comes from Latin, literally means “two-sided” (bi = two, lateral = side) or “from both sides.” This implies that a bilateral conversation ideally takes place on an equal footing. Both conversation partners are willing to listen to each other and are open to each other’s arguments. Both sides reveal something about themselves. This should lead to greater understanding and appreciation for one another.

The Purpose of a Bilateral Conversation

Bilateral conversations are primarily intended to discuss matters relevant to the employee, topics related to his or her personal life. In an informal setting, the conversation should provide insight into the employee’s state of being, both inside and outside the workplace . This makes this type of conversation fundamentally different from other types of conversations that focus much more specifically on the employee’s performance, development, competencies, or goals. The focus is on questions such as: What specific issues are on the employee’s mind at work? What is bothering them? Are there things in their home life that are important to know? Discover the HR Conversation Cycles

The Pitfalls of a One-on-One Conversation

It is undoubtedly a noble goal to conduct a one-on-one conversation. Yet it is not that simple at all. People often struggle to communicate openly. One’s own ego and personality can be major stumbling blocks, creating potential pitfalls. Much depends on the mindset with which the conversation is approached.
  • As a manager, do you dominate the conversation, or are you willing to listen to what the employee has to say?
  • Do you want to demonstrate your superiority, or do you engage in a conversation based on equality-and, as a manager, can you put yourself in the employee’s shoes?
  • Can you distinguish between a performance review and a one-on-one conversation?
  • Are you able to avoid becoming too informal and turning the conversation into a casual get-together?
 

Frequently Asked Questions About Conducting Bilateral Conversations:

  • How often should bilateral meetings be scheduled to ensure they remain effective and meaningful for both managers and employees?
    • The ideal frequency for one-on-one meetings varies depending on the organization’s needs, the employee’s role, and the specific project timelines. However, a common recommendation is quarterly, to strike a balance between ongoing feedback and development discussions without overwhelming either party. Explore this page on HR discussion cycles for more information about the different types of discussions.
 
  • What specific training or preparation can managers undergo to improve their skills in conducting one-on-one meetings so they can avoid common pitfalls?
    • Managers can improve their skills through workshops focused on active listening, effective questioning techniques, and empathetic communication. Leadership coaching and feedback training also help managers conduct more productive conversations.
 
  • How effective are one-on-one conversations compared to other forms of feedback and development discussions with employees-such as performance reviews or 360-degree feedback-when it comes to fostering personal and professional growth?
    • One-on-one conversations offer a unique, direct form of feedback that is immediate and personal, complementing broader feedback mechanisms such as performance reviews or 360-degree feedback. These conversations are particularly effective for addressing specific issues in real time and fostering personal growth through direct dialogue.
Discover the HR Conversation Cycles

Conclusion

One-on-one conversations can be valuable when conducted properly and with the right mindset—that is, when they are truly a two-way conversation. It is up to the manager to understand how the employee approaches their work as an individual. Here are a few examples of how you can give the employee the opportunity to share their perspective:
  • What would you like to discuss over the next half hour?
  • What changes would you like to see?
  • What have you learned over the past month?
